title: Discourse analysis in Ulysses and The Sound and the Fury
venue: Academic journal of business, administration, law and social sciences
abstract: The literary style of modernist authors like James Joyce (1882-1941) and William Faulkner (1897-1962) is deeply experimental. Their complexity is intertwined with the desire to retell local, national stories as seen through the eyes of losers from which small literary cosmoses are the desires result to re-adapt domestic spaces. This research does not leave a path for the use of language as a transparent means of expression, but at the same time makes it impossible to express fiction through more linear and elaborative methods, leaving the direct elaboration subordinate, shown from the viewpoint of the marginalized, the oppressed. Their speaking variety is conveyed through repetitions, fixations, alienations, and disturbing endings. The two authors create neologisms that signal dissatisfaction with the limitations of conventional language. Joyce includes Hiberno-English in Ulysses (1920) as a means of cacophonous addition to the voices and styles, just as Faulkner includes the African American speech of the American South. They operate on the differences of their traditions. Joyce attacks the use of syntax, being more interested in the order of words within the sentence, the same concern with syntactic structure that we also see in Faulkner.

title: The Search for Salvation through T. S. Eliot’s The Waste Land
abstract: T. S. Eliot’s poem ‘The Waste Land’ delves into the theme of self-reflexivity, portraying the lives of individuals alienated and isolated due to World War I. Many suffered from paranoia, leading lives devoid of purpose. The poem paints a vivid picture of the social characteristics of people in London during this period. T. S. Eliot, influenced by Indian philosophy, drew references from Hindu texts, offering a glimmer of hope. It suggests persevering through life with compassion, extending charity, and mastering inner thoughts to attain inner peace. This philosophy is captured in the resonant word ‘DA’, symbolizing the sound of thunder. It echoes thrice, representing ‘Datta’ (charity), ‘Dayadvata’ (compassion towards others), and ‘Damyata’ (control over inner thoughts). Despite the fragmented psyche of humanity post World War I, Eliot held hope for positive transformations in the years to come, contingent on people’s faith in God and the power of prayer.

title: The Causes of Spiritual Imbalance in The Sound and the Fury
venue: Saudi Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences
abstract: This paper analyzes the causes of the spiritual imbalance of the female characters Caddy, Mrs Compson and Dilsey in The Sound and the Fury from three aspects, namely ideological restriction, alienated existence and spiritual wasteland.

title: An alienated person in the novels “Do not Feed or Touch the Pelicans” by Andrey Astvatsaturov and “A Brief Life” by Juan Carlos Onetti Borges
venue: Вестник Костромского государственного университета им. Н.А. Некрасова
abstract: The article compares the methods of describing the “alienated person”, landscape and interpersonal relationships in the novel “Do not Feed or Touch the Pelicans” by the contemporary Russian writer Andrey Astvatsaturov and in the novel “A Brief Lifeˮ by the Uruguayan prose writer Juan Carlos Onetti Borges. The aim of the work is to identify the points of contact between the texts of the Uruguayan and the Russian authors within the framework of the hermeneutic approach. The research reveals a number of similarities in the authors' poetics at the narratological, compositional, philosophical and socio-psychological levels. Particular attention is paid to the analysis and commenting of dialogues in Andrey Astvatsaturov and J.C. Onetti. The communication of the characters in the texts is unproductive, the characters are alienated from each other and from the “soilˮ, and the spiritual in them is in irreconcilable conflict with the bodily. Montevideo and Santa Maria with J.C. Onetti as loci are Latin American analogues of St. Petersburg with Andrey Astvatsaturov. The “carnivalˮ finals of the novels are compared. The conclusion is made about the typological similarity of Andrey Astvatsaturov and J.C. Onetti as authors who hold pessimistic views of the real world and model fictional worlds in an attempt to overcome the oppressive longing of reality. The authors borrow techniques and strategies for text arrangement from authors such as William Cuthbert Faulkner, Jerome David Salinger, and Jean-Paul Charles Aymard Sartre while working on his novels. The question is raised about the further observation of the evolution of the poetics of Andrey Astvatsaturov and the subsequent comparison of his new texts with the novels of J.C. Onetti.

title: CLASSIFICATION OF SOCIAL CLASSES IN WILLIAM FAULKNER’S A ROSE FOR EMILY : AS A MARXIST STUDY
abstract: This thesis is an analysis of a short story entitled A Rose for Emily written by William Faulkner. The purpose of this study is to find the classification of the social classes that is reflected, the cause of classification of the social classes, and the effects of classification of the social classes on the short story A Rose for Emily. To analyze the short story, the writer uses the theory of sociology, namely Marxism from Karl Marx. The Karl Marx theory used is a class theory. After completing the analysis, the writer gets the results of the study, namely the discovery of classification of the social classes that are reflected in some characters there are the bourgouisie and the proletariat, there are cause of classification of social classes namely class awareness, and there are two effects of classification of the social classes namely alienation and conflict social.

title: 'Let me make myself crystal'. T. S. Eliot, postmodernism, and the deceptive transparency of clichés in the poetry of Carol Ann Duffy
abstract: This essay approaches the concept of “poetic transparency” from two interconnected perspectives, i.e., the modern and the postmodern. Starting from T. S. Eliot’s reflections on poetry and transparency, the essay addresses how Eliot’s modernist aesthetics becomes a site of Carol Ann Duffy’s poetic and critical exploration. The former Poet Laureate (2009-19) and her literary predecessor follow two opposite, and yet interconnected paths: while Eliot claims to work through artificiality striving to reach the “essence” of poetry, Duffy digs through the apparent naturalness of everyday language to unveil its opacity. In Duffy’s dramatic monologues – among which a prominent role is given to “Psychopath”, from Selling Manhattan (1987) – the concept of transparency is linked to a reflection on the medial presence of language. Duffy manipulates clichés and conventions to undertake a critical process which is strictly linked with Derridean différance. She exploits the superficiality of the structures of language to create a sense of alienation and disorientation in readers, who are presented with the experience of marginalized characters – “Others” towards whom sympathy is often impossible, and yet whose identities come into being through a variety of clichés which readers will easily recognize as part of their experience.

title: Alienation of the American Dream in the Context of Consumer Culture Taking Sister Carrie for Example
venue: International Conference on Contemporary Education, Social Sciences and Ecological Studies (CESSES)
abstract: The beginning of the twentieth century witnessed the emergence of consumer culture, under which context humanism and Puritan ethics embraced by tradition have been replaced by naturalism and hedonism. Dominating the American society, the ideology of naturalism is based on "the survival of the fittest" put forward by Darwin, while hedonism greatly emphasizes sensational relish and desire for current pleasure. Sister Carrie, a vivid portrayal of the early twentieth America, reveals profound influence of consumer culture over Theodore Dreiser and his naturalistic preference in both his objective narrative techniques and ideological proposition. In Sister Carrie, Dreiser depicts the American dream of three social strata, i.e. the underclass, the upper-middle class and the class trapped between the above two. Classified into the respective parts of applicable objects, means to achieve the dream and its anticipated outcomes, the American dream went through a tripartite alienation procedure, thereby being alienated as a whole. This representative novel has thrown America into a waste land, a nihilistic world where everywhere permeates shattered dreams, demonized evaluation system and lost souls.

title: Fictions of Home: Narratives of Alienation and Belonging, 1850-2000
abstract: This doctoral thesis examines the concept of home as a tool for literary critical and cultural analysis. In addition to discussing various theoretical concepts established by earlier critics (e.g. the Freudian uncanny, the Russian formalist idea of defamiliarization, or Marx's concept of alienation), this thesis proposes that fiction itself ought to be considered as a home-making practice, and that any analysis of fictions of home ought to bear in mind seven critical precepts. These seven precepts are formulated in the introduction and then applied in the discussion of one film (Steven Spielberg's E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial) and six novels (Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick: or, The Whale; George Eliot’s The Mill on the Floss; Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway; William Faulkner’s Absalom, Absalom!; Pat Barker’s Union Street; and Jeffrey Eugenides’s The Virgin Suicides).

title: Ethnic American Literature, Iowa, and the American Tradition
abstract: In the fall of 2008, Nam Le, a recent graduate of the Iowa Writer's Workshop, published a thematic collection of stories. first is entitled Love and Honor and Pity and Pride and Compassion and Sacrifice and the last is entitled The Boat. But it was the first story that most provoked my thinking, because the title was extracted from William Faulkner's famous Nobel Prize speech. All his life William Faulkner avoided speeches--I'm just a farmer who likes to tell stories, he said. That's why there was so much interest when he traveled to Stockholm to receive the Nobel Prize on December 10, 1950. Evidently, Faulkner wanted to set right the misinterpretation that his work was pessimistic. And post World War II and post Hiroshima, he felt obligated to address the radically altered world situation, especially for the writer. In the speech, Faulkner urges writers to focus on the verities of the heart, the old universal truths lacking which any story is ephemeral and doomed--love and honor and pity and and compassion and sacrifice. Nam Le's Faulkner-entitled meta-story concerns Nam Le as a character struggling at the end of his time at the Iowa Workshop to write his final story to earn his degree. He adamantly wants to resist the pressure to write, as a Vietnamese American, a story about his ethnic experience just because that's what ethnic and immigrant Americans are supposed to write about, which only produces, in the narrator's mind, a fiction filled with stereo-typed predictable enigmas and the usual presentation of exotic ethnic food (9). Love and honor and pity and pride then, is a self-conscious exploration into someone not wanting to write the story he is supposed to write, and then ironically writing it. And the story ends up including the narrator's self-proclaimed traits of ethnic American literature--stereo-typed enigmas and exotic Vietnamese food. So it is a story about immigrant experience after all, and about a writer with double consciousness whose mother was once a Vietnamese boat refugee; the plot becoming complicated by Nam Le's father showing up in Iowa, whom Nam doesn't want to deal with, and Nam staying up late in a cliched manner drinking Scotch as he moils over completing his story. writing is impressive, but one ends up wondering about the character's ultimate goal. Is he a precocious Iowa Workshop writer exploiting Faulkner's great speech to prove a self-reflexive literary point about ethnic American literature? Or is he a post-modern author writing a story about writing a story about someone who doesn't want to write the story he is writing? And/or does his book offer a new direction for ethnic American literature in the context of Faulkner and the American Tradition? Moreover, the first story is nothing like the ones that follow, which are virtuoso performances conjuring up characters and places far removed from the world of Nam Le: a graphic story about war children in Colombia; a story about human suffering in Iran; and another called Meeting Elise, about a pathetic and unhappy painter in New York City who suffers from hemorrhoids and is trying to find a way to reconnect with his estranged violinist daughter. Perhaps Nam Le is trying to prove that he can indeed write about anything. final story, The Boat, brings the book full circle in a masterful way by offering a moving threnody, with painful detail, about the narrator's mother narrowly surviving her experience as a Vietnamese boat refugee. Perhaps this is the connection to Faulkner's love and pity and compassion and sacrifice. In 1979, I had a chance to meet with Susan Sontag after a colloquium and I asked her what she thought about the state of the American novel that many believed to be dead or dying. She replied by asking me which work I thought came closest to being the Great American Novel. And I told her Faulkner's Sound and the Fury. She then talked about how all American novels are, on some level, about American history or American identity, and this was because the country itself was still young and therefore hung up on the question of who it really is. …

title: An Ecomythic Reading of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land
abstract: T S Eliot’s famous poem The Waste Land represents not only the spiritual malaise he sensed in modern society, but the alienation between the human psyche and the rest of the natural world as well. Analysis of some of the most potent imagery in the poem reveals a high modernist sense of extreme anxiety that presages much ecocritical discourse since. With reference to mythic icons Tiresias the blind seer and the mystery of the Holy Grail, this article pinpoints the way that Eliot maintains a homology between psyche and environment – in this case, the urban habitat of modern society – while showing how living in the city breaks down the individual’s links to the sacred element of the natural world. In spite of this sense of desolation, Eliot’s ritualistic use of repetition provides some clues to a nascent ecopsychology within the text.

title: Brands on a wet, black bough: marketing the masterworks of modernism
abstract: Purpose – In a world where commerce and culture are still somewhat estranged, the purpose of this paper is to show that high culture’s supreme exponents were commercially minded masters of marketing. Design/methodology/approach – Historically situated, the paper adopts a biographical approach to the making of modernism’s literary masterworks. It focuses on Ezra Pound, T.S. Eliot and James Joyce, who were responsible for the modernist classics,UlyssesandThe Waste Land. Findings – The analysis identifies five fundamental marketing principles that appear paradoxical from a traditional, customer-centric standpoint, yet are in accord with latter-day, post-Kotlerite conceptualisations. The marketing of modernism did not rely on “modern” marketing. Practical implications – If, at the height of the anti-bourgeois modernist movement, the “great divide” between elite and popular culture was bridged by marketing, there is no reason why contemporary culture and commerce cannot collaborate, co-operate, co-exist, coalesce. Originality/value – The paper complements prior studies of “painterpreneurs”, by drawing attention to the marketing of literary masterworks.

title: Elegy of the Decaying Aristocracy——Body Narrative of “A Rose for Emily” Written by Faulkner
venue: Journal of Chongqing College of Electronic Engineering
abstract: From the body narrative point of view, the interpretation of A Rose for Emily, a famous short story written by William Faulkner, can reveal the rich text content such as the decline of American southern civilization, feminist recovery and alienation, and patriarchal tyranny and cold.

title: Exploring Spatiality in T. S. Eliot’s The Waste Land and Four Quartets
venue: The International Journal of Literary Humanities
abstract: In recent years, spatiality in literature has evolved beyond being a mere backdrop for the story, revealing its complex nature. Space is now a multifaceted structure with various meanings, social implications, and historical significance. It shapes people’s perception of the physical environment and plays a crucial role in defining people’s understanding of the world around them. This understanding of space extends beyond literature and can be applied to urban spaces. Modern travel poetry has evolved to engage with the changing nature of travel, exploration, and globalization. This study aims to show how T. S. Eliot’s poetry was influenced by his experiences and travels. His exposure to different cultures during his travels is reflected in the multicultural references and themes found in his poetry, such as in The Waste Land, where he draws upon many cultural and historical allusions from various civilizations, and his use of fragmented narratives, multiple voices, and nonlinear structures. Additionally, Eliot’s sense of alienation and dislocation in his poetry can be seen as a reflection of his experiences as an American expatriate living in Europe. Furthermore, Eliot’s poetic creations draw inspiration from various specific locations he has either visited or resided in, such as Burnt Norton and East Coker in Four Quartets, which serve as both physical settings and metaphors for deeper philosophical and spiritual contemplation. For this, his poems often serve as a kind of literary travelogue through the landscapes of the modern world and the human condition.

title: Taste of Defiance: Culinary Identity in William Faulkner’s Intruder in the Dust and the Palestinian Context
abstract: Generally approached as a source of sustenance, food can transcend its basic function, evolving into a powerful nonverbal idiom articulating identity, resilience and cultural continuity. This concept is vividly illustrated in William Faulkner’s Intruder in the Dust (1948), through the character of Lucas Beauchamp, whose culinary practices serve as a profound expression of his identity and resistance against white marginalisation. Similarly, for the Palestinian people, food becomes a vital emblem of cultural heritage and defiance in the face of colonial oppression. By employing post-colonial theories, this article examines how food operates as a medium of expression that captures the complexities of identity, community, and survival amidst the forces of erasure and alienation. Through a comparative analysis of Lucas’s relationship with food and that of the Palestinian colonised people, the essay unveils the intricate ways in which culinary practices serve not merely as acts of sustenance but as profound statements of existence, resilience, and assertion of identity.

title: The Commonalities of Ecofeminism Writing Between Hemingway and Faulkner -- Based on the Interpretation of Hills Like White Elephants and There Was a Queen
venue: Research and commentary on humanities and arts.
abstract: Based on specific text analysis about Ernest Hemingway s Hills Like White Elephants and William Faulkner s There Was a Queen, this paper adopts the perspective of ecofeminism and specifically elaborates from the three aspects of the intimacy between nature and women, the alienation between nature and men, and the imparity between men and women, with the intention of exploring the commonalities in the ecofeminism writing wisdom of the two literary creators, who are identical representatives of loss of generation but shares adverse writing styles.

title: Towards Prejudiced Unhomeliness and Corrective Alterity: Ontology, Hermeneutics, and Transgressive Myth in T. S. Eliot’s The Waste Land
venue: Journal of Critical Studies in language and literature
abstract: With the advent of today’s cross-cultural alterities, the percolating notions of ‘home’, ‘self’, and ‘other’, have undergone radical transformations. This alterity, if at all, has bred a world of changing identities under the indefatigable pretext of a global consciousness. In Totality and Infinity, Emmanuel Levinas has made us leery of forging a reality that never existed; a ‘saraband of cultures’ where nomadic figures become rootless subjects. Amid these palpable alterities, the ‘self’ has embraced the transient tropes of a planetary world and a diasporic consciousness. The question remains: how is it possible to think of postcolonial subjectivity amid a world of mobility and displacement? Or, more precisely, how can we conceive of subjectivity and alterity? Overridden by these questions, this article critiques the tacit roots of the poststructuralist subject whose rootless wandering demeans the primacy of historical rootedness. The subject’s errant rootlessness necessitates a thinking that is neither absolute nor homeless. The postmodern nomad forsakes the facticity of home and forges an otherness that is irreducibly errant. In doing so, the nomad grants the ‘other’ its own myths and ideals. Postcolonial subjectivity, as this article underscores, possesses an indispensable rootedness in the facticity of shared existence. This article re-thinks postcolonial subjectivity in accordance with the hermeneutic horizon of ‘factical rootedness’ in a world of impeding prejudices. While the Western hero represents the ‘other’, the postmodern nomad transcends the land. Both models of subjectivity are culturally and politically suspect. Whereas the colonial subject reduces the ‘other’ to an object of experience, the postmodern nomad does not defy the ‘other’s myths and idols. It so happens that instead of forging an alterity that evinces the self/other dichotomy by embracing an absolute otherness, hermeneutic prejudice encourages an alterity that defies the chauvinistic logic of the subject and the ‘other’s’ claim to absolute estrangement. The discussion on hermeneutic subjectivity calls for a radical return to the soil to which only the figure of the prejudiced subject can uphold. In The Waste Land, the Greek seer Tiresias, defied by Eliot’s prejudiced stance, trespasses the threshold of pure subjectivity and forges a transformative subjectivity that illuminates the corrective alterity of prejudice (Vorurteil).

title: A Modernist Education in Pandemics
abstract: “Whatever pain achieves,” insists Elaine Scarry in her seminal study of bodily suffering, “it achieves in part through its unsharability,” reinforcing “this unsharability through its resistance to language” (4). It has been striking to me, in working on fictional and autobiographical narratives concerned with illness, disability, and grief over the past decade how dynamically writers are resisting this now-standard account of representational resistance. While reading Elizabeth Outka's absorbing, scrupulously historicized account of modernist literature in the context of the 1918–19 influenza pandemic, I was reminded of one recent example of this defiance of the ineffable: Anne Boyer's The Undying (2019). In this fierce pathography, Boyer undercuts the supposition that the suffering she endures at the hands of aggressive breast cancer is indescribable. And she does that by exposing the complacencies and misconceptions that bolster the notion of pain's inexpressibility as a critical commonplace. “Pain is widely declared inarticulate,” Boyer observes, “for the reason that we are not supposed to share a language for how we really feel” (213). The very insistence that “pain is incommunicable,” she argues, “is a lie in the face of the near-constant, trans-species, and universal communicability of pain” (215). Boyer's opposition to this lie is mobilized through what she calls an “education in pain” afforded not only by disease itself but also by the resulting physical, emotional, professional, social, and economic precarity that followed her treatment: “pain's education is an education in everything,” she concludes (242). Such an assertion poignantly resonates with the astonishing range and urgency of Outka's own education in pandemics.Airborne, invisible, virulent: claiming between 50 and 100 million lives worldwide, the 1918–19 flu caused “the most vicious type of Pneumonia that has ever been seen” (9). Eerily proleptic, these observations from one doctor in late September 1918 have been echoed a century later by countless healthcare workers on the frontline of COVID-19 who throughout the spring of 2020 recorded their grim astonishment at this new coronavirus's aggressive impact on the lungs, its stimulation of stroke-causing blood clots as the body's immune system goes into overdrive, its currently unfathomed repercussions for memory and cognition. By the lights of this still-unfolding crisis, Viral Modernism presents us with an appallingly familiar scene of sudden upheaval followed by prolonged trepidation. For we now know firsthand how a pandemic can radically alter “public life—closing schools, churches, and businesses and filling hospitals to overflowing” (75). And we also know how rapidly such an outbreak can expose scandalous inequalities in healthcare accessibility, subsidy, and distribution, while a militaristic rhetoric of national self-protection adopted by several governments has furnished metaphorical wars against infection that only “obscure the victims of the pandemic” (36). At the same time, though, as the sheer proliferation of isolation journals and lockdown-inspired meditations on a world governed by physical distancing attest, we've also witnessed a collective attempt not to repeat the way the “anguish” of 1918–19 “happened privately and within the domestic space” in such a way that left its lived consequences “unphotographed and unrecorded” (75). Returning to a moment that witnessed modernist literature's own attempts to supply “other, often intrinsically concealed, stories of illness,” Outka sets out to “launch us into new narrative streams, allowing us to hear voices long ignored in part because the viral, dust-like form at the heart of the story was itself invisible and silent” (37).To accomplish this work of “recover[ing] the ‘specters’ that the war's frame has excluded for so long” in modernist studies, Outka divides the book into three sections. The first, “Pandemic Realism,” takes in Willa Cather's One of Ours (1922), Katherine Anne Porter's Pale Horse, Pale Rider (1939), Thomas Wolfe's Look Homeward, Angel (1929), and William Maxwell's They Came Like Swallows (1937) as an interconnected corpus of “overt pandemic works” (40). Taken together, these fictions delineate the study's tripartite concerns: the pandemic's formidable challenges to literary depiction; the seemingly intractable, “miasmic world the virus created,” dissolving “distinctions between life and death”; and finally the theme to which Outka later turns in a closing chapter on the curious compensations of revenants and proto-zombies who furnish a tropology of “resurrection”—distilled in “the eerie sense that memories of the pandemic were being both buried and relentlessly remembered” (40–41).Part 2, “Pandemic Modernism,” offers bravura readings of an iconic trauma trio: Mrs Dalloway (1925), The Waste Land (1922), and “The Second Coming” (1920). For each, the question of how style itself dynamically responds to the psychic and intersubjective effects of the outbreak receives astute attention. Outka is careful about assigning intentionality when addressing the force with which particular narrative techniques evoke an emotional, social, and epidemiological environment whose “representation will not always be deliberate or clear” (100–101). Consequently, instead of speculating about whether and how writers consciously shaped their works in response to the crisis, she makes a compelling case for seeing “the pandemic as an essential presence in the style and structure” of these formally audacious texts, with the view to “retooling” the way modernist scholarship itself attends to “violence and the body” (101).Part 3, “Pandemic Cultures,” turns to what Outka intriguingly terms the “consolation spectrum” of “post-pandemic spiritualism” (200). Nimbly attending to narratives that feature ameliorating returns of the dead, she considers Arthur Conan Doyle's The Land of Mist (1926), a novel whose effort to “reimagine pandemic bodies and the sense of ever-present death” coincided with its “era's larger interest in ectoplasm and the renewed popularity of spirit photography” (200). Outka suggests that “for those grieving the pandemic dead, spiritualism's insistence on the literal truth of continued life granted a heady combination of religiously tinged yet scientifically based consolation” (242), yielding a fascinating account of disturbing yet understandably comforting figurations of resurrection.Aptly enough, Viral Modernism closes with a coda devoted to what is perhaps modernism's most formally ambitious novel of ambivalent solace, To the Lighthouse (1927). In Outka's perceptive reading, Woolf not only “shapes an aesthetics of ineffability” but obliquely reengages the “vast hidden trauma” of the pandemic and in doing so “makes linguistically tangible the ineffable quality of a viral threat” (253). This crystallizes the generative paradox that runs across Viral Modernism's preceding chapters, which reintroduce us to works that may evoke the pandemic's events and effects only indirectly while nonetheless realizing “the seemingly impossible” by “granting form to loss and emptiness, making visible what is invisible” (253). By the same stroke, the coda also reminds us of the interpretive challenge Outka has set herself in purposefully searching for resonances of illness in the structural and rhetorical anatomy of works that aren't explicitly concerned with the outbreak and its physiological or psychosocial legacies. Where To the Lighthouse is concerned, Outka points out that the novel is not “really” about the pandemic but rather employs “elements closely aligned to illness to express the scope and scale of the era's losses” (245). This distinction between intention and alignment is not only shrewdly acknowledged but also sustained throughout the book. And indeed that seems important: it becomes crucial for justifying Outka's scrutiny of how the “reality-shattering delirium,” unrelieved dread, and “miasmic atmosphere” that prevailed in the pandemic's aftermath entered the fabric of literary form, even if the virus wasn't always diegetically legible (168, 169). As for Woolf, so in W. B. Yeats's case Outka warns that intentions are ultimately hard to pin down; despite his pregnant wife's near-fatal encounter with the flu, “the pandemic's presence might have been less deliberate, a product of his recent experience but not something he consciously wove into the language, given how little time he had had to process the event” (169). If anything, Outka argues, he did not “need to write the pandemic” noticeably into the world of “The Second Coming” “for its effects to be registered,” because “the poem suggests how hard such an experience was to see clearly” (170).Seeing illness with invigorated clarity, though, despite the way it “challenges the very possibility of adequate representation” (243), is an achievement Outka registers in Mrs Dalloway. In one of Viral Modernism's most rewarding chapters, she reexamines Woolf's 1925 work as a kind of athletic deliberation on—if not an answer to—the frustration Woolf would subsequently air in “On Being Ill” (1926) over the paucity of vocabularies for imparting the quiddity of illness. The novel “offers a vivid picture of the post-pandemic body and how that body's experiences shape what it sees,” particularly through the figure of Septimus, who becomes the cipher for what Outka calls Woolf's “hallucinatory-delirium mode” (105). From Clarissa's perspective, meanwhile, “Woolf grants a portrait of a post-pandemic survivor, focusing not on the pandemic's initial outbreak or the immediacy of the illness's acute phase but on the lingering aftermath” (113). Once again, the potential for modernist style to supply aesthetic redress for the trauma and incomprehensibility of the pandemic becomes apparent, especially in “moments when contagion . . . is reimagined in ways that grant representation and at times consolation” (121). Mrs Dalloway's celebrated network of metaphors of invisible connection across public space “reflect in language the ineffable ways an entity living in one body may transfer into another,” showing how “Woolf's language encodes some of the representational difficulties that the flu (and illness in general) presented and finds a way to represent them anyway” (121). This particular reading hinges on the early scene where the impacting sound of a passing dignitary's car echoes beyond Bond Street in a “ripple” of sonically initiated relationality between the city's torn constituencies. Outka concedes that “Woolf is certainly speaking of the war here,” along with the interlacing pain and patriotism that emanate in its wake (121). But she nonetheless hypothesizes that the episode “constructs an image that speaks to the way a virus might move—and be remembered” (121).This critical maneuver encapsulates the combined risk and richness of Viral Modernism as it spots the pandemic's unseen presence in the imagery, formal mechanics, and social situations of modernist works that are apparently occupied with something other than illness on a mass scale, even if the process of “bringing death to everyone's mind” could well be seen as commensurate with memorializing a plague (121). For example, when Outka zeroes in on Clarissa ruminating on death while wandering down Bond Street, we're told that she “animates the dead and reinvents the mode of living death,” a vision reinforced by a “quintessentially Woolfian sentence structure” that threads “different clauses together with a semi-colon, the punctuation mark, we might say, of living death, hinting at a sense of ending yet also of continuity and connection” (123). “We might say”: indeed, we might. But this is also where Outka's approach—a sort of hauntological poetics of the epidemic's stylistic traces—starts to press against the perimeters of tenability. Granted, the abundant metaphoricity of dying and surviving can itself become rather contagious. And in this instance, modes of living death combine with broader social legacies of suffering to permeate undeniably penetrating readings of the connotations of syntactic structure. But in order to reveal how suggestively a novel like Mrs Dalloway facilitates “a creative reenvisioning of how contagion might move,” such readings depend upon largely analogical correlations between formal expression and epidemiological environment (122).For the most part, however, these risks pay off. Modernist scholars and students, along with those of us working in the health humanities, will be thoroughly engaged and frequently moved by Outka's determination to show that revisiting modernism's attunement to the “silences and residues of pandemic suffering may alert us,” as she reiterates elsewhere, “to precarious lives” at the mercy of “subterranean forces that extract costs from bodies and minds and communities.” Just over a hundred years on, our own planetary pandemic is inextricable from “systemic racism” and “environmental degradation.” And the very fact that the 1918–19 pandemic has for so long taken second place to global military conflict in modernist studies ought to remind us, she argues, of the necessity of resetting the frame—allowing modernist writing itself to pinpoint “the blind spots we have inherited and the tools we need to effect change” (“Grievability”).Which is another reason why leaving unquestioned those assumptions about pain's inexpressibility is not really an option. If anything, we need resources for renewed legibility when it comes to evoking and sharing the social and ontological pain of a pandemic, especially if we are to get “our leaders to interrogate the ways existing frames determine recognition” (“Grievability”). Viral Modernism's investment in reconfiguring those representational frames made me wonder whether in fact there's something deeply reassuring about the solemnity of ineffability. Deeming an experience indescribable is to confer upon it a degree of sanctity that forestalls the work of aesthetic description and historical explanation. Inexpressibility can thus offer the critic a soothing daybreak: once a situation and its sensorium are revered for being allegedly beyond words, then by implication they're also elevated beyond the very stuff that requests and rewards our analytical labors. Outka refuses to take that easy route out, while remaining sensitive to the formal and ethical challenges the flu pandemic posed for early twentieth-century writers.In this task, Outka's coda feels all the more affecting, memorably so. She shows how Woolf captures what otherwise seems inexpressible by giving dynamic form to the chronically traumatic legacies of the pandemic's losses. What is more, this lyrical “experiment in reading” dramatizes the book's eerily prophetic currency, as Outka contends that the very language of To the Lighthouse also “captures the pandemic's disappearance from cultural memory and a post-traumatic moment more generally” (253). As Woolf well knew, the “temptation is to forget,” not least “when guests start to arrive again at the house and a sense of ‘normal’ life resumes” (253). We will have to see—when the current escalation of online quarantine diaries and COVID chronicles abates, when shocking memories of front pages bearing daily fatalities are nudged into the distance by perpetually restless headlines, when high streets no longer inspire pedestrians to swerve each other with demonstrative cautiousness, when we can finally dial down the clamor of New Normal evangelism—whether that temptation will play out in our own era of post-pandemic grief.

title: ‘Making Strange’: Non-Translation in The Waste Land
abstract: This chapter employs concepts and terms drawn from Russian Formalism to assist reading key moments of non-translation in The Waste Land. Treated as avant-garde linguistic ‘shifts’ that disrupt and estrange the poetic form, particular instances of non-translation in the poem—from the epigraph to the wild cacophony of different languages at the end of the poem—are seen as covert and coded expressions of powerful affect. This chapter considers these experimental disruptions of form in the social and political contexts of post-war avant-garde revolt and recognition of individual and collective trauma.

title: The aeroplane as a modernist symbol : aviation in the works of H.G. Wells, Virginia Woolf, William Faulkner, and John Dos Passos
authors: Rinni Haji Amran; Rinni Haji Amran
abstract: This thesis investigates the rise of aviation and its influence on modernist literature in the first half of the twentieth century, arguing that the emergence of heavier-than-air flight facilitated experimentation and innovation in modernist writing in order to capture the new experience of flight and its impact on the modern world. Previous critical discussions largely focus on militarist and nationalist ideas and beliefs regarding the uses of the aeroplane, and in doing so overlook the diversity of attitudes and approaches towards aviation that had greater influence on modernist thought. Through a historicist reading of a selection of modernist texts, this study extends scholarly debates by linking alternative views of aviation and modernist literary and narrative experimentation. I begin my study by exploring how H.G. Wells’s calls for the establishment of a world government (necessitated by the emergence of aviation) led to an increasingly assertive and urgent tone in his later writings. His works serve as a useful starting point to read the more experimental, modernist prose forms that follow in his wake. While Wells’s texts were affected on a pragmatic level, those of the modernists were affected in a more imaginative, perceptual, and sensory way, which highlights the deeper extent to which aviation influenced modernist thought. For Virginia Woolf, the all-encompassing aerial view offered a new way of seeing the connections between living things, leading to an expanded narrative scope in her later writings. For William Faulkner, flight as aerial performance and spectacle was a liberating experience and became a metaphor for escape from an increasingly capitalistic and creativity-deprived world. John Dos Passos, in contrast, saw the effects of air travel as harmful to the human senses and perceptions of the world around, leading him to incorporate aspects of flight into his fast-paced, multi-modal narratives in order to convey and critique the disorienting and alienating experience of flight. Collectively, these chapters show that as much as the aeroplane was capable of causing mass destruction, it was also constructive in the way that it enabled these new ways of thinking, and it is this complex and paradoxical nature, this thesis proposes, that makes the aeroplane an important modernist symbol.

title: 物言えぬ「白痴」と黒人の声 : 『響きと怒り』におけるベンジーの「黒さ」
abstract: The question of racial blackness in white writers' works, which is still a moot point in the field of literary studies, arises when we consider William Faulkner's description of Reverend Shegog's sermon in The Sound and the Fury. Though some critics argue that the representation of black speech and accent assumes the character of Afro-American traditional counter-culture, it holds the possibility of arousing criticism for the white artist's appropriation of black linguistics. With this problem in mind, John N. Duvall evaluates Faulkner's use of the figures of racial blackness as markers of white writers' embodiment of "blackness" that afford a critical clue to the question of whiteness. According to Duvall, Faulkner figuratively becomes black in search for his artistic identity as he writes his main male characters as "black Caucasians," men who are racially white but embody the quality of racial blackness. In this view, Shegog, as well as Faulkner's "black" white men, figures the possibility of "an artistic identity that is black." This paper aims to examine the question of these conflicting critical attitudes toward Faulkner's "blackness" by reading racial connotations into Benjy Compson and his inability to speak. In the first section of the novel, Benjy assumes the image of black masculinity when his yearning for Caddy is implied with the episodes concerning his verbal difficulties. When he remembers the day of his sister's loss of virginity, Benjy tries to avoid the anguishing memory by performing the imaginary play of incestuous miscegenation. The association between the white man-child and the black conjurer is established by the fact that Benjy is mentally handicapped and unable to speak. His verbal inability and incestual yearning for Caddy take another shape of racial blackness when he is castrated after he was "trying to say." Suspected of sexual assault, the white man with the mental age of a three-years-old child embodies the racial stereotypes of "black rapist" and submissive and childish "Sambo." In addition, castration serves to elicit the patriarchal nature of the white South that caused feminization of black male southerners. What allows us to read Benjy as a "black Caucasian," however, turns into markers of his whiteness when he is juxtaposed with black characters in the fourth section. A conversation between Dilsey and Frony indicates that Benjy is alienated from the white community due to his "black" qualities but cannot wholly assimilate into the black community due to the fact that he is a white. The vague description of Benjy's response to Shegog's sermon makes it ambiguous how deeply he gets immersed in both the power of his linguistic performance and the wordless communication to which it leads the black congregation. The nature of Benjy's whiteness can be also found in his final cry, which represents the difficulties of articulating the inbetween character of his racial status. Benjy's inbetween whiteness leads us to examine the racial aspect of Faulkner's artistry that is neither appropriation of racial blackness nor dependence on ambiguous blackness. It is based on the history of racial division and his creative imagination with self-critical reference to its own whiteness.

title: Faulkner’s Queer Violences: Quentin Compson and Gail Hightower’s Wife
abstract: Literary representations of suicide among queer characters often symbolize critiques of complex hegemonic constraints. However, critical readings of these suicides easily slip into viewing queerness as the cause of self-violence, thus making difficult the task of imagining queer futures within these literary worlds. And symbolic interpretations of literary suicide, specifically, run the risk of conflating literary representation and lived experience. Criticism focused on the suicide of Quentin Compson has produced a plethora of symbolic readings that tie queerness to violence. On the other hand, the death of Gail Hightower’s wife in Light in August has received much less critical attention, even though her narrative is, I contend, an iteration of Quentin’s narrative. Reading these two deaths together can illuminate the potential meanings of self-violence in Faulkner’s works better than reading Quentin’s suicide in isolation can, and leaves little room for the easy equation of queerness and violence.

title: Delta Down: The Plantationocene in William Faulkner’s "Go Down, Moses"
authors: Calley Overton; Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona. Facultat de Filosofia i Lletres
venue: Dipòsit Digital de Documents de la UAB (Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona)
abstract: This dissertation examines William Faulkner's Go Down, Moses (1942) through the Plantationocene, a framework that names the exploitation of land and the displacement of people as prerequisites for extraction. Where scholarship has often treated the novel's racial and environmental concerns as competing claims, and its seven parts as separable units, this dissertation argues that the Plantationocene holds the two together, a unity the novel's polyvocality reveals only when read whole. It traces how the plantation persists through contested inheritance, how the Big Woods are incorporated into plantation logic, and how the novel's most marginalized sections expose what that persistence costs.

title: The Irrecoverable Trauma of Emily: A Study of Trauma in William Faulkner’s A Rose for Emily
venue: Advances in Social Science and Culture
abstract: William Faulkner’s A Rose for Emily is a short story that describes the tragic life experiences of Emily, who goes through various traumas and becomes psychologically distorted. Based on Judith Herman’s work, Trauma and Recovery, this thesis first analyzes the traumatic symptoms of Emily, using Herman’s three main categories of traumatic symptoms, which includes the symptom of hyperarousal, intrusion and constriction. Then, the causes of Emily’s trauma will be analyzed, focusing on analyzing the constraints of family, the social oppression and isolation, and the betrayal by her lover. Ultimately, under the guidance of Judith Herman’s three stage model of trauma recovery, this thesis manages to demonstrate the inevitable failure of Emily’s trauma recovery, focusing on analyzing Emily’s failure in the establishment of safety, remembrance and mourning, and the reconnection with ordinary life.

title: Blue Fathoms
abstract: I was halfway through my pregnancy when labor called me up from a deep sleep. Later, I would decide it reminded me of whale song, like I was being summoned from the blue depths of a dream. I rose with the pain, ascending one contraction at a time, until I was fully awake in the dark at 2 a.m. Outside, the March sky was cold and punctured by a handful of watery stars. In the introduction to an unpublished edition of The Sound and the Fury, William Faulkner wrote about how the idea for the novel came to him from imagining the sister he never had. This imagined sister became Caddy, a character whose emotional warmth permeates the novel, making her forced estrangement from her family unbearable when she becomes a woman who has a child—also a daughter—out of wedlock. It was as if Faulkner had created Caddy out of longing for something he desired but couldn't have. And then he constructed a kind of death for her through banishment.What Faulkner didn't know at the time of writing the novel was that his own first child, a daughter named Alabama, would die in infancy after being delivered two months early in a rural hospital in Oxford, Mississippi, where he lived with his wife Estelle. In 1931 the technology to save some premature infants existed, but the hospital where Estelle delivered didn't have an incubator. Since then, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) care has evolved to perform routine miracles. Premature babies are regularly resuscitated and successfully treated. Even extreme premies—babies born between roughly 22 and 24 weeks, who exist in the fluid, nebulous space that doctors term periviable—have, according to variable factors, a slim but significant chance of surviving.The Faulkners, heartbroken at the loss of their daughter, donated an incubator to the hospital where Estelle had given birth. For the past eight years, I'd had an IUD. I didn't want to be pregnant. I'd decided not to have another baby for many reasons, but the primary reason is that one child felt like enough. Then one day, about a week after the start of a weird, spotty period that never seemed to begin or end, I took a test, because how could I be pregnant? And yet there it was, a faint second pink line.I halfheartedly made myself consider abortion. I made myself think rationally about this pregnancy I didn't want. But even despite the fact that I didn't want it, I chose to stay pregnant. I did so partly because I knew Dominic had always wanted another baby. But I also continued the pregnancy because I thought, well, maybe this is one of those situations where I concede control and try something new, and it ends up being good for me. Maybe it ends up being good for my family.I cried in the shower so loudly my son heard me. I got a therapist. I envisioned my life as a series of waves barreling toward me one after another, and I told myself that I was a strong swimmer, that I could stay afloat. Twenty weeks into my pregnancy, I started bleeding: lightly at first, and then more and steadily. My doctor told me to go the hospital. On the first day, the staff broke COVID protocols and allowed my son to visit, but later when I asked permission to see him again, I was told no. The only reason the rule had been broken before was because my doctors considered me to be in danger of bleeding to death. Every day, sometimes twice a day, my blood was drawn so that it could be measured. But even though I bled steadily, my blood count was normal, and the longer I stayed at the hospital, the more it became evident that not only was my blood count stable, but thankfully, I was stable. My baby was also stable, with a strong, persistent heartbeat that the nurses measured at least twice a day. Despite these things, however, the partition between being pregnant and going into labor was still tissue-thin.I asked to talk to the chaplain. Though I grew up attending church with my family regularly, I am no longer religious. Still, I draw comfort from religious rituals. I also draw comfort from mystery, from the bigness and strangeness of life. I draw comfort from a forest full of new-growth longleaf pine trees. From my cat's pink toe pads. From a roadside ditch of yellow compass flowers. From the blue tide coming in. I draw comfort and meaning from my relationships with my family, my friends, my husband, and my son. I love the earthly things I can touch, and I love that there are ethereal mysteries that lie beyond my understanding.The chaplain was a neat, trim man with a teacherly demeanor. I don't know if he cried with all his patients, but he cried when I told him my story. That I hadn't wanted to be pregnant. That I was anyway. That my husband had been overjoyed. That I had slowly grown to accept the pregnancy, to want this baby.“And now what happens?” I asked him. “If I lose her, do I try again, even though I hadn't wanted to be pregnant in the first place? Do I try again, knowing I could lose the next baby too?” I don't have anything of my daughter's, not really. There's no proof she existed, except for a handful of items. A small urn of her ashes that fits in the palm of my hand. A paper with her tiny, bony, doll's feet imprinted in ink. A birth certificate. A death certificate.As I write this essay, I find myself wanting to apologize for asking you to read about a dead baby. I want to apologize to myself for having to bear the fact that there is a dead baby, and she is my baby. I want to capture the complexity and reality of this somewhere where I can be both emotional and composed. I want to fix my emotions in such a way that they can be comprehendible, observable, revisable, as if building a dollhouse and outfitting it with miniature furniture, miniature kitchenware, a miniature grandfather clock, miniature slippers by the bed. A meticulously arranged dollhouse is a domestic space, but it's rendered somewhat sideways, outside the realm of reality. It's frozen, for a while, in time and space.I have not been able to have many conversations about what happened to me with anyone other than Dominic and my therapist, but I can arrange the basic facts of it on a page. I can fix that page in time. I can be vulnerable. I can be a woman who gave birth to a baby who died. When I was pregnant with my daughter, I started writing a short story. I thought about the worst thing I could imagine happening, and I began writing about a woman who loses her baby at birth. I was about three-quarters finished with the story when I started bleeding.Though sometimes doctors in the United States will intervene in a birth as early as 21 weeks, it is extraordinarily rare. My own doctors strongly discouraged NICU intervention before 24 weeks. When I entered the hospital, I was four weeks away from that point, a span of time that distended before me like an unbridgeable stretch of water. I spent a week in the hospital, stable yet fragile. My doctors couldn't tell me why I had gone into labor early or what had caused it. When I asked if the IUD still present in my uterus was responsible, they didn't know.I was discharged from the hospital on a sunny, blustery Friday morning. I went home, showered, took a Tylenol, and went to bed. I woke up in the early morning hours with contractions that pulled me up from a deep ocean of sleep.I don't believe that we conjure things into existence, that Faulkner manifested a future tragedy for himself by creating and mistreating Caddy, or that by creating a character whose baby died, I sparked some sort of cosmic turn of events that lead to my own baby dying, but I do wonder about writerly obsessions and how those obsessions reach back not only into the past but, in some cases, into a future that hasn't even happened yet. I wonder if grief is a thing that arrives in us fully formed. I wonder if we are destined to uncover it day by day, year by year, as more pieces of it are revealed. I wonder if I am sifting through a domestic landscape—a small and tragic dollhouse—that, while personal and private, has resonance for anyone who has experienced loss and grief. When he was a child, the poet Gregory Orr went on a hunting trip with his father and brother, and in a terrible accident, Orr's gun fired erratically, killing his younger brother. Two years later, his mother died during a routine hospital procedure. In his book Poetry as Survival, Orr recounts the awful unmooring of self these deaths caused, how he had no joy or hope or way to understand these traumatic events until a kind librarian introduced him to poetry. Suddenly, Orr had a way of taking the miserable chaos of his life and ordering it into poems.Orr's book focuses specifically on poetry as the means to give order to disorder and shape tragedy into narrative. Because I'm a poet, I've written poems about losing my daughter, and in doing so I have experienced the relief that Orr promises. In poetry, the “lyric I,” as he calls it, helps to augment the senseless events of her birth and death. But there are things poetry isn't capable of doing, or at least I am not a good enough poet, yet, to conjure them.Some relevant details: The way I pulled my tear-soaked mask over my nose every time another doctor or nurse walked into my room. The steady stream of blood and mucus soaking the industrial-strength hospital pads. The “basket” that sat in the toilet, which was designed to catch my urine so that the nurses could record how much blood and mucus I was expelling. How my urine was always scarlet and thick with dark clots. How I had blood drawn every day, sometimes twice a day, first thing in the morning at 5 a.m. How I had to listen to her healthy heartbeat multiple times a day. How, even when I was in labor with a baby I knew would die as soon as she was born, I was forced to listen to her heartbeat. How I begged for pain relief, but none of the five nurses who tried could run an IV into my small and dehydrated veins. How they stuck me with needles at least eight times over the course of an hour and a half. One needle they tried to put in my hand hurt me so badly it dwarfed even my contractions. The next day, half my hand bloomed blue, purple, and yellow. A gruesome garden.These are details I could put into poems, and some I have, but what I need to do even more than use the personal lyric is to contextualize these things that happened to me. What does it mean to get accidentally pregnant at the age of 38 even though I had an IUD that had worked perfectly for eight years? Why did this happen during the middle of the most significant global event of my life: a sweeping, worldwide pandemic? Why did my healthy body suddenly go into devastating early labor? Why did I not deliver right away when labor started? Why did I remain in the hospital in limbo for an entire week until the day I was discharged? Why on that day did I suddenly descend into the rest of labor? When is a baby a baby and no longer a fetus, and how do I divorce this question from a pro-life/forced-birth context? Why do I insist that she was a baby when technically she was not viable? Why do I need her to be a baby when she never really was and will never really be a baby in any real sense, in that babies cry and shit and nurse and sleep and need their mothers? These are questions that are more difficult for me to explore in poems.But in an essay, I can at least try. One of the weirdest things my brain has had to sort through is the very fine line, medically, between what is classified as a late miscarriage and what is classified as a premature birth. In the United States, anything prior to 20 weeks is a miscarriage, and anything afterward is a birth. Had I gone into labor a week or two before, what happened to me would have been considered a miscarriage. It wouldn't have been much different—the nuts and bolts of my body expelling a pregnancy. And phrasing it that way, as “expelling,” is so brutal that it hurts me to write it. But it's true. Even though a late miscarriage would have been nearly the same, I clung—I still cling—to the technicality that what happened to me was, in fact, birth and not a miscarriage.And because I've given birth before, and because I've been in labor before, it was very clear to me that my body was in labor. As the contractions rolled through me in waves, it was exactly like nine years before when I had been in labor with my son. The only difference was that because I had essentially been in labor for a week, she came very quickly, and when she came she was so small there was no pushing for me to do. During the week I spent in the hospital, the nurses had told me she could be born alive, and I was terrified of that, terrified of what seemed like a final suffering that my baby would have to endure. And maybe it was suffering, but in the moment that's not what it looked like. It didn't look like much of anything. It looked like a baby, an almost-baby, quiet and still. She never struggled to breathe. She never struggled to do anything. After asking me, my doctor placed her on my chest just like any baby after they're born. At some point, before she was taken away, Dominic held her in a pink and blue receiving blanket, gazing at her delicate nose, the fine lines of her eyelids, the shadow on her scalp where her dark hair was coming in.How could this experience be similar to a miscarriage? And this baby on my chest, this baby in my husband's arms, who in my body had been a fetus and who could not live outside my body, how could she be anything but a baby? My baby?Afterward, friends and acquaintances who wanted to comfort me shared their stories of miscarriage. And I have no doubt that there are similarities between these stories of pregnancy loss and my experience giving birth very prematurely. But in my mind I have needed a firm line, a demarcation, between these two experiences. I think, perhaps, my grief demands that what I experienced was infant loss, not pregnancy loss. My grief demands a daughter, not a fetus. Holding her on my chest as she died begs for personhood, but of course she was not quite a person, was she? And though she was a baby, and my baby, she was also not quite a baby. She never cried or nursed or opened her eyes. She never gripped my thumb with her fist. Though she was born alive, she never breathed. A few nights after I lost her, I had a dream. In my dream, I swam out to a sandbar in an ocean and stayed there for a long time, buoyant in the waves rolling in. After a while, I looked back to shore, but I could no longer see it. The waves were big, jewel-blue and rolling in the opposite direction toward me. I knew I could not swim against them to reach the beach again. There was no way back.I haven't opened the blue velvet case that holds her urn since I picked it up from the funeral home. For infant cremains, urns are tiny. They look sample-sized. I remember standing in front of a wall of urns with Dominic, picking one out. But I don't remember what her urn looks like, and I can't bring myself to open the case to remind myself.At night, I descend into the blue depths of sleep, sometimes easily, sometimes slowly and with great difficulty. I don't know what makes a baby a baby, what makes a person a person, but I know I had a daughter. And I know that in recording this as fact I can restore her, even if temporarily, if in a way that leaves dissatisfaction and grief in its wake. When I went into labor with her, it felt like a whale was summoning me up from the blue fathoms of the deep.Whales are the loudest creatures on earth. Sperm whale songs can rupture a diver's eardrums. If a scientist places a hydrophone off the shore of Virginia, she can hear blue whales singing near Ireland. On better days, I think of my baby like that—no longer seen or felt, but here, nonetheless, in the dark waters of my heart, calling to me. Nowhere and everywhere at once.

title: Subject Alienation in a Morbid Society—Illness Narrative in A Rose for Emily
abstract: As an iconic writer of the Southern Renaissance, William Faulkner applied his distinctive stream- of-consciousness style and masterful narrative skills to paint a picture of the decaying and gro-tesque South. In his most celebrated short story, A Rose for Emily, based on the richly layered imagery of illnesses such as autism, aphasia, and madness, Faulkner revealed the undercurrents of heterogeneous ideologies that lurked beneath the seemingly peaceful town of Jefferson. At the same time, the alienation of the individual subjects in the novel has a distinct orientation of social deformity, indicating a morbid post-war American Southern society caught up in the “confusion” and eroded by Puritanism. The two main narrative threads were intertwined under the cover of the disease, suggesting the “fullness” of the social statute and the “emptiness” of the subject’s consciousness, revealing the silence and dissonance of the individual in his struggle against society, and further denouncing the prohibition, discipline, and persecution of the subject by the pathological society.

title: Realism and Modernism, Solipsism and Solidarity
abstract: Although it adopts and adapts both realism and naturalism, Richard Wright’s Native Son (1940) becomes, by Book Three (“Fate”), a modernist drama of consciousness. Native Son thus calls for a broad definition of the modern novel, one that reaches from Dostoevsky to Faulkner, includes Dreiser as well as Proust, and extends to Wright himself. Wright’s protagonist Bigger Thomas embodies the realist vision of the individual immersed in society and history as well as the modernist idea of alienation, for Bigger is both the doomed victim of forces beyond his control and the shaper of his own inner world of consciousness. By means of the tension between these perspectives, and by immersing the reader in Bigger’s internal quest for meaning at great length, Wright succeeds in crafting a novel that is modernist in its rejection of outmoded epistemologies yet eloquent on behalf of the voiceless.

title: Lords of Sounds and Lesser Things
abstract: Lords of Sounds and Lesser Things Joshua Bennett (bio) Work might be better conceptualized by examining the range of work that African-American women actually perform. Work as alienated labor can be economically exploitative, physically demanding, and intellectually deadening—the type of work long associated with Black women's status as "mule." Alienated labor can be paid—the case of Black women in domestic service, those Black women working as dishwashers, dry-cleaning assistants, cooks, and health-care assistants, as well as some professional Black women engaged in corporate mammy work; or it can be unpaid, as with the seemingly never-ending chores of many Black grandmothers and Black single mothers. But work can also be empowering and creative, even if it physically challenging and appears to be demeaning. —Patricia Hill Collins, Black Feminist Thought1 My principal question, phrased plainly, is: what different modalities of the human come to light if we do not take the liberal humanist figure of Man as the master-subject but focus on how humanity has been imagined and lived by those subjects excluded from this domain? —Alexander G. Weheliye, Habeas Viscus: Racializing Assemblages, Biopolitics, and Black Feminist Theories of the Human2 Let's face it. I am a marked woman, but not everybody knows my name. "Peaches" and "Brown Sugar," "Sapphire" and "Earth Mother," "Aunty," "Granny," God's "Holy Fool," a "Miss Ebony First," or "Black Woman at the Podium": I describe a locus of confounded identities, a meeting ground of investments and privations in the national treasury of rhetorical wealth. My country needs me, and if I were not here, I would have to be invented. —Hortense Spillers, "Mama's Baby, Papa's Maybe: An American Grammar Book" Throughout Zora Neale Hurston's corpus, we find any number of moments marked by the presence of nonhuman animals that buck expectations rooted in a normative zoological framework for creaturely behavior—consider the goat that flags a train in Mules and Men or the revenge-seeking rattlesnake in her short story "Sweat"—but nowhere is this desire to render the insurgent potential of animal life more vividly on display than [End Page 29] in her 1937 masterwork Their Eyes Were Watching God. Therein, Hurston crafts a world in which animals perform species in a fashion that destabilizes and defamiliarizes normative expectations around not only animal interiority but also animal sociality. My aim herein is to offer an alternative reading of the way that the figure of the mule, in particular, appears in the text, one that strains against the grain of how the mule has historically been marked in twentieth-century literary criticism and elsewhere, that is, as largely or solely a site of gendered oppression, labor that is taken for granted and rendered imperceptible. Though I will argue that these regulatory forces are often at work when the mule appears on the scene as a signifier, I will also argue that such forces are never the totality of what is present, that muleness indeed represents otherworldly duress but also the potential for an otherwise world, that is, a radically different set of social and political relations, in the midst of and in spite of that constraint. Hence, what follows is an extended reading of the way that muleness moves through the text as an analytic of power, how Hurston returns to the figure of the mule again and again—sometimes even when there are no mules as such present in a given scene—in order to elucidate the power relations that produce the mule as a form of animal life, which is also to say, a creature invented for the sake of labor and labor alone, as well as a useful metonym for describing the experiences of black women living under patriarchy's unremitting pressures. Through a close reading of several key scenes from the text and an engagement with black feminist thinkers such as Hortense Spillers, I intend to make an argument for the mule as an especially generative site of inquiry and imagination not only in Hurston's oeuvre but in the field of black literary theory more broadly.
