abstract: For his style-forming mastery of the art of modern narration, Hemingway was awarded the Noble Prize in 1954 and is still widely considered as the major American novelist of the mid-twentieth century. The works of Hemingway, by portraying how man utterly threw himself upon to survive in an indifferent world, reveal man's impotence and his despairing courage to assert himself against overwhelming odds. Antagonism toward institutions, alienation from society and its values and traditions, were all illustrated by Hemingway in a figurative style and his philosophy corresponding to the Existentialism in the modern West.

title: Marx and Modern Fiction (review)
abstract: Reviews209 Marx and Modern Fiction, by Edward Ahearn; xv & 231 pp. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1989, $22.00. In Marx and Modern Fiction, Edward Ahearn argues convincingly that Marx's writings provide the key to understanding major themes and narrative form in modern Western fiction. Byjuxtaposing sets of novels written between 1836 and 1936 from England, Ireland, France, and America, he shows that our great writers of the last two centuries consciously point out the links between history and cultural creations. In doing so, Professor Ahearn corrects earlier Marxist critics, such as Lukács, Benjamin, and Jameson, draws upon feminist critics, especially Irigaray, and comes up with useful insights into Balzac, Austen, Flaubert, Joyce, Melville, James, and Faulkner in a book that is eminendy readable. The opening chapter draws upon a list of Marxist themes, namely the division oflabor, the creation ofcapital, modes ofproduction, the enslavementofwomen through marriage, and the perversion of erotic desire into lust for possessions that recur in all of the novels Ahearn studies. He suggests, moreover, that Marx's desire to formulate a comprehensive view ofhistory as well as to unmask the contradictions and deceptions inherent in capitalism is echoed by these artists' use of irony and complicated narrative techniques. A comparison of Pride and Prejudice and Madame Bovary establishes these books as complementary treatments of bondage to material objects, of the impact of industrialization on provincial life, and of the struggles between the aristocracy and the middle class. Together, these works "frame the period of the onset of the bourgeois order" (p. 31). Their largely impersonal narratives parallel Marx's efforts to overcome a subjective, ideologically tainted point of view in favor of objective social criticism. The pairing of Henry James's TL· Golden Bowl and James Joyce's Ulysses reveals two works haunted by colonial oppression which nevertheless "attain a cosmopolitan vision" (p. 76) in their awareness of international economic relations, racism, and "the prostitution of the human to the monetary in modern society" (p. 95).James and Joyce portray the extremes ofclass and wealth resulting from conquest and the accumulation of capital. These authors, often criticized for their complicated narrative techniques , such as the use of inner monologues, do not remove themselves to the aesthetic realm but rather underline the individual's alienation in the bourgeois world. Both Balzac's Le Père Goriot and Faulkner's Absalom, Absalom grapple with two significant events in the history of class struggle, the French Revolution and the American Civil War. They offer a panorama of socio-economic development from Marx's tribal stage to the blossoming of urban, bureaucratic capitalism and stress the patriarchal character of bourgeois society. Although they differ in form—Balzac projects toward the future while Faulkner reconstitutes the past—both insist upon "the relationship between personal fate and 210Philosophy and Literature (inter) national history" (p. 152). A final chapter explores Moby Dick as a synthesis of Marxist elements. Melville's true subject is global exploration and commerce; he consistendy questions the values of American democracy and religion, envisages eroticism in economic terms and pushes alienation to schizophrenia. His style, which alternates between third-person narration and direct address, documentation and story telling, blurs the distinctions between fiction and historical facts and, "like Marx's writing, is a powerful incentive to liberation" (p. 198). One can only regret the brevity of this book, which hints at, but does not elucidate, either the relationship between Melville and the French symbolist tradition or Marxist interpretations of Balzac's other novels. Ahearn, nevertheless , is an admirable defender of both Marx and the novelists he examines. Perhaps the greatest merit of this study is its refusal to see these artists as naive, or as victims of ideology. As Ahearn asserts in every chapter, even if they do not come to the same conclusions as Marx, their complex, even contradictory, perspectives are based on an understanding of the economic forces that created their world and ofhuman beings as both pawns and shapers of history. Ahearn proves that Marxist thought does not impose reductive views on modern fiction but rather opens exciting avenues of literary exploration. title: Heroes with a Hundred Names: Mythology and Folklore in the Early Fiction of Robert Penn Warren
abstract: Leverett Butts’ Heroes with a Hundred Names: Mythology and Folklore in the Early Fiction of Robert Penn Warren is a daring and insightful reading of Penn Warren's use of mythological and folkloric materials in the four novels of his major phase, beginning with Night Rider in 1939 (Houghton Mifflin), and closing with Band of Angels in 1955 (Random House). The book reflects Butts’ deep immersion in Warren's fiction; his grasp of Warren's key themes and of Warren's critique of the materialism and rootlessness of contemporary society; his sensitive understanding of the characters’ psychologies and moral predicaments; and the investment he shares with Warren in comparative mythology. Like Warren, Butts uses the term “myth” not merely to describe an inherited fund of traditional stories from cultures around the world, but also the underlying patterns of belief and value that individuals and societies embrace in order to make sense of the world and to find their purpose in it.A century ago, in his 1923 essay “Ulysses, Order, and Myth,” T. S. Eliot coined the phrase “mythic method” to describe the way in which James Joyce's Ulysses, and his own The Waste Land, rooted themselves in a substratum of ancient traditional stories. In each case, the mythic method was not merely a description of the authors’ interests and techniques, but a way for them to examine and engage their transcendent sources of value. Eliot believed that our age is a disenchanted one, in which people are alienated from the divine, and because they are alienated from the divine, are alienated also from nature and from each other.The mythic method might be taken as a way to use literature to heal the brokenness of modernity by calling readers back to a value-laden, traditional, organic world order. But the mythic method might just as well be taken as only a diagnostic tool, registering how lost we are in a world in which we can never recover our footing. Even registering that cultural loss is a not-inconsiderable achievement, however, because self-awareness, of however dark a kind, is a good thing in itself, and such self-knowledge at least promises the ability to manage—even if it is powerless to solve—the original problem of world-alienation. In his 1955 essay “Knowledge and the Image of Man,” originally a speech to the American Philosophical Society, Warren treats this kind of rueful knowledge about human lostness as the best literature can do, even if it amounts only to a second bite of the original apple, because even if it does not offer redemption, it at least offers a chastened wisdom.Butts shows that Warren uses mythological thinking to come to grips with human lostness in all five of the novels of Warren's major period: All five use mythology and folklore to underline the ways in which modernity has become deracinated and has sacrificed authentic relationships to the natural world and authentic relationships among people. In each case, Butts reads a Warren text against a different mythological archive, bringing out the thematic depth of the novels by mapping the characters and the moral arc of the story against a mythological ur-text in startling detail.Butts places Night Rider alongside the Arthurian cycle, showing affinities among the characters in each text that reflect his critical insight into their moral predicaments. Percy Munn really is the blunderer that Sir Percival is; his investment in the Bunk Trevelyan case really does involve an impulsive investment in Trevelyan's wife such as Percival might, as an amateurish knight-errant on the make, have made to a lady; and Munn's failures to live up to his impulsive and ill-advised promises really do parallel the failures of the Arthurian knight. Bill Christian really is a bull-headed blusterer like Gawain. Captain Todd really is a noble but failed Lancelot, and his son Benton is purer and more noble, like Galahad.In At Heaven's Gate, the characters Jerry Calhoun, Slim Sarrett, Jason Sweetwater, and even Sue Murdock develop the combined themes of the Wandering Jew and the banished Cain in interestingly contrasting ways, bringing out the contradictory resonances of the novel's anti-urban and anti-capitalist themes. And both Cain and the Wandering Jew offer the reader good ways of understanding the predicament of modernity.The way Butts lays the characters of All the King's Men against the characters from Norse mythology is still more daring and more counterintuitive. Whether or not Willie is a plausible Odin, Jack Burden is certainly a plausible Loki, although, as Butts points out, Loki is positively evil in ways that Jack never is, and Tiny Duffy seems to step into the role of Loki at the novel's conclusion. Willie's desire to wiggle out of his deal with Gummy Larson to build his great hospital does have affinities with Odin's desire to wiggle out of the deal he has made with the dwarves to build his Valhalla. Both heroes are destroyed by the consequences of what they did to build the structure they hope to be remembered for.Butts’ reading of the novel is persuasive because it turns on suggestive echoes rather than upon rigorous patterning. Where the reading works, it works by making illuminating comparisons rather than by suggesting a comprehensive and consistent design.The connection Butts develops between the action of World Enough and Time and the mythology of the King of the Wood that Sir James Frazer developed in his monumental The Golden Bough is given plausibility not only by the patricidal rage Jeremiah Beaumont works up against Cassius Fort, his once mentor and patron, and by their mutual erotic investment in Rachel Jordan, but also by those moments of mystic connection with nature that Beaumont feels when he touches the beech tree in the forest, a moment that, as Butts points out, repeats itself with a telling difference when Beaumont is waiting among the lilacs in Fort's garden just before he murders him. The rise and fall of an ecstatic Dionysian relationship to nature (in which I also feel resonances from Frazer) is, Butts argues, this book's lyric version of the Agrarian complaint against modernity.The most daring connections Butts draws in his book tie the characters of Band of Angels to the collection of loas (spirits) who figure in the Haitian vodou religion. Now Warren would have learned quite a bit about this subject from Hurston's Mules and Men, which he certainly knew. And Butts backs up his analysis with very persuasive readings of the characters. Band of Angels has always been the poor cousin among Warren's novels. Butts’ readings reclaim that novel as a subject of interest.Some readers, however, might be forgiven for wondering whether the complex, systematic mapping of these novels onto mythological precursors that he develops was in Warren's focal consciousness when he wrote the novels. The best answer to these readers is to point to Leverett Butts’ other work, his brilliant retellings of the Arthurian stories as Westerns, in the novel series Guns of the Waste Land (Lume Books, 2016). The joy of that series is the way the two sets of stories unexpectedly click when seen next to each other. Seeing a Western as an Arthurian romance luminously (and completely persuasively) clarifies the stakes of the Western. And if one turns the connection around, seeing a Western as an Arthurian romance revivifies the Arthurian romance as well. “Seeing as” is an interpretive art not because it decodes the author's hidden design but because it brings into the light implicit aspects of the author's imagination. Butts’ fascinating readings richly bring out the implicit dimensions of these novels. They made me read all five of them with new eyes.

abstract: 2023 saw the publication of a smaller number of titles focused on Virginia Woolf than 2022, with two dedicated monographs and a significant edited collection. The latter is the impressively comprehensive The Oxford Handbook of Virginia Woolf, edited by Anne E. Fernald and first published in hardback in 2021 (but not reviewed in this title that year), and now available in a paperback edition. The collection begins with an introduction by Fernald that emphasizes Woolf’s ‘feminism and her experiments in language as foundational to her legacy’ (p. 1). It also briefly but effectively situates Woolf in relation to her work’s challenge to conventional genre boundaries, her education and upbringing, her friends and social networks, and her relationship to feminism, gender and race, all of which are topics central to the contributions that follow. The collection is organized into six parts: ‘Life’, ‘Texts’, ‘Experiments in Form and Style’, ‘Professions of Writing’, ‘Contexts’ and ‘Afterlives’. Part I, ‘Life’, begins with Urmila Seshagiri’s chapter on ‘Family and Place’, which situates Woolf not only in relation to her various homes or addresses but more significantly as a writer who profoundly questioned the meaning and experience of home across her works. Kathryn Simpson’s chapter, ‘Friends and Lovers’, considers Woolf’s many relationships, platonic and otherwise, through focusing on six of her friends: Violet Dickinson, E. M. Forster, Lytton Strachey, Katherine Mansfield, Vita Sackville-West and Ethel Smyth, considering the mutual impact they had on each other’s life and work. Regina Marler’s wide-ranging chapter, ‘Traditions and Transformations’ looks at the many ways that Woolf’s childhood and upbringing, and her more general relationship to, and memory of, the Victorian era, continued to shape her later self and writing in complex ways. Part II, ‘Texts’, opens with Caroline Pollentier’s theoretically deft chapter, ‘Private Writings’, which reads Woolf’s notebooks, letters and diaries as ‘techniques of living’ (p. 64, quoting Foucault) that conjoin aesthetics to ethics via quotidian practices of everyday life(writing). Jocelyn Rodal’s chapter ‘Early Novels and Stories (1915–1923)’ situates Woolf’s essays and fiction of this period in relation to Victorian precedents, while at the same time showing how their thematic representations of reading, writers and writing, gestures proleptically towards literary modernism, including Woolf’s own. Gabrielle McIntire’s chapter ‘Mature Works I (1924–1927)’ reads Woolf’s essays and fiction of this period in relation to its intervention into an array of philosophical questions spanning ethics, morality, ontology and epistemology, with a particular focus on how Woolf’s high modernist experiments in genre, mode and style were committed to representing the truth of what Woolf called the soul. Elsa Högberg’s chapter ‘Mature Works II (1928–1932)’ conceives the lyrical features and ‘formal-generic hybridity’ (p. 102) of Woolf’s work as the most powerful site of her social and political commitments, demonstrating how the lyrical prose of both Orlando [1928] and The Waves [1931] engages in a feminist and anti-imperialist textual politics. Alice Wood’s chapter ‘Late Works (1933–1941)’ takes a thematic approach to Woolf’s work of this period, organized into sections on ‘Mixing Art and Politics’, ‘Patriarchy and Fascism’ and ‘Nationalism and War’, and focusing on The Years [1937], Three Guineas [1938] and Between the Acts [1941]. Part III, ‘Experiments in Form and Style’, begins with Dora Zhang’s chapter ‘Stream of Consciousness’. Zhang expands this central category of modernism from a narrow conception as interior monologue into a broader genre with three key attributes: free indirect discourse, the narration of collectivity and the use of analogy to represent ‘being conscious’ (p. 134), a quality that affiliates Woolf with William James. Amy Bromley’s chapter ‘Character, Form, and Fiction’ traces Woolf’s conception of character through essays such as ‘Character in Fiction’ [1924] and ‘Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown’ [1923] before turning to three novelistic examples of character in Jacob’s Room [1922], Mrs Dalloway [1925] and Orlando, demonstrating throughout the connections between characterization and broader questions of literary form. Jesse Matz’s chapter ‘Time’ contextualizes Woolf’s many experiments in literary temporality in relation to material and philosophical changes in the organization and phenomenology of time, and develops a Ricoeurian conception of the historical dialectic between temporal and narrative form throughout her works. Janine Utell’s chapter ‘Narrative Ethics’ explores three interrelated ethical strands of Woolf’s work: the relationship between the good life and reading, the recognition of alterity and unknowability and the limits of humanist ethics, with a particular focus on Mrs Dalloway and The Years. Jane de Gay’s chapter ‘Allusion and Metaphor’ considers how Woolf’s use of allusion departed from male modernists such as Eliot and Joyce in its focus on creative transformation rather than canonical authority, and argues for the importance of metaphors of nature in conceptualizing allusion across Woolf’s literary works. Laura Marcus’s chapter ‘Biography and Autobiography’ unpacks Woolf’s innovations in both these modes with particular attention to Orlando and Roger Fry [1940], and in relation to questions of truth, identity, embodiment and memory. Part IV, ‘Professions of Writing’, opens with Helen Southworth’s chapter ‘Literary London’, which traces Woolf’s movements from Kensington to Bloomsbury to Richmond (and then back to Bloomsbury) between 1905 and 1924, considering how these different physical places and social milieus filtered into Woolf’s writing. Alice Staveley’s chapter ‘The Hogarth Press’ surveys the changing trends in scholarship about the press and the Woolfs’ roles in it, as well as offering a materialist feminist reading of how the manual and professional labour of printing shaped the emergence of Woolf’s modernist style in ‘The Mark on the Wall’ [1917] and elsewhere. Eleanor McNees’s chapter ‘Woolf as Reviewer-Critic’ tracks her critical and review essays across her career, identifying core formal features such as metaphor, analogy, character and ventriloquism, as well as the displacement of the model of the reviewer-critic by that of the common reader. Beth C. Rosenberg’s chapter ‘The Essays’ develops an account of Woolf’s feminine and feminist appropriation of the essay form from male predecessors such as Walter Pater, Max Beerbohm, Montaigne and Hazlitt, with an extended reading of A Room of One’s Own [1929] and its use of a personal voice and embodied emotion. Claire Davison’s chapter ‘The Lyrical Mode of Translating’ draws a suggestive parallel between Woolf’s recurrent figure of ‘Anon’ and the historical role of translators, often also anonymous, female and elided, using this to frame a broader investigation into Woolf’s representation of, and work in, translation, via what she calls the ‘lyrical mode’ (p. 292). Part V, ‘Contexts’, starts with Stephanie J. Brown’s chapter ‘Woolf’s Feminism’. Brown traces Woolf’s feminist commitments across her life and writing, considering how these commitments traverse the changing landscape of feminism at large, and how they intersect with other concerns such as race, class and literary aesthetics. Chris Coffman’s chapter ‘Queer Theory’ takes a comparative approach to Woolf, reading Orlando, Mrs Dalloway and A Room of One’s Own in conversation with mid-century Indian and late-century North African fiction, as well as contemporary British literature by Jeanette Winterson, to reveal the full range and scope of Woolf’s imagination of ‘new possibilities for desire and gendered embodiment’ (p. 342). Anna Snaith’s chapter ‘Woolf and Education’ is split into three sections, the first tracing Woolf’s own engagement with formal educational institutions, the second her critique and reconceptualization of education in her novels and essays, and the third her thinking of education beyond institutions, in forms such as public libraries and common readers. Barbara Green’s chapter ‘Woolf and Suffrage’ reads the backward-looking temporalities of the suffrage movement in Night and Day [1919] and The Years as a sign of Woolf’s ambivalence towards its progressive impulses, but also de-exceptionalizes that ambivalence by locating it as a common feature of more mainstream movement novels. Tamar Katz’s chapter ‘Impressionism and Post-Impressionism’ traces the influences and changing iterations of these styles across Woolf’s oeuvre, with a particular focus on Jacob’s Room and To the Lighthouse [1927]. Maxwell Uphaus’s chapter ‘Oceans and Empire’ reads Woolf’s figurations of the ocean as a key site of her feminist anti-imperialism, as well as its limitations, focusing on The Voyage Out [1915] and the 1931 short story, ‘Scenes from the life of a British Naval Officer’. Madelyn Detloff’s chapter ‘Biopower’ offers a Foucauldian interpretation of Three Guineas and ‘Thoughts of Peace in an Air Raid’ [1940], demonstrating how they both challenge and reaffirm the logics underpinning state racism and genderism. Cliff Mak’s chapter ‘The Natural World and the Anthropocene’ reads Woolf’s attachment to the aristocratic sport of fly-fishing in her 1936 review of John Waller’s My Sporting Life [1936] as both disrupting and reinforcing the limits of human-centred conceptions of ethics and agency, connecting this discussion to her more well-known essays, short stories and novels such as Flush [1933] and The Waves. Beryl Pong’s chapter ‘War and Peace’ argues that prolepsis provided Woolf’s novels with ‘a narrative style that responds to the temporal politics of war with a pacifist politics of time’ (p. 455). Mary Wilson’s chapter ‘Work’ demonstrates Woolf’s vexed proximity to the labour of domestic service, which both supported her own writerly work—and the work of her middleclass protagonists—at the same
