title: Strange Fruit and Patriotic Flowers: E. McKnight Kauffer's Illustrated South
abstract: This article discusses literary works by Langston Hughes and William Faulkner in relation to their dust jackets and illustrations by the modernist expatriate American poster artist E. McKnight Kauffer (1890–1954). It argues that Kauffer's life and art are best understood in the context of displacement and exile in response to two world wars, which forced his return to an America in which he no longer felt "at home" by 1940. His prolific output left its mark—on high modernism, on the evolution of book and poster design, even on ads to buy war bonds for textile mills in the South. A globally engaged modernist who for many years abroad looked from the outside in at the U.S., Kauffer made unique contributions to cultural and political representations of African Americans and the South. Most dramatically, in cover art for Faulkner's Intruder in the Dust (1948)—a dust jacket only now being recognized for its subversive implications—Kauffer encodes his own paratextual interpretation of the novel's lynching theme.

title: A Study on the Self-Construction of Joe Christmas in Light in August
abstract: On the basis of Lacan’s theories of Mirror Stage and Three Orders, the paper analyses the process of seeking and constructing of protagonist’s self-identity in William Faulkner’s Light in August, exploring the inevitability of self-lost. Joe Christmas has been abandoned in an orphanage by his grandfather since the day he was born because his grandfather has suspected that Joe has the black blood. Joe became aware of his black identity as a result of the verbal abuse of the word “nigger” in other’s mouth. After that, he has been searching for his identity in the thirty years of short life. However, in the conflict between the self in the mirror and the name of the father in the symbolic order, Joe, on the one hand, gradually admitted his black blood without hesitation in front of the outsiders, and on the other hand, he extremely despised the black blood in his heart. In the extreme alienation, Joe gradually lost self and eventually died. According to Lacan’s theory, the self always exists in the connection with the other, and establishes self-identity by obtaining recognition from the other. It will easily lead to the self-alienation once the relationship cannot be handled correctly. Joe’s tragic fate caused by failure construction of self-identity not only arouses the sympathy of the readers but also arouses people’s reflection about their own identity. Even in the face of abnormal beliefs about race, religion, and so on, people should complete the construction of self-identity and recover ourselves.

title: F. O. Matthiessen's Modernist Hawthorne
abstract: F.O. Matthiessen and Newton Arvin have a few things in common. They were of the same generation (Matthiessen was born in 1902, two years after Arvin). They were educated at Harvard (Arvin as an undergraduate, Matthiessen as a graduate student). They were both gay and both sympathetic to the political left. Their sexuality and their politics would bring unwelcome scrutiny to both men near the ends of their lives (Matthiessen committed suicide in 1950, and Arvin died in 1963 after retiring in disgrace from Smith College in 1960). They both wrote important scholarship on the work of Nathaniel Hawthorne, Arvin's book appearing in 1929 (reviewed by Matthiessen in the New Republic in 1930) and Matthiessen's book-within-a-book, his section on Hawthorne in American Renaissance, in 1941. In their treatment of Hawthorne, these two vital critics of nineteenth-century American literature interestingly diverge. In what follows, I explore the difference between Arvin's and Matthiessen's analyses of Hawthorne, and I offer a couple of explanations for the distinctive turn that Matthiessen's reading of Hawthorne takes, a turn that puts him at odds with the main current of Arvin's reading.Arvin's Hawthorne is a writer struggling with the tension, which the scholar names as a central preoccupation of American literature, between the individual and society. He opens his book with the contrast between Hawthorne and his Bowdoin classmates: where they go on to success in the professions, he consigns himself for the next dozen years to his third-story room on Herbert Street in Salem and writes in solitude (Arvin, Hawthorne 6). There, Hawthorne produced his sketches, stories, and early romances, but there, too, he suffered, according to Arvin, something like exile from the social and erotic possibilities of community: His imagination, instead of playing freely and flexibly over the intricate facts of human existence was entangling itself in the briars of a special and abnormal experience; was looking at the world from a distorted angle and through colored lenses. (58) This solitude was ultimately to create the central (if powerfully moving) failure of Hawthorne's literary production, to overcast the play of his imagination with a cloudy and obfuscating sense of the presence of guilt at the heart of all human relations, and hide from him those sources of spiritual joy that lie beyond the springs of spiritual confusion (58). The fault is not entirely Hawthorne's. As Christopher Castiglia argues, Arvin blames Hawthorne's society at least as much as he blames the writer himself, condemning Hawthorne's era for its uncritical investment in public and private conformity that offered a free-thinking and imaginative individual no choice but to withdraw from public life (Castiglia 125).Matthiessen diagnoses a similar problematic for Hawthorne, noting Hawthorne's frequent exploration of the tensions between the individual and society and casting these in terms of tragedy. But Matthiessen sees Hawthorne neither as suffering in isolation nor as failing to engage his society. Reading Hawthorne's central works in terms of allegory and tragedy, inserting the works at once in the long traditions of these genres and in the welter of democratic ideas and arguments of the 1830s and 1840s, Matthiessen finds in Hawthorne's work powerful resources precisely for overcoming the painful division between self and society, for merging the self into the democratic social whole. Tellingly, those resources, for Matthiessen, have more to do with the form of Hawthorne's works than with positions they seem explicitly or implicitly to take on or the questions with which they are concerned.We might hazard a variety of explanations for how Matthiessen's reading of Hawthorne, conducted just a dozen years after and in full awareness of Arvin's, differs so dramatically from Arvin's. The decade or so between Arvin's and Matthiessen's books saw the emergence of new scholarship on the American Puritans, especially Herbert Schneider's The Puritan Mind (1930), which helped Matthiessen to situate Hawthorne as a religious and tragic writer. More than this, Matthiessen's frequent invocations of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and his use of Hawthorne's readingas recorded in his journals but also as discovered through the records of books he took out of the Concord public librarypoint to the influence of Matthiessen's graduate adviser and senior Harvard colleague, John Livingston Lowes, whose The Road to Xanadu: A Study of the Ways of the Imagination (1927) was an attempt to reconstruct the mind of the poet through his reading (Lowes did extensive research in Coleridge's journals), to show how the poet's synthesis of the intellectual culture of his moment can be found in the poem and/or how the poem illustrates the poet's synthetic work via the poetic imagination. More than anything else, it is through attention to Hawthorne's reading that Matthiessen substantiates his opening claim that, while [m]any have remarked [on Hawthorne's] tragic depth, very few have realized that his thought bore an immediate relation to the issues of his own day (Matthiessen American Renaissance 192). But while the scholarly fingerprints of both Schneider and Lowes are on Matthiessen's discussion of Hawthorne, the most important and influential presence in the two hundred pages Matthiessen spends on Hawthorne is T.S. Eliot.Matthiessen concludes Book Two of American Renaissance with a chapter titled From Hawthorne to James to Eliot, exemplifying there the practice he promises in the book's opening pages, to follow these books through their implications, to situate them at once in their own time and in his own (xi). Just as Matthiessen's understanding of Hawthorne hinges on the author's tragic dramatization of evil as the violation of norms that would enable communal flourishing, his connection of Hawthorne to James and then Eliot develops from Hawthorne's late-career worries over the dissolution and dispersal of those communally held moral norms. While no really integrated principles can be made out of his varying reflections on his social and economic milieu, Matthiessen writes, Hawthorne was acutely conscious of the slow disintegration of the bases upon which the earlier moral values had depended (361). By the 1920s, Matthiessen concludes, Hawthorne's anxiety had become, for Eliot, the certainty that personality, as opposed to the authorization and discipline of tradition, posed existential aesthetic and social dangers. Eliot came to believe that the choice lay between further disintegration of the sort that Hawthorne already foresaw, and a return to dogma upon which to base more adequate values than those of James (368). Eliotic modernism seems simply to be the fruition of Hawthornean anxiety.But Eliot appears not only in this concluding moment. He is a crucial figure for Matthiessen's interpretation of Hawthorne in key moments throughout the chapters. Indeed, Matthiessen invokes Eliot along with Herman Melville in the opening pages of his Hawthorne section: It is significant that Eliot, in whose own work the dark strain of Hawthorne is more visible than in the work of any other writer of the present, has judged him by criteria analogous to Melville's. He goes on to quote Eliot on Hawthorne in a way that suggests just how Eliotic Matthiessen's own reading of Hawthorne will be: The work of Hawthorne is truly a criticismtrue because a fidelity of the artist and not a mere conviction of the manof the Puritan morality, of the Transcendentalist morality, and of the world which Hawthorne knew (American Renaissance 193). When Matthiessen wants to distinguish Hawthorne from a character who might seem to be his textual avatar, he invokes Eliot: [I]n risking such parallels between his life and his art, we must remember that Coverdale is not Hawthorne any more than Prufrock is Eliot (229). When he wants to specify the character of Hawthorne's fidelity to historical realities, he invokes Eliot: What Eliot called Hawthorne's realism could not depend on a notation of rich surface details; its very starvation made it a truer facing of the tragedy of provincial New England (236). And on and on.The ubiquity of Eliot in Matthiessen's chapters on Hawthorne should perhaps not be surprising. By the late 1930s, Eliot was a dominant voice in Anglo-American literary culture, famous not only for The Waste Land and other poems but also for the taste-making, canon-forming, and critical-practice-modeling essays he had published in The Criterion and gathered in The Sacred Wood and Selected Essays. His work and ideas had been examined by such critics as R. P. Blackmur (who published a crucial two-part essay on Eliot in Hound and Horn in 1928) and Edmund Wilson (who included a chapter on Eliot in Axel's Castle [1931]). (Matthiessen, by the way, reviewed the latter in the Yale Review.) Most importantly, Eliot had spent the 193233 academic year at Harvard (where Matthiessen had just been appointed Chairman of the Board of Tutors in History and Literature and Senior Tutor in the new Eliot House) delivering the Charles Eliot Norton lectures. While they never became close, Matthiessen did spend time with Eliot during his time in Cambridge, and the poet had a profound impact on the critic. Matthiessen taught and wrote on Eliot's work throughout the rest of his career, and, in 1935, he published The Achievement of T.S. Eliot, the first academic monograph on the poet's work. As Giles Gunn points out in his analysis of Matthiessen's Eliot book, the critic develops in that study the theory of literature that will shape his critical methods in American Renaissance. At the very center of that theory is the notion of organic form, the idea that it is through the text's production of wholeness (rather than its articulation of any doctrine or position) that the literary work achieves its deepest significance. Matthiessen states his foundational assumption most clearly here: [I]t is particularly necessary to be plain at a time when works of art are increasingly being confused with the doctrines which they embody. The confusion is especially great when dealing with literature since, in approaching an art whose medium is words, it is very hard to make relevant distinctions between content and form, to distinguish the idea from the expression . It is equally true that although a poem grows organically out of the life of its time, it is not a document but a work of art; that is to say, it possesses in a very real sense a life of its own which is distinct from the biography of its creator and also from any idea or belief that it expresses. (Achievement of T.S. Eliot vii) It is easy to see how such assumptions would produce an interpretation of Hawthorne quite different from Arvin's, not least because Arvin is as openly opposed to Eliot's formalism (and that of the emergent New Critics influenced by Eliot) as Matthiessen is sympathetic to it. In American Pantheon, he writes that he is quite willing and even eager to be impressionistic, intuitional, appreciative, unsystematic, and all the other sins in the tight little Eliotic decalogue (xvi). Where Arvin elaborates a Hawthorne whose fictions provide models for mediation between a culture's demands for conformity and the Other's requirements of difference, Matthiessen finds a Hawthorne whose works' tradition-influenced formal management of their internal conflicts produces effects of unity that train readers in a capacity for wholeness otherwise absent in the world as it is.We can find these Eliotic imperatives woven through the methodological choices that give American Renaissance its distinctive power, as well as in the theory of literature and its value that shapes his methods. In Method and Scope, the preface to American Renaissance, Matthiessen writes that the critic's chief responsibility and obligation in limning a literary work's value for readers in their own moment is not the simple reading off of political or social values of potential utility in that moment (as he elsewhere accuses such critics as V. F. Calverton and V. L. Parrington of doing), but, instead, is to examine an author's resources of language and of genres, in a word, to be preoccupied with form (xi).This imperative is most clearly and illuminatingly on display in Matthiessen's chapter, The Haunted Mind, which might just as easily have been titled Hawthorne and the Dissociation of Sensibility. There, Matthiessen again divines the chief difficulty Hawthorne faces as divisionboth between individual and society and within the individualand offers Hawthorne's wholeness as the imagined resolution of the difficulty. He distinguishes Hawthorne from Henry David Thoreau and Henry James, the latter characterized as metaphysical and thereby evoking Eliot's idea that the dissociation of the sensibility occurs after the seventeenth-century moment dominated by the poetics of John Donne. Hawthorne, Matthiessen argues, also draws his influences from the seventeenth century; his conception of permanent truth, however, is Miltonic rather than metaphysical. For Hawthorne, what holds us together, individually and socially, is our inherent capacity for evil, a capacity that, like the imagination, wells up from within and is not entirely susceptible to conscious control. If the point was that we might derive from this thematic content some principle applicable to our lives in the present, this would seem a paradox, or at least an unwelcome prescription: the solution to the problem of disunity and fragmentation is acceptance of evil as the permanent human condition. But for Matthiessen, any such thematic principle is beside the point. What is applicable for later readers is not the idea of evil as universal but the formal process through which Hawthorne orders an aesthetic unity out of the fragmentation and division with which his narratives are concerned. The resources for wholeness that Hawthorne offers arise, for example, from the unity of his style and his themes: [I]f his art was to fulfill its function by remaining true to what his deepest intuitions had known, there must inevitably have been woven into the texture of his style some thinness and bleakness, the consequences of the long domination of Puritan thought, and of the lack of any developed artistic traditions from which he could start. (235) Or we might find the possibility of unity in the way Hawthorne narrated the relationships among characters, each of whom allegorically represents something beyond himself or herself as individual: Hawthorne was trying to encompass the range of society by presenting a procession of types, grouped together, not by the external accidents of their trades or professions, but by their hidden desires or their deeper bond of suffering. (239) In other words, Hawthorne's stories and romances work a lot like The Waste Land works, and they are more like Eliot's poems than, say, Honoré de Balzac's novels.For the generation of American literary critics and literary historians trained after the appearance of American Renaissance, it was Matthiessen's ability to fuse the formal emphasis drawn from Eliot and central to the emergent (and soon dominant) New Criticism with his attention to historical context and contemporary relevance that made him so influential. While Matthiessen's modernism leads William Cain to produce a vigorous takedown, it gives his analyses staying power that has led to a renewal of interest in his work over the last decade or so (see, e.g., the chapter on Matthiessen in Henry Abelove's Deep Gossip or Samuel Otter's much more recent essay, American Renaissance and Us). But the implicit dialogue with Arvin's earlier work on Hawthorne suggests that it is not just Matthiessen's attention to form that later critics found enabling. In his review of Arvin's book, Matthiessen notes that the critic's sharp analysis discovers an essence in Hawthorne's work that we cannot afford to forget: [T]he guilt that Hawthorne broods over rises invariably out of isolation (Nathaniel Hawthorne 21011). Focusing on how the operations of form keep the thematic tensions that Arvin importantly identified in balance, demonstrating that Hawthorne's formal perfection produces effects of unity and coherence, Matthiessen's modernist reading style adumbrates Arvin's moral poetics. Together, these critics' approaches continue to offer important resources for literary studies' distinctive value in a culture often inclined to focus on the what of an utterance rather than the vital and telling how.

title: T. S. Eliot’s Modernist Techniques in ‘The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
abstract: This paper explores T. S. Eliot’s modernist techniques in “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” (1915) acclaimed as the first poem in Modernism constructed upon Baudelaire’s concept of modernity. The representative modernist poet Eliot is incomparably different from the Romantic or Victorian poets, influenced by Freudian psychoanalysis which classifies the human self into the Id, the Ego and the Super-ego, and by Jamesian “stream of consciousness.” Through the “interior monologue” or daydream of the prudent and indecisive Prufrock, Eliot remarkably presents “alienation” in urban life, a theme of Modernism by describing the incommunicative speaker who is unable to have a rendezvous with the sensual women in his unconsciousness. Furthermore, the poet superbly depicts psychological time in Prufrock’s consciousness rather than mechanical or chronological time under the influence of the Bergsonian concept of time. Eliot’s modernist technique also is obviously displayed through the peculiar metaphor, simile, metonymy, symbol, and the more complex conceit than the conceit of the metaphysical poets. In conclusion, Eliot’s “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” projecting the speaker’s vacillating (un)consciousness or subconsciousness is indeed the first innovative modernist poem bridging the chasm between his conventional Harvard juvenilia and the modernist masterpiece The Waste Land.

title: Jonathan Franzen: The Comedy of Rage
abstract: Jonathan Franzen, considered by many to be the most important writer of serious fiction of his generation, has proven in his most successfully realized novels that humor serves a serious function in his work. No reader of The Corrections (2001) can forget Chip Lambert stuffing an expensive salmon fillet into his pants at a haute supermarket called Nightmare of Consumption or, pages later, Chip's drugged, impassioned lovemaking to an antique chaise lounge, nor will readers fail to recall the repellant Joey Berglund of Freedom (2010) forced to knead his own excrement in search of the wedding band he had ingested. Franzen's enormous potential is apparent as a novelist in general and as a comic writer in particular, so it is unsurprising that he has become the subject of academic scrutiny. With The Comedy of Rage, Philip Weinstein offers the first critical biography of Franzen to date. Weinstein, a Swarthmore professor and the author of several books on literary modernism and Faulkner most especially, offers an overview of Franzen's life and works up to the time before his latest novel, Purity, was published in 2015.Weinstein describes a central tension that animates Franzen's body of fiction, a tension between what he sees as highbrow rage on the one hand and mainstream acceptance and love on the other, and he grounds his claims in the biographical evidence he amasses. Weinstein's project raises the question of how “a suspicious intellectual loner and the mainstream writer idolized by millions … come together as one person” (2), and for Weinstein, the answer is that Franzen's once-corrosive rage becomes tempered over time by love and that this “oppositional encounter produces … the inimitable comedy of his work” (3). Weinstein charts the early childhood of Franzen as one of alienation and uncertainty, characterized by a distant and taciturn father and an emotionally suffocating mother. He recounts Franzen's formative years as a German major at Swarthmore and details the harrowing dissolution of his marriage, life experiences figured here as the necessary constituents for his career as a novelist.Weinstein, like most commentators on Franzen's fiction, argues that Franzen's first two novels, while promising and intermittently brilliant, are less than wholly successful. The Twenty-Seventh City (1988) and Strong Motion (1992) are ambitious but also marred by postmodernist pretensions, and both suffer because Franzen creates caricatures—strawmen—on whom he heaps his curdling invective rather than complexly realized characters capable of evoking compassion and censure in readers. At this stage of his evolution as a writer, Franzen had not tamed his dogmatic predilection for withering highbrow critique of a bankrupt America. In Weinstein's binary reckoning, Franzen chose a “status” over “contract” ethos (Franzen's terms) in his early novels (89). Significantly, Franzen's decision to mine his own fraught family's struggles and transmute the personal into art signals his claim to greatness for Weinstein. The Corrections (2001) abandons formulaic types and gains emotional heft from Franzen's choice to love the characters enough not to judge them; we now witness Franzen's generous attention to dynamic, complex characters drawn from his reimagining of his own father and mother. Likewise, Freedom (2010) features his most complex female character in the person of Patty Berglund, whose many sides are revealed in his sustained and pitch-perfect dramatization of marital discord and resilience. Weinstein's concluding chapters are devoted to Franzen's sometimes notorious New Yorker essays and a cursory overview of Purity (2015), still an unpublished manuscript when Jonathan Franzen went to press.Despite Weinstein's contention that substantial parts of his biographical portrayal of Franzen have been gleaned from interviews and private email exchanges with the author, the evidence suggests that actual engagements with Franzen were limited. Instead, most of the biographical data has been cobbled from previously available and well-known sources, including Franzen's own autobiographical essays, his memoir The Discomfort Zone (2006), and published interviews, such as the lengthy one in the 2010 Paris Review.1 For the rest of the book, Weinstein builds his claims about his subject's steady maturation on what amounts to character studies of Franzen's five novels.In the end, the most perplexing problem posed by Weinstein's book is one of purpose. Why write a critical biography of a young novelist (Franzen was born in 1959) who is, God willing, so emphatically mid-career? In a book-length study, conclusions about such a novelist's place in literary history can be only contingent at best. Moreover, can one really lay claim to writing a biography if the resulting work is more or less a compendium of existing biographical factoids and autobiographical admissions?The book reveals other lapses as well. When stripped to its essence, Weinstein's central argument is simplistic, a variation on the cliché uttered in creative writing workshops: “Write what you know.” In Weinstein's estimation, Franzen's fiction assumes an urgent potency only when he ceases to write difficult postmodernist fiction and instead creatively reworks the particulars of his family life as he does in The Corrections and Freedom. It is unfortunate that Weinstein's book was published before Purity was released; if he had been able to read the final version, he might have found he could no longer endorse such a biographically informed thesis.In his treatment of the biographical evidence of Franzen's life, especially with regard to Franzen's parents, Weinstein is bluntly Freudian in his pronouncements. He avows that Franzen's mother is the prototype for all his female characters over five novels. He asks rather breezily, “Is there any doubt that, behind these troubled maternal portraits, there lies the clamorous figure of Irene Franzen?” (19). He argues that son Jonathan is locked in Oedipal agon with his father, Earl, and with other strong novelists such as Thomas Pynchon and most pointedly David Foster Wallace, concluding that “this Oedipal model lodges at the core of Franzen's imaginary” (22). Readers, however, may well find such psychologizing dated and perhaps a little hackneyed. And just because Franzen has admitted in an essay to a youthful fondness for the muted somberness of comic strip character Charlie Brown, it does not follow that the adult Franzen would relish, as Weinstein maintains, the “Schultzian comedy of his former identity” (38). The comparison to Charles Schultz seems unnecessarily infantilizing.The book is marred by stylistic infelicities, too. The phrase “warts and all” is used no fewer than four times. The book is studded with examples of tortured syntax and at least one mixed metaphor: “This new scene sprays its poison like a second electric chair” (132). Stilted phrasing is too common. “You cannot ride with the horses of Status and at the same time run with the hounds of Contract” (94) may be whimsical, but an observant editor would have excised it. Even more awkward are the several instances where, one presumes, Weinstein wishes to normalize vulgarities in the most casual, hip way, but results in producing howlers like this: “Granting how powerfully dick and cunt see what they want, we may ask: can they see—and let us see—beyond what they want” (170)? Or this: “The mother's vagina was a pussy prior to becoming a womb” (209).If the book is bedeviled by Weinstein's hazy sense of purpose, it is also beset by his unsure sense of the work's intended audience. Whom will this book serve? Academic readers will have no doubt read Franzen's autobiographical essays in their original form and would not need Freud's concept of eros explained (88). But neither would scholars necessarily be gratified by a long account of Franzen's abortive attempts to adapt The Corrections as an HBO series. Conversely, would nonspecialized readers find any merit in Weinstein's lengthy explication of Franzen's labor of love, The Kraus Project (2013), his translation with footnotes of the Viennese intellectual Karl Kraus's essays? It would seem that Philip Weinstein's The Comedy of Rage wrestles with the same conundrum that he argues for in Franzen's work, a confused tendency to write for an academic audience that wants more analytic depth and a general readership that wants less.

title: Paris as ‘unreal city’: Modernist conceptions in Michiel Heyns’s Invisible Furies
abstract: Michiel Heyns's sixth novel, Invisible Furies (2012) is deeply inscribed in the author's profound engagement in and knowledge of the grand modernist tradition. The article aims to illuminate and discuss this underrated novel in terms of some of its modernist attributes by relating the work conceptually to the works of great modernist writers, particularly T. S. Eliot and E. M. Forster, in order to demonstrate its impressive literary scope and density of meaning. While there are direct allusions to Eliot's poetry in the text, it is a certain sensibility and perspective that reminds the reader forcibly of Eliot's vision, particularly in The Waste Land (1922) and The Hollow Men (1925). Eliot's image of the "Unreal city", derived from Baudelaire's Les sept veillards, is particularly pertinent. A number of modernist concerns or themes are addressed in this context, in particular the ambiguous merits and value of the aesthetic, social alienation, the city and the concept of Forster's "eternal moment" (his equivalent to Joyce's "epiphany", Virginia Woolf's "moment of being" and Eliot's "moment in and out of time") as a possible means of salvation in the face of the meaninglessness of a spiritu- ally and emotionally arid, modern existence.

title: Precarious Voices
abstract: This chapter takes up questions of ‘‘moods and voices’ in the modern British novel. In its focus on ‘moving epochs’ it also offers a critique of literary periodization and of approaches to modernist literature and culture which have rendered the rich and complex novels of the mid-twentieth century merely an ‘after modernism’: the texts of this period, it is argued, are too often misunderstood or diminished. It points in particular to the ‘distributed’ exposition of mind, through a broadly phenomenological grasp of the structures of experience, running throughout the fiction of the twentieth century from Franz Kafka, Virginia Woolf, Marcel Proust, and William Faulkner onwards. Many of the most compelling novels of the 1950s (including work by Muriel Spark, William Sansom, William Golding, Elizabeth Bowen, and Samuel Beckett) employed expressionist techniques, born of phenomenological insights, to imagine worlds that reflect disturbed minds and alienated outsiders.

title: Backwater Blues: The Mississippi Flood of 1927 in the African American ImaginationAin’t Got No Home: America’s Great Migrations and the Making of an Interracial LeftWriting through Jane Crow: Race and Gender Politics in African American LiteratureThe Other Blacklist: The African American Literary and Cultural Left of the 1950s
abstract: In 1995, Farah Jasmine Griffin’s foundational “Who Set You Flowin’?”: The African-American Migration Narrative argued that the migration narrative and movement itself played a definitive role in African American literary production across the twentieth century. Citing Jean Toomer’s Cane (1923), Griffin associated the movement of African Americans across space with the liquid (blood and water) metaphor of flow. Almost twenty years later, a new set of literary, cultural, and historical studies is bringing attention to the literature produced during the Great Migration period. Offering readings of literary and cultural texts informed by the context of institutions, from the American Red Cross to the Communist Party and the CIA, these texts deepen an ongoing conversation about the implications of the physical movement of black bodies across space and the relationship between black creative practice and social movements.In Backwater Blues, Richard Mizelle references Bessie Smith’s “Backwater Blues,” and the blues tradition broadly, to understand black experiences of disaster that become undocumentable due to the profound disenfranchisement of the black people most vulnerable to the social impact of “natural” disasters and the nonlinearity of racial trauma. Mizelle argues that, “like griots of the past, black blues musicians kept the experiences of those displaced and marginalized folks alive in the music” (11). This sentence hints at the fact that Mizelle’s concept of “racial flood diaspora” (which includes the dispersal of people; shifts in labor structures; and the expression of racialized experiences through art, protest, and cultural critique) is also linked to a concept of diaspora that craves or at least implies a connection to a pre-enslavement black history. This pre-enslavement history is represented by “griots,” which, in an otherwise sharply geographically specific and historicized work, Mizelle chooses to place in a vague “past.” He doesn’t have to say Africa. Or perhaps he cannot afford to say Africa without risking the terms of the specific contours of the US-based racial flood diaspora he seeks to describe in this project.Mizelle’s use of blues as both a mode of analysis and a source of alternative experiential evidence is compelling. His description of the history of displacement trajectories between Louisiana and Houston, Texas, becomes a work song–inflected blues, as do his depictions of the persistence and suppression of black protest work by Ida B. Wells, W. E. B. DuBois, Roy Wilkins, and others at the time. His descriptions of the violence of forced labor in the aftermath of disaster, and the ways white Southern planters used American Red Cross labor camps to restrict black people from migrating and to force them into debt-based labor after a direct emergency, are supplemented by his rereadings of Richard Wright’s flood-themed short stories. While he goes to great length to describe the violence that black men in Wright’s stories face as they try to protect and maintain their families in the aftermath of the flood, playing out their decisions step by step, he only briefly mentions Tea Cake’s conscripted labor in Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) and never mentions the brutal decision that Janie (Hurston’s black female protagonist) has to make when Tea Cake contracts rabies during this forced labor and she has to shoot him.Mizelle’s study is certainly useful for scholars who are interested in connections between contemporary social disasters such as Katrina and the racialized history of disaster perpetuation and response in the United States (and by the Red Cross), but I also find it useful as a way of thinking about the rest of the works under consideration here. What if we think about the work of writers moving through the decades that follow the flood, and continue the migration in terms of the multiple disasters of racism, sexism, homophobia, capitalism, and a culture of sexual violence?Ain’t Got No Home seeks to describe an interracial left through a rereading of migration narratives. Like Griffin’s Who Set You Flowin’?, Battat’s work features a Jacob Lawrence classic on the cover, alongside the vernacularized migratory statement “Ain’t Got No Home.” But while Mizelle cites the racially critical “Boll Weevil Blues”: “The white man he got half the crop, boll weevil took the rest; I ain’t got no home” (the phrase immediately bringing to mind the first words of Nina Simone’s later rendition of “I Got Life,” which are also “I ain’t got no home”), Battat refers to white folk singer Woody Guthrie’s dust-bowl migration song: “Rich man took my home and he drove me from my door / And I ain’t got no home in this world anymore” (Mizelle, 28–29; Battat, 5). Battat’s work seeks to emphasize the class connections between migration narratives of black and white survivors of the Great Depression and their relationship to the efforts of the Communist Popular Front to use the economic crash to substantially change conditions for workers.While Battat’s project seeks to displace John Steinbeck’s Grapes of Wrath (1939) and Dorothea Lange’s image of the migrant mother, by offering readings of work from the same period by Wright, Elizabeth Catlett, William Attaway, Ann Petry, Marita Bonner, Chester Himes, and Sanora Babb, her project ultimately works to integrate the artists of color (and Babb as a lesser-known white woman) into a preexisting white Left that remains dominant in the text. It is rare for many pages of this book to pass without Steinbeck coming up. In fact, except for the chapter on Himes, every chapter (including the introduction) grounds itself in Steinbeck by comparison or contextualization. Tellingly, while Battat marks when she is talking about an African American, or otherwise nonwhite person, she consistently leaves the whiteness of white people unmarked. The fact that Catlett is African American must be spoken while the fact the Lange is white never is. This undermines Battat’s own argument that, “deriving solely from a European aesthetic tradition,” Lange’s image and the use of it as an icon feeds into an “idea of universal motherhood [which] elides the historical experiences of colonialism, slavery, segregation, and internment that gave rise to vastly different meanings of motherhood and different priorities for social change” (99), an argument that is affirmed by a nuanced reading of Catlett on her own terms.The dominance of the white subject shows up in another way in Battat’s readings of Petry and Himes. While Battat spends quite a bit of time discussing the implications of Himes’s discussions of sexual violence against white women in his autobiography, in her gloss of Petry’s The Street (1946), she skips over the rape that the protagonist defends herself against in the climactic action of the book, writing only “Lutie murders the man who wants to prostitute her.” Without mentioning the rape in the process, Battat is able to describe Lutie’s action not as self-defense but as “a self-destructive, militant act of violence” (108). While I certainly feel that Himes’s discussions of sexual violence against white women have much to teach us about race, class, sexuality, and rape culture, we may also have a lot to learn from the visibility of the idea of sexual violence against white women (which Battat also talks about in terms of the Scottsboro case) in the face of the refusal to even acknowledge sexual violence against black women. Battat draws on the life of black feminist Pauli Murray for her elaborations on the figure of the hobo, draws her examples of “girl hobos” from her archive, and later uses them to contextualize the relationship between the labor movement and civil rights in Elizabeth Catlett’s work, referring to her recurring presence without sustained attention to her work. Murray appears as “the African American woman mentioned earlier” (21), and then “the African American woman hobo discussed in chapter 1” (109). Does Murray haunt this less-than-intersectional work? Ayesha Hardison might suggest that the contours of Jane Crow, the matrix of racism and sexism that black women experience, are exactly what allow Murray to be a figure convenient in order to make multiple points, but too complicated to discuss fully in Battat’s work.This exact matrix of intersectional violence shapes Hardison’s Writing through Jane Crow. Hardison looks at how literature centering black women in the mid-twentieth century takes on intersectional oppression before the further articulations of the Civil Rights and Black Feminist movements, and creates precedents from which later liberation texts benefit. Hardison gives sustained attention to Murray’s autobiography and points out how Murray’s insistence on the simultaneity of sexism and racism, while carefully eliding her own lifelong struggle with her sexuality and gender identity, typifies the limits, challenges, and possibilities of the time period characterized by Jane Crow. This text is a breakthrough, offering Murray’s analysis to justify and enact readings of several underread texts by many of the most important writers of the period, including Hurston, Gwendolyn Brooks, Petry, and Wright. Connecting Hurston’s Seraph on the Suwanee (1948) to her first short story “Drenched in Light” (1924) and her autobiography (1942) to question the complexity of white patronage for black women artists is a transformative move. Ultimately, through her nuanced readings of The Street, Dorothy West’s The Living is Easy (1948), and other texts, Hardison arrives at a depiction of Jane Crow as not simply an intersection, but a disaster flooding the lives of black women in a manner that destroys lives, suppresses manuscripts, forces hurtful compromises, and demands incredible creativity.In The Other Blacklist, Mary Helen Washington, known for her crucial list-making work in her multiple anthologies of and about black women writers, offers another disaster in the lives of black artists: explicit state surveillance. Drawing on the FBI Freedom of Information Act files of several black artists, including Brooks, Alice Childress, and Lorraine Hansberry, Washington offers a countersurveillance, or what Steve Mann might call a sousveillance. Deciding to go back and overhear the conversations about black radicalism and communism that she did not notice as a child growing up in an anticommunist climate, she offers that reckoning with the direct and implicit connections between black artists and the Communist Party may be important for contemporary radical artists. Communist-contextualized portraits of the artists she chooses to profile offer ways of rereading classic works, and her chapter on spycraft and the CIA-funded “First Negro Writers Conference” is terrifying and revolutionary, as it reveals the repressive state to be one of the most consistent and attentive readers of African American literature in the twentieth century.As they describe the multiple disasters contextualizing black art and life in the mid-twentieth century in the United States, none of these texts escape the disastrous impacts of the flow of ideological, physical, and state violence. And the disaster is not over.

title: The place of short stories in modernist fiction
abstract: It is especially noteworthy that many of the short stories and short stories collections written during the early to mid-twentieth century take place in a single town or city designated by the author. The place setting may be fictitious, like that of Sherwood Anderson’s Winesburg and William Faulkner’s Yoknapatawpha or in the case of Joyce’s Dubliners, an actual city. By virtue of the fact that they take place within the confines of a single location, these short stories already deceive readers from the beginning by providing them with a false expectation of unity and coherence. In actuality, the only unifying aspect of these short stories, besides their static background is the fact that their characters are all in one way or another, dealing with their own demons. They neither notice nor acknowledge the pain and suffering of their fellow townsmen. The utter alienation that the each of the characters experiences prevents them from reaching out to one another, thus, creating a cavernous sense of disconnect and loss within the community. \n\tAccording to author and critic, Michael Levenson, “crisis is inevitably the central term in discussion” during the Modernism period (Cambridge Companion 4). One of the ways in which modernist works explore this “crisis” brought about by the deteriorating “stabilities of society, religion and culture” (Stallworthy and Ramazani 1828), is by conveying the deep-seated scepticism of man towards the belief that “the world, things, and selves were knowable” (1838), and that they have a fixed meaning, which can be represented with absolute certainty. As such, this essay will explore the inherent cynicism in short stories by examining and drawing attention to the paradoxical nature of the short story as a traditionally realist form, the universal loneliness of man and the irreconcilable discrepancy between language and reality. These are fundamental features that make short stories invaluable and relevant to the Modernism period where there is a distinct propensity to capture the inherent meaninglessness of life and the profound sense of disengagement one experiences in spite of living in such a physically interconnected world.

title: Speaking American
venue: American book review/The American book review
abstract: Speaking American Gayle Rogers (bio) Accented America: The Cultural Politics of Multilingual Modernism Joshua L. Miller Oxford University Press www.globaloup,com 432 Pages; Print, $26.95 Modernist literature is famous for its multilingual experiments: Ezra Pound’s The Cantos (1917–69) contains everything from Provençal fragments to Chinese characters; James Joyce’s Ulysses (1922) asks its reader to know at least a half-dozen tongues (and his Finnegans Wake [1939] is not even in any single language); and T. S. Eliot’s The Waste Land (1922) concludes with a jumble of quotations from works in five different languages. Scholars have spent decades studying and theorizing the origins of this impulse: the modern metropolis and its cacophony of languages, the apex and disintegration of European imperialism, or a writerly elitism aimed at alienating the mass of common readers. Joshua Miller’s Accented America proposes a new historical context for multilingual modernism—one specific to the American condition yet pertinent to reading modernist works from beyond the US. American modernism, he notes, arose in the face of a powerful nativist and English–only movement. In the early 1900s, America was transformed from a country in which the diverse tongues of its immigrant populations were accepted to one in which they were suppressed or outlawed. Theodore Roosevelt declared in 1907, “We have room for but one language here [in this country], and that is the English language, for we intend to see that the crucible turns our people out as Americans, of American nationality, and not as dwellers in a polyglot boardinghouse.” Bilingual schools in places like Louisiana were closed, and translations had to be screened by authorities; German was demonized as the language of the enemy, while Russian was feared as a subversive, insurrectionist tongue. Modernists, Miller argues, took arms against this trend by twisting and contorting English, pushing it to new regions, and experimenting with its own limits by staging its collisions with America’s “other” languages. The influential literary critic H. L. Mencken theorized an “American language” that was, as Miller writes, “lexically dynamic but racially stable,” grounded in the diverse tongues that formed the “American experience” but subsumed and assimilated by a hegemonic whiteness. The figures that Miller analyzes, including the American novelists Gertrude Stein, John Dos Passos, Jean Toomer, Henry Roth, and Nella Larsen, along with the Anglophone Filipino Carlos Bulosan and the Mexican American Américo Paredes, defamiliarized this version of American English as a means of resisting, among other things, the model of uniform citizenship that Roosevelt and others elaborated. Furthermore, they used literature to “crystalliz[e] popular opinion and...to inform the beliefs and practices of future communities of readers”—readers who might understand the socio-political processes that had “contrived” the apparently natural evolution of their American vernaculars. In multiform ways, these authors “made geographical and linguistic dislocations central to their self-reflexively internationalist narrative idioms.” For its range, its incisiveness, its persuasive argument, and its stylistic elegance, Miller’s book is an impressive achievement. It is bracketed by two moments of America’s political internationalism: 1898 and 1945. In the former year, the US launched its overseas empire and acquired territories of non-English-speaking peoples; in the latter, it consolidated its global influence with further military engagements abroad but all but stopped its official period of territorial expansion. The writers he treats found themselves on the various margins of the new US empire; they were, by and large, political leftists and anti-imperialists, and they bemoaned what Dos Passos characterized as the mechanized, homogeneous style of literature that had come to reign during this period of American history. They employed everything from jarring syntax (Stein) to code-switching (Toomer, Larsen) to broken English (Roth) to Spanglish (Paredes) in order to disrupt the blanketing effect of what Miller aptly dubs “linguistic nationalism.” In other words, they implicitly traced and counteracted the reduction of America’s “Englishes” to one “English,” which was at the time called “Anglo-Saxon” English. In examining the “transformative energy” that modernist experimentalism and “multilingual and vernacular cultural expression” infused one another, Miller himself harnesses a critical energy that shines in his brilliant account. title: Her Own Spook: Colorism, Vision, and the Dark Female Body
abstract: This chapter concentrates on colorism's deployment of vision to mark and decipher difference and value. It considers the two plays about colorism by black women playwrights—Dael Orlandersmith's Yellowman and Zora Neale Hurston's Color Struck—which were part of a tradition of work by black women that covers color/gender/class distinctions among blacks. These plays revealed how visuality is interlaced with narrative in the medium of theatre. and, in addition, presented insights into the visual and psychic effect and affect of the state-sanctioned system of colorism. Hurston's play and the scholarship on Color Struck were useful for engaging Yellowman's depiction of the traumatic relationship between vision and black female corporeality due to colorism. In the world of Yellowman, it was a totalizing system where one must kill her/his kinship to escape the legacy of black-on-black terror and the visual regime that regulates relations of alienation.

title: Joseph Brodsky and T.S. Eliot
abstract: Joseph Brodsky's critical essays, Less Than One (1986) and On Grief and Reason (1995), provide the necessary context for his long Russian poem Verses on the Death of T. S. Eliot. Brodsky-who's also written elegies on John Donne, W. H. Auden and Robert Lowell-explains, with characteristic wit, his personal attraction to this kind of poetry at time when wasn't quite real to him: was young then and therefore particularly keen on elegies as genre, having nobody around dying to write one for. So 1 read them perhaps more avidly than anything else. He soon realized that contemplating an author's made him aware of his own mortality: most interesting feature of the genre was the authors' unwitting attempts at self-portrayal with which nearly every poem 'in memoriam' is strewn--or soiled. He adds that death as theme always produces self-portrait. Remembering his exile by the Soviet government and fear of an early from heart disease at the time he wrote his elegy on Eliot, Brodsky insists, there is nothing more moving than an alienated man resorting to But he also believes that by writing elegies poets learn to shift the focus to their subjects and exclude themselves from thoughts of death. Like his heroine and mentor, Anna Akhmatova, he continues to address the dead as though they were alive. (1) Finally, he says that poems about the dead revive them and make them as real as when they were living: Elegy is retrospective genre, the most common of all poetic genres. The reason for this, in part, is the natural human feeling that our life becomes truly real only after the fact, that moving pen across piece of paper is, strictly chronologically, also retrospective process. (2) Brodsky, not influenced by as he was by Auden and Lowell, is surprisingly critical of the older poet. Alluding to Pound's Cantos and to the notes in The Waste Land, he writes that unlike number of his illustrious contemporaries, Frost never wears his learning on his sleeve. (3) ... can be shrugged off.... is outwardly obscure, so he obviates the reader's need to think (4)--the scholarly notes, he feels, provide the explanation. Quoting Eliot's quotation in The Waste Land_of the Burial of the Dead service in The Book of Common Prayer--I will show you fear in handful of dust--Brodsky scornfully asserts that needs the minatory presence of a handful of dust to perceive terror. (5) His dislike of Eliot's pedantic and allusive technique blinds him to the impact of this marvelous quote. But he also admires for making the vital connection, in his essay on Metaphysical Poets (1921), between himself and John Donne, between seventeenth and twentieth century poetry: Eliot was one of the first to point out the similarity between modernist and metaphysical poets; he saw modernism as contemporary manifestation of baroque sensibility. (6) Sentenced to forced labor and exiled in the Arctic Circle when died on January 4,1965, Brodsky did not learn of his until week later, but completed the poem within day after hearing the news. title: T.S. Eliot's Virtual Europe: The Flaneur and the Textual Flanerie
abstract: I. Introduction T. S. Eliot repeatedly shifted from one urban culture to another: from St. Louis to Boston, from Harvard to the Sorbonne, from Paris to London, and from Marburg to Oxford. The trajectory of Eliot's urban detour finally settles down in London, and Eliot's choice of living in London remains his signature effort to attuned to the total phenomenon and sensibility of the age, resolute advance to the city as the primary solution to the oscillation between social and intellectual conflict. However, Eliot is less traveling poet than an avowed collector who abandons nothing en route, be it Shakespeare, Homer, or the rock drawing of the Magdalenian draughtsmen. (1) Of all the intellectuals writing in the first great heyday of modernism, in my view it is Eliot who turns out to be the one who speaks most eloquently to the postmodernist sense of de-centralization, fragmentation, syncretism, hybridization, and indeterminacy. Though professed anglo-catholic (Eliot's own uncapitalized terms, see Eliot's preface to For Lancelot Andrewes vii), Eliot includes unorthodox, un-Christian, and even seemingly incompatible elements in his works. Though great defender of tradition, Eliot is interested in the artist as alien and he aspires to maintain the role of foreigner with integrity, to be perpetual outsider with a source of authority (Eliot, Turgenev 172; qtd. in Jeffreys 400). Eliot's life as literary Baedeker is devoted to re/mapping Europe and European culture/literature imbued with alternate otherness, diversity, and heterogeneity: It is the final perfection, the perfection, the consummation of the American to become, not an Englishman, but European--something which no born European, no person of any European nationality can become (Eliot, Memory of Henry James 1). As John G. Cawelti points out, exile is both central theme and characteristic biographical pattern of artistic modernism (38). With Eliot, exile was both voluntary and involuntary: it began before he was born, was repeated early in his life, and then became his own chosen way of life. Eliot's forefather, Andrew Eliott, emigrated around 1668-1669 from East Coker, Somerset, to New (Massachusetts, Bay Colony), America. Eliot's grandfather, William Greenleaf Eliot, left New for St. Louis in 1834, where he established Unitarian Church and founded Washington University. His father and mother brought the family back to the North Shore every summer, and in 1896 built substantial house at Eastern Point, Gloucester, Massachusetts. In retrospect, Eliot is heard confessing sense of alienation and displacement caused by such complicated familial background: perceived that I myself had always been New Englander in the South West, and South Westerner in New England (Eliot's Preface to Edgar A. Mowrer's This American World). In 1906, Eliot entered Harvard and remained there until he took his B.A. in 1909 and M.A. in 1910. Peter Ackroyd presumes that Eliot must have felt that he was not perfectly educated at Harvard, and that Eliot may have recognized--as most Bostonians did--the narrowness of the horizon (Ackroyd 39), for he eventually persuaded his father to subsidize his first trip to Europe in October 1910. He stayed mainly in Paris until July 1911, attended lectures at the Sorbonne University, and visited Italy and briefly. Having been given Sheldon Travelling Fellowship, which Harvard offered him to return to Europe in 1914, Eliot arrived in London by mischance in August 1914. The First World War made him an exile just as he had begun his study at the University of Marburg. Eliot stayed in London until the Michaelmas term at Oxford began in October, and then he took refuge in Merton College to begin work under Harold Joachim. Eliot took the first step of self-imposed exile in June 1915 when he married Vivienne Haigh-Wood on impulse at the Hampstead Registry Office, which shocked and agitated his parents. …

title: Violence and the Hearth: Lynching and Resistance in Go Down, Moses
abstract: EDWARD CLOUGH University of East Anglia Violence and the Hearth: Lynching and Resistance in Go Down, Moses I THROUGHOUT HIS MID-CAREER WORKS, FAULKNER REPEATEDLY RETURNED to the same scene: a black child and a white child, raised together, come to sense their racial, and so social, difference. Their intimacy is broken, and with it their innocence, and the two become irrevocably estranged. This discovery of racial difference marks the end of childhood, and its loss haunts Faulkner’s white protagonists, much as it clearly haunted his own mind. Again and again—in The Unvanquished (1938), Intruder in the Dust (1948), or his semi-fictional article “Mississippi” (1954)— Faulkner reenacted this primal rupture, as though compelled by some nostalgic impulse toward some lost childhood innocence, some lost security of home. Yet he directly depicted this as a single, definable moment of rupture only once, in the Go Down, Moses (1942) story “The Fire and the Hearth,” where it resonates with particular poignancy amid the novel’s larger themes of possession and loss. Roth Edmonds, the son of white planter Zack Edmonds, and Henry Beauchamp,thesonofblacktenant-farmerLucasBeauchamp,havebeen raised together as “foster-brothers,” nursed together at Henry’s mother’s breast following the death of Roth’s mother in childbirth; they are also, as a result of their mutual ancestor Carothers McCaslin’s rape of his slaves, distant kinsmen. The two boys hunt together, share food at the same table, sleep in the same beds, treat one another’s homes as “interchangeable” (GDM 85). In particular, Roth loves the hearth in Henry’s home, an open fire that Henry’s father, Lucas, has kept burning constantly since his wedding-night, and in which Roth finds a source of “centering” order, a source of life. One day, at the age of seven, Roth suddenly becomes aware of their racial difference; he takes the bed, and makes Henry sleep on a pallet on the floor. When Roth awakes the next morning, still wracked with grief and a “shame he would not admit,” he finds the pallet empty and Henry wordlessly departed. “They never slept in the same room again and never again ate at the same table,” Faulkner writes, “because he admitted 392 Edward Clough to himself it was shame now” (87). This is Roth’s moment of irreversible action, then—but significantly, it is not his moment of actual loss. For a month Roth distances himself from Henry until eventually, wracked with guilt and shame that he cannot adequately articulate, he finally goes to Henry’s home. In a clumsy attempt to undo his past actions, Roth tells Henry’s family that he is staying for dinner, and for a brief, blissful few moments, he is able to believe that his relationship with Henry has been restored, that “it was as if it had never happened at all” (87). But when he is called for dinner, he finds that Henry’s family has already eaten separately, and the table has been laid for him alone. “Are you ashamed to eat when I eat?” Roth tearfully confronts Henry. “I aint shamed of nobody,” is Henry’s mild, devastating reply. “Not even me” (88). The episode’s power arises through its depiction of the collision of two worlds: the formative, resonant spaces of childhood and the structured spaces of Southern adult society. The loss of innocence and stability is at the same time the creation of order, and the intimate and seemingly neutral spaces of domesticity—the bed, the meal-table, the hearth—become reconstituted not simply as scenes of instruction, but as the highly political divisions between private and social that they have always been. By forcing Henry to sleep alone on the pallet below, Roth vertically asserts his new hierarchical consciousness. Yet by eating the same food at the same table as Roth, but at different times, Henry’s family horizontally undermines this same hierarchy—quite literally turning the tables on him.
