title: T. S. Eliot and Organicism by Jeremy Diaper (review)
abstract: Reviewed by: T. S. Eliot and Organicism by Jeremy Diaper Philip Irving Mitchell T. S. Eliot and Organicism. By Jeremy Diaper. Clemson, SC: Clemson University Press, 2021. ISBN 978-1-80085-961-8. Pp. xiii + 218. $44.95. Jeremy Diaper wants to convince readers that agrarian concerns are more central to T. S. Eliot's prose and poetry than many have assumed, and he mostly succeeds in that purpose. Diaper makes the case that agrarian and organicist ideals and motifs are spread throughout Eliot's work, especially in the 1930s and 1940s, and that this is reflective of a growing, nuanced understanding. Eliot neither romanticized rural life, nor did he reject the strengths of the urban world. Instead, he advocated for a balance of the two with some individuals dwelling predominately in one or the other, but both being teachable and subject to correction. This included for Eliot a defense of rural autonomy in some things, for the rural world did not need the urban to teach it culture. Given that the organicism movement in Britain eventually faded, one can ask whether Eliot finally held these convictions in a life-changing way, or were they perhaps more ideals that he explored for a season? The cover of T. S. Eliot and Organicism, for instance, features a photograph of Eliot proudly displaying a loaf of homemade bread which he baked at Pike's Farm in 1933. Is this an amusing exception, or something indicative of a more constant concern in Eliot's career? [End Page 461] While Diaper will admit that Eliot's emphasis on organic ideals, like much of his social criticism, became softer in the 1950s, he nonetheless argues that Eliot continued to hold to organicist values, in part because Eliot idealized from rather early on certain aspects of rural life and the natural world. Diaper begins to build his case for Eliot's life-long concern on what some might see as more shaky ground. He argues that in the early poetry, especially in The Waste Land, imagery of wasted places, both of the city and the desert, foreshadow an organicist concern with poor food and land misuse, as well as with general displacement and lack of physical, social, and spiritual rootedness. Eliot's early interest in James Frazer's The Golden Bough can suggest that the parched imagery of The Waste Land still has the potential for a spiritual renewal. This is true as well of "The Hollow Men": "This is the dead land/This is cactus land/… The supplication of a dead man's hand/Under the twinkle of a fading star" (qtd. 9). The urban world is often the banal world, and since Eliot would come to have a concern with culinary skill and healthy cuisine, it is possible to see these early poetic images as either indicative of a nascent concern or at least as preparatory in an imaginative way. Diaper likewise connects this concern to Eliot's dramatic spectacle, The Rock. There, Eliot explores the connection between Christian faith, agriculture, and the opportunity for cultural revitalization: "When the field is tilled/ And the wheat is bread/They shall not die in a shortened bed/ And a narrow sheet" (qtd. 31). In other words, The Waste Land may be said to prepare for The Rock, and what was implicit now becomes explicit. Diaper is on more solid ground when he focuses on Eliot's social criticism, and he explores how Eliot's Criterion was often a center for discussing the ideas and texts of key organic movement leaders, including Viscount Lymington, R. G. Stapledon, Montague Fordham, and K. E. Barlow. Both the Commentary and the Books of the Quarter sections of the Criterion are important for measuring awareness of organic ideas. In Commentaries, Eliot wrote in defense of countryside that should be preserved and of the need for healthy foodstuffs not only for rural communities but also urban ones. Eliot also advocated for a close alliance between agriculture and church. This included shared concerns with historian Christopher Dawson's call for a cultural recovery of the spiritual principle that informs both social and organic/economic life. title: Rachael Gilmour . Bad English: Literature, Multilingualism and the Politics of Language in Contemporary Britain
abstract: An elusive subfield has taken shape over the past 20 years, focused on literary writing in non-standard and experimental Englishes. With our pockets bulging with borrowed linguistic terms, literary critics have given new attention to Anglophone multiplicity and the dilemmas of vernacular representation. This constellation is hard to define, but (disparate) touchstones might include Evelyn Nien-Ming Ch’ien’s Weird English (2004), Dohra Ahmad’s Rotten English: A Literary Anthology (2007) and Matthew Hart’s Nations of Nothing But Poetry (2010). Buoyed by the mainstreaming of postcolonial critique, these scholars are especially drawn to codes of otherness and belonging generated through linguistic estrangement. Viewed in this frame, fascinating parallels begin to crackle between (say) Hugh MacDiarmid, Zora Neale Hurston and Junot Díaz, without revoking the specificities of their aims and techniques. Although energized by transnational writing, criticism in this niche tends to follow established contours of modernist and American literary studies, from Michael North’s The Dialect of Modernism (1994) to Joshua L. Miller’s Accented America (2011). British and Irish writers are recognized as important figures in the remaking of English as a global literary language (from Linton Kwesi Johnson to Roddy Doyle and Irvine Welsh), but with the exception of Scotland there have been few sustained attempts to ground this writing in UK political context. This is the path-breaking achievement of Rachael Gilmour’s Bad English. This brilliant study is a compelling advance for the inchoate field of ‘Other English’ criticism, but is also a major contribution to scholarship on contemporary British literature, postcolonial studies and translation theory.

title: Re-Visiting T.S. Eliot’s Poetry through Henri Lefebvre’s Rhythmanalysis
venue: Celal Bayar Üniversitesi Sosyal Bilimler Dergisi
abstract: This paper explores the elements of rhythm in the social space in T.S. Eliot’s early poems and The Waste Land. One of the leading literary figures of the modernist era, Eliot dealt with the representation of the alienated individual within the boundary of the upper-middle class which can be followed especially in “The Lovesong of J. Alfred Prufrock.” Regarding the theoretical context of the study, Henri Lefebvre’s rhythmanalysis theory is applied to reveal how Eliot observed, understood and listened to the rhythms of city life. While observing people within the culture of the city, Eliot listened to the mechanisms present in this space. However, his concern of space and sound did not follow a single route, yet led to a wide, universal level. Thus, this paper intends to display Eliot’s perception of rhythm in his poems from the perspective of Lefebvre’s rhythmanalysis.

title: Mark Sandy . Transatlantic Transformations of Romanticism: Aesthetics, Subjectivity and the Environment.
abstract: Mark Sandy has written a ghost story. This is a book in which the influence of British Romanticism on American literature is described in terms of haunting, echo and poetic resonance. Sandy argues that American writers performed a failed and somewhat half-hearted, exorcism. He suggests that they used their Romantic inheritance to fashion an aesthetic of self and nature that appeared to be—and wanted to be—more independent and existentially charged than that of their British forbears. And yet, in the very act of trying to defeat the spectre of influence, they confronted kindred spirits and ‘summoned those spectres of alienation, disconnection and solipsism that already stalked and were latent within, earlier Romantic concepts of the aesthetic, subjectivity and nature.’ The result, Sandy argues, was something of a double haunting: a confrontation with the spectre of British Romantic writing that manifested as a ghostly self-reflexive feeling of alienation. The central conceits of haunting, echo and resonance speak strongly to Sandy’s methodology. This is not a book that traces specific points of influence and dissonance by way of readings, meetings, friendships and historical contexts. Readers looking for a more concrete and historically focused understanding of transatlantic cultures of exchange might justifiably be frustrated by the way in which Sandy’s extended discussion of Romantic ‘echo’ and ‘presence’ eschews new investigation into specific contexts of reading and reception. But for those looking for a broader understanding of the ways that Romantic ideas of nature have registered in the prose and poetry of a select number of American writers, this book will certainly add something. Following the introduction, Sandy moves to a reassessment of the well-known British Romantic influence on Emerson and Thoreau, discussing ‘the poetic presences of Byron, Shelley and Keats’ as ‘important touchstones’ in the representation of interactions between self and world. In a concluding section to the chapter, Sandy devotes a couple of pages to the Keatsian influence on Whitman and Dickinson—to whom he also returns at the end of the book. In covering such broad ground, Sandy gives us a feel for transatlantic connectedness—finding particular mileage in the expansive Keatsian concept of ‘negative capability’. In fact, Keats seems such an important figure in Sandy’s reading that one does wonder whether a book about Keats’ literary reception in America might have told a more incisive story of poetic and cultural influence. Chapter three opens a new section entitled ‘Subjects in Nature’ and makes a sudden jump to the twentieth century and the influence of Keats on F. Scott Fitzgerald. Sandy argues that Fitzgerald’s fictive mode ‘is itself an exercise in Keats’ negatively capable poetics’. Sandy finds productive parallels between Keatsian negative capability and Fitzgerald’s treatment of self-dissolution and interior space, describing the Romantic self as a disenchanted journey home, an act of mourning for a lost imaginary world that resonated in a post-war context. But, while the discussion of selfhood is illuminating, ‘nature’ remains a rather vague idea in this chapter, and Fitzgerald perhaps an odd choice to illuminate its meaning. Chapter four moves the discussion to Wordsworthian shadows and Byronic shades in William Faulkner. Like negative capability, shadow-play allows Sandy to be suggestive and the reading of resonance—for example, of Wordsworth’s Idiot Boy in Benjy Compson—is often revealing and persuasive. Part Three, titled ‘Fictional Selves and Nature’, moves to chapters on Saul Bellow and Toni Morrison. Sandy admits that he is selective in his choice of material—and there is no reason why he should have been comprehensive. But the rationale for selection does remain rather obscure, and at this point the balletic geographical and historical leaps and the seemingly interchangeable use of ‘nature’ and ‘environment’ did start to feel a little frustrating. It matters so much to Bellow that he is a city writer—like Augie March, ‘Chicago born’—and his frustration with Romanticism is so closely connected to what he saw as the sham Romanticism of mid-twentieth-century American counterculture and his anxiety about groupthink as an echo of Nazi terror that it seems odd to read his interest in Romantic selfhood so entirely without this cultural and historical context. The chapter on Morrison was fresher to me, and there is no doubt that Sandy produces some individually insightful close readings, but I would have liked more overall logic and rationale for selection—even if just on grounds of personal taste, interest and value. The book ends with a surprising return to the nineteenth century and a discussion of Dickinson and Whitman, which then extends to Wallace Stevens. This deliberately ahistorical structure is consistent with Sandy’s approach, emphasizing ghostly points of contact, resonance and divergence rather than telling a particular story of transatlantic exchange that is culturally and historically situated. Sandy ends by quoting Stevens’s chiasmic assertion that: ‘The enigmatical beauty / Of each beautiful enigma / Becomes amassed in a total double-thing’. He concludes: for post-Romantic poetics, this enigmatic ‘double-thing’, comprising the sacred and the profane, perceived and created, the real and non-real, the something and nothing, constitutes our elusory and inescapable sense of self, beauty, death and nature.

title: Living Through the In-Between: T. S Eliot’s Philosophy of Human Existence
abstract: This research paper aims to highlight the philosophical perspective of T. S. Eliot on the existence of modern human beings on earth. The recurring meaninglessness and alienation expressed in the poems “The Waste Land” and “The Hollow Man” are discussed based on the context in which the poet correlateswith the reality experienced by the people. The encroachment of modernity of the twentieth-century civilization points to the loss of individual traditions, rootlessness and disorientation. The perpetual enquiries on the binaries are negated through the introduction of the intermediary space of existence. Certain vocabulary used in the poems throws light onto the existence of the poetic subjects in their in-between states referring to the presence of neither/nor situations. The fundamental nature of the reality and existence characterised by Eliot is revealed through the analysis of the poems as an experience of identity crisis amidst the politico-social situations leading to uncertain, anxious and ambiguous states of living. The paper concludes with the discovery of liminality and liminal existence of the poetic subjects that represent the existence of human beings regardless of time and place.

title: “Unreal City”: The Image of the City in T. S. Eliot’s Poetry
abstract: As a modernist poet writing in London during World War I and in the postwar period, Eliot takes the City of London as the background of his poems and presents a bleak image of the city through his lines.In "The love song of J. Alfred Prufrock" and in "The waste land" the reader follows the poet personae through the streets of London by experiencing each element that defines London as Eliot gives life to the city by personifying its elements such as the London fog.The image of the city in Modernist literature is always a pessimistic one and this is not only the result of the Great War and its aftermath but also an image that is borrowed from late nineteenth-century concerns in literature such as industrialization, migration to the big city, crowded and suffocating city life, and so on.However, modernist literature also depicts a conflicting relationship between the metropolis and the modern individual in which one closely identifies with the city but feels alienated in it at the same time.This paper aims to discuss that the city has its own life and character created by the language used to describe the city by Eliot, and endeavours to scrutinize the conflicting nature of the individual's relation to the big city, which s/he both antagonizes and identifies with in Eliot's poetry.

title: The Wasteland of the Modern Soul: Symbolism and Myth in the Literary Works of T.S. Eliot
venue: International journal of humanities and social science invention.
abstract: T.S. Eliot created the Modernist poetic style through his complex and innovative use of symbols together with his "mythic method" approach. This article provides a rigorous examination of how Eliot weaponized these literary tools to navigate the profound spiritual, cultural, and ontological fragmentation which emerged during the postWorld War I period. The study investigates his artistic development from The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock which used "objective correlative" techniques to represent urban alienation to The Waste Land which employed multiple mythological elements and finally to Four Quartets which used sacred liturgical symbols. The study demonstrates that Eliot's entire body of work serves as a crucial connection between the spoiled historical past and the ongoing quest for eternal spiritual truth. The analysis centersonEliot's fundamental conviction about myth which he believed creates an ongoing link between present-day life and ancient times. Myth functions as a structural framework which supports the vast display of present-day historical events that exhibit both uselessness and disorder. The study investigates the impact of French Symbolism and Cambridge Ritualists on Eliot's symbolic system which he developed to show his personal emotional struggles through symbols that represent human experiences. Through its exploration of modernity's "broken images" and traditional stories' unifying force the article demonstrates thatEliot's mythopoetic method served as the foundational basis for mid-century philosophers who studied faith and time. The research shows thatEliot created his own modern poetic language through historical symbols which he used to express his vision beyond the urgent problems of his time.

title: Palimpsests and Doubles: Echoes of The Rubáiyát in T. S. Eliot's Poetry after Vinnie-Marie D'Ambrosio
venue: The Journal of the Midwest Modern Language Association
abstract: Palimpsests and Doubles:Echoes of The Rubáiyát in T. S. Eliot's Poetry after Vinnie-Marie D'Ambrosio Russell Brickey (bio) In his 1933 Norton Lecture "The Use of Poetry and the Use of Criticism,"1 T. S. Eliot related the following anecdote to explain his emergence as a poet: I can recall clearly enough the moment when, at the age of fourteen or so, I happened to pick up a copy of Fitzgerald's [sic] Omar which was lying about, and the almost overwhelming introduction to a new world of feeling which this poem was the occasion of giving me. It was like a sudden conversion; the world appeared anew, painted with bright, delicious and painful colours. (25) Eliot's anecdote was by no means recondite, but its significance was never truly evaluated until Vinnie-Marie D'Ambrosio's 1989 Eliot Possessed: T. S. Eliot and FitzGerald's Rubáiyát. D'Ambrosio takes T. S. Eliot's brief recollection about Edward FitzGerald's The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, The Astronomer Poet of Persia and traces the putative effect of the medieval Persian-cum-Victorian [End Page 79] poem on Eliot's seminal modernist poetry. D'Ambrosio's thesis is fairly succinct: The themes that the Rubáiyát shares with The Waste Land are fruitful to explore: sterility and fertility, isolation and alienation, time, the questioning attitude, power, the ambiguity of the "you" address. A few of the many symbols shared, but transformed by Eliot's forceful originality, are the waste, the desert, washing rituals, Nothingness, broken images, rebirth after burial, wind, Procne, checkerboard games. Even structural parallels exist, though transformed. (182) Simply put, The Rubáiyát seems to have given Eliot his poetic instinct, an instinct that follows a "good writers borrow" process rather than the "great writers steal" dictate that Eliot espoused. This paper compares these aspects of FitzGerald's aesthetic and Eliot's later poetry, as well as their relation to their literary progenitor, Omar Khayyám, who by the time of FitzGerald's Rubáiyát was more legendary construct and caricature than actual author. Buried in history and revived by concepts that are untrammeled Orientalism, the Omar of the poem (as opposed to the real Omar Khayyám designated by his full name in this paper) rails against Persian aristocracy, petty bureaucracy, and Sufism, but the true subject matter is civilization itself. The Rubáiyát is about humanity, even if the ostensible marriage between Victorian England and medieval Persia is the implied provenance. In the same way that "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" describes St. Louis or that The Waste Land invokes post–World War II Europe or that both could be set in London, The Rubáiyát evokes a specific landscape, depending on the reader's lens, or it can represent the world. As there are many readership communities in action at any one time, the onus of meaning falls on which fiction the community believes—the poem belongs to either the country of origin or the world at large—and thus both readings depend on how the community views the authors. This is a long way around to suggest that the authorial fallacy is unusually strong in these poems and that the patrilineal relationship between these poets is more pronounced than is usually the case. [End Page 80] With its great geographic, literary, and temporal leaps, the continuum between these poets suggests two doublings: the Imaginary-Double of Omar Khayyám when reinscribed by Edward FitzGerald's pseudotranslation (which FitzGerald referred to as "transmogrification" and which is often referred to as "FitzOmar" in critical literature today) and the Obscured-Double of FitzOmar within Eliot's poetry—a Double who speaks through the author, in this case a historical parent-author, from behind a textual veil. The Imaginary-Double (as I am using the term here) begins with a falsified literary source, initially presented as fact, that allows the actual author-translator-transcriber to speak with the assumed authority of a spurious historical figure. The Imaginary-Double can work only with a fiction of original source material. Readers must accept, no matter...

title: Inability of Self-expression in the Selected Works of Eliot and Anderson
abstract: At first glance, T. S. Eliot and Sherwood Anderson do not seem to have much in common when their works are considered.Eliot is known primarily for his poetry and Anderson for his short stories.The former is often considered an English author and the latter an American one.The first is one of the most recognizable names of Modernism, and the second is often considered a realist.Eliot is known for the complexity and inaccessibility of his poetry and Anderson's works appear much simpler in comparison.Eliot is famous for his urban imagery and Anderson for his rural setting.However, there is one theme they have in common: the exploration of an individual's inability of self-expression in his surroundings, where the expression is affected by materialistic, artistic, sexual or other issues with accompanying repressions.This desire for self-expression or self-realization contrasts with the mores of one's society and their failed attempts to express themselves bring along depression, frustration, repression and alienation, something that both Eliot and Anderson knew well, because they also struggled with some of the issues of their protagonists.An important notion here is that the exploration of this inability seems to suggest its universality or ubiquity, regardless if the individual is living in a big city or a small rural community.Upon closer analysis of these themes, the differences start to fade and other connections appear, such as Eliot's use of the caricature or grotesque to heighten certain states of mind, something that Anderson also does;FILOZOFSKI_Hum_22.indd 194 4.6.2020.20:22:57 195 prosinca 2019.indeed, the first story in his work Winesburg, Ohio is called Book of the Grotesque, but with a more sympathetic and less ironic flavour.Evening and night are very important times for both authors, as that is when an individual's introspection, mostly unconscious, is intensified.Social critique is very prominent and the compatibility of public and private lives is also explored.

title: Ulysses as Modern Prototype of Homo Viator
venue: Journal of Humanistic and Social Studies
abstract: This paper emphasises, through the notion of generic intertextuality, the Homeric inheritance in the literary modernity. Specific techniques of transtextual communication are employed to analyse how the myth of Odyssey was valued in modern literature, i.e. the novels of two emblematic writers, Joyce and Faulkner. In Ulysses, desacralisation is visible at all levels, but it does not eliminate the identity of the protagonists who are saved by their humanity. Soldiers’ Pay, a rewriting based on allusions to the myth of Odysseus, denies the perspective of recovery. Ulysses’ counterpart is an alienated being suffocated by the superficial world he lives in, an example of de-heroisation that modernity uses without restraint.

title: Imperialism and the Politics of Childhood Innocence in Peter Pan and Wendy
abstract: Imperialism and the Politics of Childhood Innocence in Peter Pan and Wendy Hyun-Joo Yoo (bio) Modernist writers such as Virginia Woolf, James Joyce, or T. S. Eliot reacted to World War I, industrialization, urbanization, immigration, and capitalism, which isolated and alienated individuals and pushed them into severe loneliness, by turning toward already existing modernist aesthetic as represented by painters, philosophers, and architects such as Salvador Dali, Henri Matisse, Friedrich Nietzsche, Henri Bergson, and Frank Lloyd Wright. Similarly, children's literature authors adopted literary techniques and thematic issues associated with Modernism in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. According to Kimberley Reynolds, who explores Modernism in children's literature in Left Out: The Forgotten Tradition of Radical Publishing for Children in Britain 1910–49, radical children's literature appeared in Britain between 1910 and 1949, influenced by "leftwing politics, modernist and avant-garde art and design, and progressive education" (10). Radical writers' works for children employed various modernist, experimental literary techniques such as multiple/unusual perspectives, streams of consciousness, two-dimensional and fragmented images/forms, anthropomorphism, carnivalesque reversal, collage effects, the mixing of registers, and open endings, as a way to disturb the dominant ideologies of capital and class (Reynolds 102–29). In Peter Pan and Wendy1 (1911), J. M. Barrie (1860–1937), like other British authors of children's literature in the modernist era, acknowledges the value of ambiguity, ambivalence, and disruptions in narrative, and consciously incorporates the complicated concerns and diverse devices of Modernism into his text. That is, Barrie effectively appropriates various sensibilities, perspectives, and experimental techniques of modernist artists on the narrative surface.2 Interestingly, however, when it comes to the deep thematic intent behind this simple story of children's adventure into an unknown world, Barrie seems to create the same world from [End Page 387] which he tries to escape in Peter Pan and Wendy—one that propagandizes the colonial ideology. Specifically, in Barrie's text, the crude imperialistic, white-supremacist, and capitalistic desire to brutally conquer the world and subjugate colonized peoples is filtered and purified through the immaculate innocence of the child and children's play and games. Far from being innocent fun, when seen through postcolonial and feminist perspectives, the activities of Peter and his comrades represent the experiences of the British Empire. I. Childhood Innocence Imperial ideologies take many forms, the most pernicious of which is the use of images of childhood innocence to perpetuate colonial oppression. If imperial conquests always begin with military intervention, they end with cultural intervention. And on the battlefield of ideas, an effective way for the dominant social class to wage war on the colonized is through children's culture, specifically the image of the child, whose innocence and goodness is made to justify the experiences and evils of imperialist thought and action. Nowhere is this more clearly evidenced than in Barrie's Peter Pan and Wendy. Superficially a supreme example of childhood innocence, Peter's play and games enact not just the business of empire, but the contradictions within colonial rule. To perpetuate the empire, the image of the innocent child as a vehicle for driving home the values of the ruling class must be constantly reconstructed, relived, and reexperienced each time as though it were new. But to remain a child, to refuse to grow up like Peter and thus constantly remain in a state of perpetual reconstruction does not immortalize the empire, but rather heralds its certain decay, for the child, like the empire, turns in on itself, feeds on itself, and destroys itself from within. Peter, "imprisoned by his inability to grow up" (Gilead 285), like the British Empire, forgets what he knows. Indeed, ironically, Peter must remember to forget, must reenact in children's games, play, and adventure that which he himself inevitably symbolizes: both the end and beginning of childhood innocence. In fact, as Marah Gubar points out, the inextricable association of children with innocence has not always been essential, but was only naturalized during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (123). It was philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–78) and Romantic poets such as William Blake (1757–1827) and William Wordsworth (1770–1850), who popularized the idea...

title: Bilingual Areas within the Territory of the Republic of Albania
abstract: This paper will be focused on the elements of religious utopia exposed in the novel “The Sound and the Fury” by William Faulkner, through the episode of Dilsey. In contrast to Quentin and Jason’s meaningless, decomposed perception of time, responsible for its perversity, Dilsey’s religious sensitivity transmits a systematic structure to the world because historic human awareness is recorded by God’s projection: all events are based on Christ’s Alpha and Omega. Religious myth utopia, anticipated by Dilsey in the last episode, achieves its climax in Shegog’s predication. Just like Dilsey, who varies from the characters of the novel with her positive utopia, even the positive utopia projected by the priest’s predication alters from the alienating caustic and mortal circumstances of the whole novel. Dilsey together with the church congregation were gathered to listen to this predication, living the joy of Easter in the novel. Shegog is a transmitter of God’s word, to touch people’s hearts and join them in a “collective dream” dedicated to the Easter celebration. The people in the church reached a small utopian dream, part of the big dream instigated by the myth of Christian religion. Impeding all negativities, the ritual enabled the unification of humanity in a common positive dream. This dream is responsible for the religious utopia in the novel. Through an empirical analysis of this episode, Dilsey, and the sermon, I will arrive to the point to present the elements of religious utopia involved in this part of the novel.

title: Making it Transitional
abstract: Late Victorian into Modern, an edited collection of 39 essays on British literature and culture between 1880 and 1920, is the latest book in Oxford University Press’s Twenty-First Century Approaches to Literature series. The series aims (according to its website) ‘to provoke rather than reassure, to challenge rather than codify’, and to ‘direct readers to areas of enlivened and unresolved debate’.1 Its newest installment does all this. The collection’s editors seek to bring together criticism that trains its focus on the transitional area between Victorian and modern, emphasizing the into and doing justice to the developments within the arts, sciences, politics, and society that were continuous across the four decades between 1880 and 1920. History, they and the scholars they gather remind us, does not politely stop to make neat boundaries. The guiding idea becomes legible in a change of voice: Marcus, Mendelssohn, and Shepherd-Barr state that their object is to open ‘the central paradoxes of a period constructed as at once radically new and very old, as modern and archaic, as a beginning and a fin’ (1). ‘A period constructed’ – by whom? By those who participated in it? By some of its participants but not others? By observers from (geographically) afar? Or by its later commentators? The collection offers an occasion to gain a clearer view into the constructive processes as they have developed over time, and as many different types of builders have taken to them. In their next sentence, Marcus, Mendelssohn, and Shepherd-Barr clarify the agent of their formerly passive construction: Their project is to attend to mid-points chronological and conceptual, to ‘the multiple centres around which this dynamic period constructed and constituted itself’ (1). The editors distinguish self-fashioning via a radical rupture from the past as a mode overtly manifested by early-twentieth-century artists – not a descriptive term, but a provocative, historicizable, ‘performative’ one (6). Thus they try to resist the term modernism, and instead explore the period’s modes and creations ‘in their own particular terms’ (1) and in their musings on ‘the question of what it means to perceive oneself as living in a transitional age’ (3). The first two sections (containing 10 essays in total) address and complicate one expected division of this period, named by the book’s title, between the chronologically earlier and later halves, and the Victorian and modern sensibilities they might, by some accounts, entail. Thus, the first section, Twilights, features essays that engage with models of 1880–1920 as a ‘decadent’ period that embraced nostalgia and decline. This section focuses on ways of looking backward, by means of medievalisms, Celticisms, and biological-psychological explanations of the death drive. Next follows the section Making it New which, by including several essays with definitional titles – ‘Cultures of the Avant-Garde’, ‘When Was Modernism?’, ‘What Was the ‘New Drama’?’, ‘Who Was the ‘New Woman’?’ – details the impartial ruptures and plentiful continuities across the twentieth century’s turn. The opening two orienting sections give way to groups of essays on Modes and Genres (exploring style and form in scientific romances, adventure, and detective stories); Sites and Spaces of Knowledge (interrogating the literary-critical currency of the terms science, the city, and empire); Political and Social Selves; Authorship, Aesthetics, and Print Cultures; and Technologies. The driving categories are intuitive but also feel fresh and surprising. They include cinema and telephony, motherhood and reproduction, sexualities, bodies and the machine, visual culture, race and biology, authorship, regionalism, reading and transmission, primitivism, time and space, selenography, technology, performance and theatricality. They place at centre stage innovations characteristic of the period, including its concerns with the occult, with quantum physics, with cosmopolitanism and imperialism. A key choice, pointed and potentially quite productive: the editors explain that they ‘have avoided author-based chapters, because the volume’s overarching strategy is to frame the period in terms of its networks, genres, and intellectual and cultural formations’ (4). Much of the book’s originality emerges in the way it highlights networks that include wide memberships, making individual authors visible as participants in a rich variety of cultural and aesthetic debates. Thus, for example, Joseph Conrad features (alongside Olive Schreiner and Rudyard Kipling) in Jarad Zimbler’s argument that novels of empire and colonialism rejected exotic adventure and romance despite their readers’ objections, but also (alongside a quite different set of companions including H. G. Wells, Virginia Woolf, D. H. Lawrence, and T. S. Eliot) in Rachel Crossland’s examination of the way scientific discoveries such as X-rays and radioactivity, the electron, and quantum theory induced literary ripples. Laurence Scott reveals Conrad (in The Secret Agent and in his collaboration with Ford Madox Ford) as a surprising colleague of Wells, Arthur Morrison, Arthur Machen, and Thomas Burke, who represented London as a city both overwhelmingly concrete and at the same time incompletely materialized, permeable to fourth dimensions that were capturing the imaginations of late-Victorian mathematicians and philosophers. And Benjamin Kohlmann, deftly revealing how thoroughly the economic thinking about welfare infused into the period’s literature, traces Conrad’s sympathies (in Chance and Nostromo) with critiques of laissez-faire economics in novels by Trollope, Gissing, Wells, and Forster. Taken together, these essays – and the permutations within the remaining essays – offer a rewarding refraction of cultural concerns into their author-specific variations, and make individual authors shimmer multifariously. The editors aim also to ‘grant new legibility’ to ‘“minor” genres such as parody and self-portrait that were familiar in their own time but from which recent criticism has become more estranged’ (4). Essays draw our attention to texts, modes, and genres that aren’t flashy, but that perhaps should be: the scientific romance, the ‘autobiografiction’, the proto-‘formalist’ occult mythology. This collection does excellent work in tracing thematic threads through texts beyond the centrally canonical. Kate Flint, for example, in pursuit of debates about photography, gathers together an array that – besides more canonical texts such as Hardy’s A Laodicean, Conan Doyle’s ‘The Man with the Twisted Lip’, Woolf’s The Voyage Out, and Arnold Bennett’s The Old Wives’ Tale – includes Amy Levy’s The Romance of a Shop, Rudyard Kipling’s ‘At the End of the Passage’, and Richard Marsh’s ‘The Photographs’, as well as more theoretical and technical texts such as P. H. Emerson’s Naturalistic Photography for Students of the Art (1889) and Charles Caffin’s Photography as a Fine Art: The Achievements and Possibilities of Photographic Art in America (1901), and Alvin Langdon Coburn’s volumes of photographic portraits, Men of Mark (1913). Or, discussing treatments of the moon, Matthew Taunton reconfigures the canon to include not only H. G. Wells and James Joyce but writers such as James Nasmyth and James Carpenter (creators of The Moon, Considered as a Planet, a World, and a Satellite, 1874) and Garrett P. Serviss (author of The Moon Metal, 1900), and Charles Hannan (who wrote Thuka of the Moon, 1906). Thorough and enterprising, the collection’s essays commit to diving into the archive in search of gems that deserve revisiting. This is admirable for its canon-stretching promise. In the abstract, this approach addresses a question that is at the heart of any literary scholarship, and perhaps especially in essay collections’ attempts to represent a time period and the terms of its own criticism of itself. That question is how to balance the canon with the archive, and the archivist’s completeness with the curator’s taste. Where the ideal fulcrum is, of course, must remain rather a matter of personal critical preference; Late Victorian into Modern seems to proceed by featuring familiar names (Conrad, Kipling, Schreiner, Wells, Woolf, Joyce, Forster) again and again at least in brief, but often giving its most extensive analyses to authors and texts that have not traditionally enjoyed as much attention. In the process, certain modes have gotten richer, more complete leafings-out than others: considerations of prose fiction, non-fiction, and theatre dominate, and comparatively few essays focus on poetry. The ideas of Eliot, Pound, Hulme, Lewis, and H. D. – especially their ideas about imagism, periodization, political ideology, and women’s authorship – figure prominently, but not so much their poetry. (Notable exceptions include Hannah Sullivan’s demonstration that earlier nineteenth-century poets such as Christina Rossetti made ‘newly’ unrhymed, roughly metered verse before Pound did; Santanu Das’s reading of soldier-poets who thematize the empathic capacities of the human hand alongside the writings of nurses, D. H. Lawrence, and Claire Goll; and Dennis Denisoff’s exploration of Michael Field’s contributions to an avant-la-lettre post-humanism). What happens, in the process, to some of the more familiar categories one might associate with the transition into modernism, categories such as difficulty, experimentalism, or a no-longer-pictorial, more psychological, realism? These remain as informing presences, though by other names. Realism, for instance, doesn’t reign as a facilely central term. Instead, adjacent categories such as naturalism, impressionism, and – as Sos Eltis and Kirsten Shepherd-Barr satisfyingly observe – even self-consciousness about one’s medium, offer more precise coordinates by which to navigate the range between mimesis and subjectivism. On the other hand, experimentation becomes specified, in Christos Hadjiyiannis’s discussion of the avant-garde, as essentially an anti-positivism and imagism (as philosophized by Hulme, Bergson, and Pound). In short, the essays’ authors put these transhistorical terms, realism and experimentation, into their contexts. For the most part, the results are positive. At times, the effort is somewhat uneven, ranging from readings that generate exciting new insights and blend historicist completeness with compelling, literary close reading, to pieces that read more like literature reviews, or foreshortened versions of more ambitious essays, projecting fruitful intervention into the field but allowing only glancing, briefly unfolded demonstrations. At other times, the terms parsing literature’s interactions with contemporaneous non-literary cultural developments produce elisions. For instance, literary art’s relationship to the other arts (especially visual arts) seems to have gotten folded into discussions of literature’s engagements with technology, or of book design and production. Essays address cinema, photography, portraiture, and book illustration, but not the ‘fine’ arts that were being rethought and made abstract or discordant – such as painting, sculpture, or music – or even the more industrial, craft-based arts that were reformed in the wake of decadence, then functionalism. The Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts movements get mentioned on a single page, and Impressionism, acknowledged as something visible in art galleries during the late 1870s, functions most prominently as a shorthand for (literary) technique that aims to ‘capture the encounter between external reality and consciousness’ (188). To a reader familiar with the history of criticism of this period – a reader who knows how much scholarly ink has already been devoted to the turn-of-the-twentieth-century revisions of the ‘sister arts’ model – this omission will feel justified. It is refreshing to search beyond the traditional analogies between literature to the ‘fine’ arts, and toward comparisons with newer technologies of vision. And yet, the book misses an opportunity to trace another continuity across the late-nineteenth and the early-twentieth centuries, giving instead the impression that the late-Victorians and moderns ceased to be interested in paint, fabric, stone, glass, or clay, which (as has been shown by Rachel Teukolsky, Elisabeth Oliver, and Victoria Rosner, among others) they did not.2 Late Victorian into Modern chooses its foci bravely and with interesting results, such that the omissions and eclipses that inevitably arise do more to shed light on the constraints of any selection process than to cripple the final product. Genre studies, theatre studies, and media studies are this collection’s stars, and they shine brightly and earn our attention.

title: The inert and the violent
abstract: The modern mind is dialectical to an extreme; it looks for division, it dramatizes oppositions. For this emphasis, Faulkner's Light in August is a classic of the modern imagination as well as perhaps the most representative of his works. Division is corruption in the world of Faulkner, and miscegenation is its vivid symbolic act. Opposed to this act of violent disorder, we understand an ideal of implicit unity, which is thereby purity. Violence is the ironically appropriate and naturalistically inevitable fate of the passive agent. Crumbling below her rigid surface, reached in her isolation, Joanna Burden falls to unlimited license. The two faces on the wheel are a supreme violent duality of blind matter and blind inhibition separated without the resolutions of the moral intelligence. Grimm and Christmas are complements of a debased substance, force meeting force in passion and repression. A third force is needed, that of the moral will and spiritual sympathy.

title: Acknowledging Addie’s Pain: Language, Wittgenstein, andAs I Lay Dying
abstract: Where Addie Bundren’s bitter statement in Faulkner’s As I Lay Dying that “words are no good” has often been read as concerning the universal shortcomings of language, this article turns to the philosophy of Faulkner’s contemporary Ludwig Wittgenstein for a more context-specific understanding of how words convey meaning. Drawing on Stanley Cavell’s distinction between knowledge and acknowledgment, this article proposes that Addie’s social position as a poor housewife in the modernizing US South prompts her to focus on language’s epistemological limits, at the expense of its empathetic possibilities. The particular words Addie repudiates—words like “motherhood” and “sin”—attest to the connection between her philosophical views and her deepest lived frustrations. In turn, Addie’s linguistic philosophy informs those of her children—particularly Dewey Dell, Darl, and Vardaman—all of whom feel alienated from their society and struggle to gain acknowledgment through language.

title: Transatlantic Poe: Eliot, Williams, and Huxley, Readers of the French Poe
abstract: “This is one of the ‘others’—a suggestive book,” noted Poe in 1844 about L'An 2440 by Sebastien Mercier, an early science fiction work that has since been quite forgotten; the same may be said enthusiastically about Maria Filippakopoulou's Transatlantic Poe, whose afterlife in scholarship deserves to be more enduring. This is a remarkable book in Poe studies that eschews a reflection on Poe's life and on the content value of his work. Instead, it foregrounds Poe as a model of what Pascale Casanova in The World Republic of Letters (2004) has called littérarisation: translation (broadly interpreted by Filippakopoulou in a book that challenges the notion of linguistic nativity) as negotiation of literary prestige both of the object's symbolic value and of its receiving agents. Transatlantic Poe, while examining the extent to which Poe became a “spectral original” (27) when adopted by the French and “an adulterated version of Poe” (128) when reassessed in the English-speaking world, rewards the reader with several insights on the poetics and ideologies of important literary figures who had to negotiate the significance of Poe across the Atlantic: Baudelaire, Williams, Eliot, and Huxley.This is also a relevant book for translation studies that does not address any single translation of Poe. Instead, it dedicates three chapters to the metadiscourses that consubstantiate what the author chooses to call “Baudelaire's project,” a critical enterprise that led to the realignment of the value of Poe in his source culture and made him pivotal for an inexhaustible stream of metadiscourses. The study of these “rewritings” was defended early on the turn toward translation in comparative studies, by Susan Bassnett and André Lefevere, as an alternative paradigm to the interpretation monograph in literary studies. This is, finally, a courageous book in reception studies, which supersedes the traditional comparative approach of the dual frameworks of original and receiving authors. Instead, it opts for a “polyprismatic or stereoscopic account” (230) that radicalizes the volatile space of the original and foregrounds value exchanges exploding bilateral considerations of source and target.In respect to the singular recognition of Poe by Baudelaire, who posited him as a transatlantic older brother, Filippakopoulou's book shares a rather understated insight of Patrick F. Quinn's The French Face of Edgar Poe (1957): that the facile criticism of American democracy by the French poet was a populist bait to enforce the more radical and modern(ist) idea of the alienation of the literary author from any nationalist generalization. Transatlantic Poe also honors a long line of research dating back to Léon Lemonnier's Les Traducteurs d'Edgar Poe in 1928 and extending to the ever-rising interest in Poe's reception and translation attested by the edited collections Poe Abroad (1999), Poe's Pervasive Influence (2012), and Translated Poe (2014).As the very title of Filippakopoulou's book indicates, however, the novelty it brings to Poe's reception scholarship is the outlook of the relatively recent field of Transatlantic studies, spurred in the cusp of the twenty-first century by academics such as Paul Giles, Will Kaufman, or the late Susan Manning (to whom this study is dedicated), to question place-based identities and monocultural visions, and to subject them to a “critical relativism” (20) mindful of the “reflective operations” (21) of the increasingly intense cross-Atlantic exchanges modeling (at least) the Western worldview. Giles's definition of transatlantic comparativism is given as a “strategy to fracture the boundaries of established institutions and scholarly disciplines” (16), and the resistance to reductively disentangle threads is procured by the author through “a conflation” between “the method and the content value” (227). How such concurrence is to be achieved is never clearly explained, but one of the keywords advanced is “argumentative development” (24), from which we may infer that the preferred method—itself a blend of methodologies from critical linguistics, close reading grounded in New Historicism, translation in its relation to comparativism and reception—is aligned with contents that do not signify independently but only as situated discourses responding to and shaping one another, in what is put forth as a bicentric cultural exchange.These dynamics might well be posited as cultural triangulation, considering not only the movements of adoption of the U.S. writer by the French and his reassessment on the grounds of American locality by William Carlos Williams or of linguistic nativity by T. S. Eliot and Aldous Huxley, but also how the two latter authors were allegedly selected for this study because, besides their texts being “norm-setters,” they themselves embodied the “hyphenated Anglo-American positionality” (193–94). On this last triangulation, Filippakopoulou's study, despite its rootedness in contextualization, does not take the “argumentative development” to the full consequences, which, should it pursue how Eliot and Huxley projected on Poe their own hesitation between European and U.S. cultural configurations, eventually would deter the too quick synonymity sometimes established between Anglo-American and Americanist (12), as well as the slippage between nationalism and “defence of linguistic nativity” (25). Certain passages, such as the introductory remark on the “attempt to describe the two national repertoires that have recorded two characteristic moments in Poe's reevaluation in modern times” (25), might misleadingly equate the term “Anglophone criticism” with the monocultural notion that the critic otherwise wishes to disperse. Moreover, the affirmation that “Eliot and Huxley's shuttling experience between the two coasts of the Atlantic … seems to have played a significant role in their heavy investment to the stability of linguistic nativity” (194) is not necessarily untrue but lacks evidence. There is little historicization of the cosmopolitanism or expatriation movement of the two authors, of their somewhat incompatible geopolitical stances, or of factual instances that should give pause, such as the provocative stance of the title of one of the last pieces on Poe by Eliot, “American Literature and the American Language” (1966). In this respect, Filippakopoulou is truer to the design of “welcomed complexity” (234) when she offers a reading of Williams's reappraisal of Poe in In the American Grain (1925) that argues for a non-nationalist redefinition of the concept of locality and permits a bifocal view of “originality,” which needs not extricate an author from tentative anterior positions in the world panorama.The book's methodology is on the whole very meritorious in offering insights on negotiations of literary prestige from the part(s) of authors involved in the setting of agendas for Western modern literature. As mentioned above, the three chapters on Baudelaire's co-option of Poe do not address the French writer's actual translations but, rather fittingly, since the remainder of the book is on the response of English-speaking writers, presents fascinating close readings of significant passages in the three extensive critical pieces meant as introductions or prefaces to Poe's works—“Edgar Poe: Sa vie et ses ouvrages” (1852), “Edgar Poe: Sa vie et ses oeuvres” (1856), and “Notes Nouvelles sur Edgar Poe” (1857). Additionally, Filippakopoulou analyzes two lesser-divulged pieces: a fictionalized letter (“To Maria Clemm” published in Le pays in 1854) and “Avis du Traducteur” (posthumously revealed in 1934). Throughout her analysis, Filippakopoulou shows how “Baudelaire's campaign of haute vulgarisation” (35), heavily drawing on nineteenth-century poetics of biography, capitalizes on the fuzzy tragedy of Poe's factual death and launches a recuperation project based on the idea of marginalization. Several compelling but conflicting identifications are unearthed by the critic's competence in discourse analysis: with a “corrected” image of Poe emplotted on the account of the French writer's increasing interest in his life and works, with the putative French admirers of Poe set apart from the frivolous Parisian literati, with the aristocrats of the spirit against the moneymaking Americans, with Maria Clemm as a figure of maternal acquiescence and understanding, et cetera. The comments on the recourse to the genre of the “filial letter,” in Chapter 2, whereby the project assumes “a mien of familial altruism and solidarity” (77), hint at how much the foregrounding of the antinomies of the particular/universal and the private/public is constitutive of literary modernity and might build up a poetics of sincerity instead of undermining it. As such, it would be interesting to conflate some of this book's arguments with Louis A. Renza's Edgar Allan Poe, Wallace Stevens, and the Poetics of American Privacy (2002) and indicate how essentially transnational is the dependence of privacy in a recurring otherness.One should note that the distinction between the different degrees of publicity of Baudelaire's metatexts could be more explicit in this book. However interesting the relations that might be elicited from the focus on lesser-known texts by Baudelaire on Poe, they should be taken as ancillary to the more extensive critical pieces, particularly the two prefaces published in Baudelaire's collections of translated Poe tales, and widely disseminated elsewhere, because these are the statements that account for “the Poe that modernists read” (123). Moreover, the study could benefit from a modalization of the identification of “Baudelaire's project” with “the French Poe,” which is the provocative title of the second part of Transatlantic Poe, devoted to the ambivalent gestures of literary retrieval by the “Anglo-American” authors. This division somewhat belies the constant cautionary remarks toward overarching generalizations, even if it expediently delimitates the grounds for the embattled “linguistic nativity” whose problematics Filippakopoulou convincingly exposes in the arguments of Eliot and Huxley.The discussion could be further nuanced by addressing a fact that is mentioned but slightly overlooked in the book: that both Eliot's and Huxley's pieces directly confront the judgment of the contemporary Paul Valéry, and perhaps only indirectly that of the subject of his 1924 conference “Situation de Baudelaire.” It could therefore be appropriate to reassess the continuum Baudelaire–Mallarmé–Valéry in the French reception of Poe and of how much these essays in English were influential in crystallizing it, especially Eliot's “From Poe to Valéry.” For, in his 1948 lecture, Eliot is quite possibly less concerned with the misprision of Poe than with the commencement and progression of a particular tradition in poetry that he believes has exhausted itself: pure poetry. Furthermore, he sees this tradition as the heightening of a consciousness of language, leading to the demise of subject matter and ultimately to the authorization of what Eliot most abhors in Poe, “irresponsibility toward the meaning of words.” But can't this disregard for the propriety of meaning signify the urge towards deterritorialization and detachment of native entrenchment, aiming at a transrational (if not indeed transnational or even universal) utopia, beyond discursive reason and beyond the nationally bounded senses serving utilitarian communication?In The Poet Edgar Allan Poe, Alien Angel (2014), Jerome McGann suggests that Eliot had to cross the Atlantic in order to make his American discovery of Poe, and he bases his insight in the verse from “Little Gidding” (1942) that takes up the famously puzzling phrase of Mallarmé's “Le Tombeau d'Egad Poe” (1876): “donner un ses plus pur aux mots de la tribu.” Eliot—in a manner no less intriguing—chooses to replace “mots” for “dialect”: “Since our concern was speech and speech impelled us / to purify the dialect of the tribe.” The transatlantic negotiation of purity in language in late Romanticism and early Modernism, and of where, how, and by whom it comes to bear elocutionary authority, is the threshold where we are left in Transatlantic Poe. The questions raised here regarding this book's scope or choice of texts result, themselves, from its courageous determination not to assign any inherent signification to Poe's work and to regard it as an “original … incapable of producing meaning independently” (228) but emerging in the light of critical narratives seen “as historical representations that negotiate a fantasy of literary essence in cultural terms” (232).

title: Modernists
abstract: This chapter discusses the early careers and work of the two most influential poets of Modernism. It contrasts the way in which Pound’s outspoken criticisms and poetic innovations alienated most of the English literary establishment, leading to his departure from England in 1920, while T. S. Eliot is shown to have skilfully negotiated his way into that establishment in the 1920s, not least through his editing of the Criterion. The chapter also considers the contribution of biography in understanding the development of a poet’s work, the role of editors and patrons in promoting Modernism, and the value of correspondence as historical evidence.

title: The "Ulysses" Delusion: Rethinking Standards of Literary Merit by Cecilia Konchar Farr
abstract: Reviewed by: The "Ulysses" Delusion: Rethinking Standards of Literary Merit by Cecilia Konchar Farr Ira Nadel (bio) THE "ULYSSES" DELUSION: RETHINKING STANDARDS OF LITERARY MERIT, by Cecilia Konchar Farr. New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2016. xx + 199 pp. $95.00. The title of Cecilia Konchar Farr's book promises a confrontation with history—or, if not history—text. It suggests a head-on collision with the reputation, status, and reception of Joyce's novel with perhaps an overturning of its modernist dominance, a full, ten-round bout with the anticipation of a knockout punch, or at least a few stinging jabs. Disappointingly, nothing like this happens. There is no match—not even an uppercut, let alone a smack-down. The title of the book is, in fact, misleading because the text is more about Harry Potter and popular fiction than Joyce and/or Ulysses. In fact, after a few opening punches in the "Preface" on how the academy has ruined reading because of its celebration of Joyce's difficult novel, the undisputed heavyweight champion of modernism, Joyce is heard from again only once and does not even appear in the index. The accusation that Ulysses and the literary establishment has held up the novel to celebrate only its complexity, counter-narratives, and allusions sustains an eagerness to counter-punch, but little serious damage is done. Yet the argument is made that readers are leaving the arena dissatisfied and finding greater satisfaction in the work of, say, Nicholas Sparks or Lee Child. The populist assumption of this study is that "[t]raining in literature teaches us that good novels are difficult" (xvi). Only novels that require constant interpretation keep the academy going, Farr argues, hence their privileged status, while alienating actual readers. Ulysses (although The Unnamable, Underworld, or Infinite Jest could easily stand in1) is the bête noire preventing the development of "honest readers." Indeed, The "Ulysses" Demon might be a more accurate title for this book. Farr is an instrumentalist, believing that reading should have the practical purpose of establishing a community agreeing on a single idea: that a certain text is "good" (143). This moralistic, Arnoldian notion has little cultural or even formalist grounding—only that novels should be set free from "insular academic discourse and high modernism" (xx).2 With its informal, user-friendly tone, the text seems more like readers [End Page 176] explaining why they like, rather than understand, a book, and it divides them into "novel-lovers" and "literary professionals" (147). The opinion of a book club, rather than a critic, seems to be the test of literary value while scholarship actually "has little to say about the novels that most people value" (151). This is democratic criticism at its fullest, but its subjectivity creates its own distraction, pulling itself away from its supposed topic. Ulysses is forgotten in the book's pursuit and celebration of popular taste, with its underlying thesis that difficult books are not what people want to read. The proof? When did you last see someone read Ulysses on a train or a plane? The subtitle, however, promises something more: "Rethinking Standards of Literary Merit," a subject previously addressed by T. S. Eliot, Walter Benjamin, and Frank Kermode among others.3 But such work finds no currency in this study. Janet Radway's A Feeling for Books: The Book-of-the-Month Club, Literary Taste, and Middle-Class Desire, which essentially focuses on literary taste (the underlying subject of Farr's study), is the guiding text, overlooking works like Stanley Fish's Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities or Terry Eagleton's How to Read Literature.4 Farr avoids any theoretical engagement with her topic, neglecting such helpful sources as the special "Literary Value" issue of the Modern Language Quarterly or Lise Jaillant's Modernism, Middlebrow and the Literary Canon: The Modern Library Series, 1917–1955, which dedicates chapter 3 to discussing Joyce.5 The work of Franco Moretti would establish a historical context for Farr's position, notably The Bourgeois: Between History and Literature, exploring the meaning of "useful" or "influence" in relation to literary works, or his study of popular reading in...

title: Introduction
abstract: Introduction Jung Jack Saebyok (bio) Born in 1908, Kim Kirim grew up to be a leading figure in the modernist movement in Korean literature in the 1930s. He earned his living as a newspaper journalist, writing reports during the day and composing poetry at night. A founding member of kuinhoe, an eclectic gathering of modernist writers and poets, he went on to befriend Yi Sang as his intellectual ally in this group. A literary rebel, Kim Kirim was not shy about criticizing many Korean poets of the earlier generation, whom he saw as being cripplingly sentimental and overly flowery in their use of language. Instead, he espoused a poetics of intellectualism and positivity, the disciplined use of adjectives, and the revitalization of our world as the poet’s chief duty. His poetry was also influenced by T. S. Eliot and I. A. Richards. In Eliot, he saw a poet whose influences had had to overcome, and in Richards, a critic he needed to emulate. In Kim Kirim’s long poem Weather Map1 (1937) a typhoon ploughs through an unprepared city. A new sun is born in the aftermath. Topical and apocalyptic, Kirim’s work consists of seven individual parts, each of which were initially published as a standalone [End Page 201] poem. They were later gathered to form a single piece and published in book form in 1936. The volume was edited by Yi Sang, who also designed its striking cover. Brought together as one long poem, the seven pieces create a collage-like canvas of a modern East Asian metropolis in the path of a great storm. The first two parts, “The Morning of the World” and “Citizen’s Parade,” show us a superficially peaceful world boiling with trouble beneath its surface. The second pair, “Typhoon’s Coughing Hour” and “Trace,” presents the storm’s approach and the destruction it brings as a metaphor for the philosophical, political, and economic transformations of the time that often proved disastrous for East Asian nations. The fifth and the penultimate parts, “Sick Landscape” and “Owl’s Incantation,” detail the dreary aftermath of the storm and stress and contain the poem’s most lyrical passages. The final part, titled “The Song of the Iron Wheel,” is a prophecy of a new age that will emerge from such ruin. Weather Map is the kind of literary experience that we hardly ever have today. Grand and daring, the poem is the product of a maker who believed without irony that poetry can make things happen on a scale involving all of humanity. With such fervent faith, Kirim’s verse functions as both diagnosis of a dying society and herald of a new world. For English readers, the experience of Kim Kirim’s Weather Map will inevitably bring to mind that other long poem brimming with modernist sensibilities. Like Eliot’s The Waste Land (1922), Kim Kirim’s work expresses in fragmented imagery a ruined city and an alienated poetic voice, searching for the redemption of a cursed civilization. But Weather Map is not a mere Korean imitation of its English predecessor. In fact, Kim Kirim criticizes The Waste Land in an essay published within a year after the publication of his Weather Map. After discussing the poetic methods of his contemporaries, Kim Kirim concludes with the following observation: [End Page 202] We have clearly seen the earlier missteps of the poet of The Waste Land, who attempted to write a mythology of the 20th Century. But all he managed was to write a mythology of spiritual slash-and-burn farmers. On top of that burnt land of the messiah, he recklessly tried to rebuild the mythology of the Middle Ages.2 Kirim’s criticism of Eliot’s work informs us of what he was attempting to do with his own poetry: create a new mythology unburdened by the limited traditions of the past. In this regard, it is clear that Kirim meant his Weather Map to be a foundational work upon which to build such a vision.
