title: Race, Politics, and Irish America: A Gothic History
abstract: The issue of race in America has been a central part of political discourse since the seventeenth century. Despite the election of Barack Obama (who has Irish roots) to the US presidency in the early twenty-first century, the creation of the 1619 Project, and the Black Lives Matter movement, progress on race equality remains fragile. In Florida recent rulings on how Black history can be taught in schools, the assiduous removal of critical race theory, and the blocking of a new Advanced Placement class on African American studies provide examples of the sensitivity and polarization that discussions on race continue to have in 2023.Race and racialized caricatures have long been part of the history of Irish people and their descendants. As the concept of Irish identity has varied over time, so has it been complicated by issues of class, gender, language, religion, and place. The “varieties of Irishness” evident in Ireland were transported overseas as people fled poverty and oppression, often, like James O’Neill’s family, settling in North America.Mary Burke’s Race, Politics, and Irish America: A Gothic History provides a timely reminder that the political debate about race extends beyond politics. Readers quickly learn that Burke will examine race by considering multiple “cultural productions,” encompassing drama, film, fashion and beauty products, songs, and much more (1). This generic breadth helps Burke create a rich, nuanced, and complex picture of what it means to be Irish. From these diverse “productions,” she extracts the “undead”—gothic—history of the Irish American story. “That unfinished past,” she observes, “replays within American contexts of race, slavery, settler-colonialism, and ethnic hierarchies” (1). Compellingly, Burke includes performers, “public women,” and queer and multiracial authors in her analyses and thus rejects the traditional focus on straight, white, male authors. She promises, and delivers, a rich, rewarding, and challenging read.Burke begins her study with two chapters on the “Scots-Irish Gothic,” which consider Edgar Alan Poe (1809–49), Henry James (1843–1916), and Irish nationalist John Mitchel (1815–75). The term “Scots Irish” refers to the approximately 400,000 Irish immigrants of Scottish descent, predominantly Presbyterian, who arrived in colonial America in the eighteenth century. The phrase was coined retrospectively as a way to distinguish this group from the largely Catholic and poor Famine and post-Famine Irish emigrants of the 1840s and later. Poe is anteceded as an accomplished writer of the American Gothic by Charles Brockden Brown, author of Edgar Huntly, published in 1799. Both writers, Burke shows, draw much from their Irish backgrounds, as would James. Sophisticated and cosmopolitan, James was acutely aware of the hierarchies of whiteness that existed in relation to Irish people and Europeans in general. Provocatively, Burke analyzes him in relation both to his closeted Irishness and his closeted homosexuality.Radicalized by the Irish Famine, John Mitchel was exiled in 1848 by the British government, initially to Bermuda but ultimately to Van Dieman’s Land, now Tasmania. In Ireland he and his fellow Young Irelanders had become frustrated by Daniel O’Connell’s outspoken criticism of slavery. When Mitchel escaped from Australia to America in 1853, he became a vocal supporter of chattel slavery and Southern secession. He argued that Black slaves were well treated compared to the intermittent starvation of the Irish poor. His grandson, John Purroy Mitchel, was elected mayor of New York in 1914. Today, the elder Mitchel remains a contested and controversial figure in Irish historiography.Chapter 3 treats Eugene O’Neill (1888–1953) and F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896–1940) jointly, as contemporary Irish Americans with much in common. Both had economically comfortable upbringings, access to Ivy League education (both flunked out of Princeton), and histories of alcoholism and depression. The backdrop of their early writings was the search for national identity on both sides of the Atlantic, though each man engaged with his Irishness in different ways. Fitzgerald’s playboy lifestyle, performed in the public eye, seemed at odds with his misleading acknowledgment, during an interview in 1927, that his mother’s family were “straight 1850 potato-famine Irish” (89). A few years later, while he was working on Tender Is the Night, Fitzgerald shared with a friend his “intense social self-consciousness” about his background: “I am half black Irish and half old American stock with the usual ancestral pretentions. The black Irish half of the family had the money and looked down on the Maryland side of the family who had … that certain series of reticences and obligations that go under the poor old, shattered word ‘breeding’ … I suppose this is just a confession of being a Gael” (91). Burke regards the phrase “half black Irish” as central to understanding how Fitzgerald viewed himself in the context of 1920s “white America,” especially its depictions of skin color and beauty. At the same time, his comments provide fascinating insights into class—and “breeding”—in America.Like Fitzgerald, Eugene O’Neill had a direct connection with Ireland’s Great Famine of 1845 to 1852. James O’Neill was from a Famine refugee from Kilkenny, a survivor of a tragedy that claimed approximately 25 percent of the country’s population in a six-year span. Unlike many who fled to North America, James was ultimately able to provide comfortably for his family. However, rather than embrace a lifestyle of white privilege, Eugene dropped out of college and spent a good deal of time living hand-to-mouth in Argentina and elsewhere. Moreover, he chastised others in Irish America who chose not to throw in their lot with oppressed and banished peoples.During his vagabond phase, O’Neill visited Trinidad and Portuguese East Africa. As part of the British Colonial Service, Irish-born Roger Casement had served in the latter location from 1895 to 1898 and had published his damning report on the Belgian Congo a few years later. Trinidad had developed as a sugar colony until the British empire’s abolition of slavery in 1838. The ending of enslavement in British colonies, however, did not create prosperity for many former slaves or their descendants. O’Neill, familiar with Irish colonization and brought up in the era of Jim Crow, explored the encounters between Irish and Africans in the Caribbean in Thirst (1913) and The Moon of the Caribbees (1917). Although not chattel slaves, many of the impoverished Irish sailors whom O’Neill depicted had been impressed as indentured servants. Burke supplies an important caveat about reading these plays: “in the seventeenth-century Caribbean, the Irish were both planter and debased deportee, and the low status of the latter should not efface the imperialist role played by some elite Irish in that sphere” (66). This is an important reminder of the complexity of race and identity. Recent historiography has explored the paradox of being Irish—and white—in the British empire. The last few years have also witnessed new research on both the role of Irish people in the slave trade and on the Irish abolitionist movement. This work has revealed fresh layers of complexity regarding interactions between Black and Irish peoples.O’Neill’s interest in Black history and identity was evident in his 1920 play, The Emperor Jones. His insistence that the lead role had to be played by a Black actor was a powerful statement of both his agency and his determination to challenge established theater conventions. Paul Robeson succeeded Charles Sidney Gilpin on the stage and eventually starred in the film version. Robeson—actor, athlete, and activist—fought for social justice his whole life and rejoined O’Neill in 1923 for All God’s Chillun Got Wings, about miscegenation. For both O’Neill and Robeson, this was a brave choice of topic: the Ku Klux Klan revived in the 1920s, and its membership exceeded two million by 1923. Interracial marriage was prominent among their targets.O’Neill returned to his Irish roots in Desire Under the Elms (1924). Burke reads this play as a challenge to white colonialism of Scots-Irish origin. The Plantation of Ireland had confiscated land belonging to Catholics in the early seventeenth century; in O’Neill’s play, Ephraim Cabot displays an analogous greed when he boasts of having killed and scalped “Injuns in the West” in his quest for land and power. In this way, too, Burke grounds the play in Irish politics of the 1920s, particularly the recent partition of Ireland, which led to more violence and displacement within the country.In her final two chapters, Burke continues to demonstrate how Irish history, most notably the Plantation of Ulster and the Great Famine, permeates questions about racial status. Frank Yerby (1916‒91), an African American author with Scots-Irish lineage, frequently used the antebellum South as the setting for his works, for example in his historical novel, The Foxes of Harrow (1946). In contrast to the ambivalence regarding the loss of the South in the writings of William Faulkner (1897–1962), Yerby proposes to, in Burke’s words, “dance upon the grave of the plantation system” (110). One of the most unexpected chapters in this volume is the last one, “White Wedding: Grace Kelly, Spectacle, and Irish Assimilation.” Kelly, like O’Neill, descended from Famine-era immigrants, appeared to personify a version of the American dream by marrying into European royalty in 1956, a spectacle watched on television by 30 million people. For Burke, Kelly was also pivotal in the creation and consolidation of Irish “whiteness.”An epilogue looks at the Kennedy dynasty, which, returning to a major theme of the book, is subtitled, “Kennedy Gothic”—a foreboding insight into American politics. Burke draws a clear link between the Kellys and the Kennedys: “the bride’s globally visible ascent to the highest social echelon paved the way for America’s ‘royals,’ the Kennedy dynasty, as well as for broader Irish America’s attainment of unconditional whiteness” (135). For her finale, to the kaleidoscope of Irish, American, and Irish American politics, she revisits several of the issues that I note above. She concludes that if things had been different, along the lines suggested by O’Neill and Yerby, Barack Obama might have been referred to as “America’s first Black Irish President” (178).Burke’s book is wide ranging topically and with respect to the “cultural productions” at issue. Oddly, while songs are included in her list of topics to be examined, there is little here on this subject—the Irish Caribbean singer Rhianna earns a brief mention, but minstrelsy is omitted. This is a shame because Thomas D. “Daddy” Rice, associated with the song “Jump Jim Crow,” was Irish American, as were many minstrel performers. Regardless, this powerful and timely examination of race and politics in Irish America challenges many stereotypes and frames well-known authors, celebrities, and politicians in a way that brings new understanding to them and their Irish identities. Burke is to be congratulated for producing such a fine, wide-ranging, and broadly appealing study.

title: Communion of Radicals: The Literary Christian Left in Twentieth-Century America by Jonathan McGregor (review)
abstract: Reviewed by: Communion of Radicals: The Literary Christian Left in Twentieth-Century America by Jonathan McGregor Martin George Holmes Communion of Radicals: The Literary Christian Left in Twentieth-Century America. By Jonathan McGregor. Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University Press, 2021. ISBN 978-0-8071-7582-8. Pp. viii + 256. $50.00. Jonathan McGregor's Communion of Radicals: The Literary Christian Left in Twentieth-Century America is a long-overdue history of the Christian literary left in the twentieth-century United States. America has strong traditions of left-wing radicalism among orthodox Christian literary figures. However, because there is a stereotype that American Christians who emphasize doctrinal orthodoxy are almost invariably right-wing, these traditions have been neglected. Scholars of American leftism, for their part, often write from an aggressively secularist perspective, and so have also tended to overlook these traditions. Jonathan McGregor, a left-wing literary historian currently teaching at Southern Methodist University, seeks to rectify this lamentable situation with his new book. His aim is twofold. First, as a scholar, he wishes to "add a new chapter to the history of the literary Left" by exploring the lives and works of these radicals in greater detail (5). He does not limit himself to discussing their lives and works in isolation; he highlights their intersection with other literary movements (such as that of the Southern Agrarians) and other scholarly paradigms (such as queer studies). Second, as a doctrinally orthodox Christian committed to social justice, he is appealing to "pilgrims in search of literary waymarks" that communicate a Christian leftist vision of social justice (16). Because of America's religious diversity, McGregor focuses on four distinct radical Christian traditions. Two are ecclesiastical: Anglo-Catholic socialism and Roman Catholic personalism. The other two are regional: left-wing Southern Agrarianism and New England dissent. [End Page 80] Chapter 1 discusses the socialism of two queer converts to Anglo-Catholicism, Vida Dutton Scudder and Ralph Adams Cram. McGregor highlights that, like so many Anglo-Catholics in the late 1800s and early 1900s, Scudder and Cram decried capitalist inequalities and bourgeois individualism. Seeking a more just world, but suspicious of secular visions of socialism, they looked to the Middle Ages for guidance, specifically the medieval religious life. Cram, pessimistic about the future of modern capitalism, favored separatist monastic communities. Scudder, inspired more by the Franciscans, favored transformative communities to work in the world. McGregor emphasizes that queerness informed their respect for, and interest in, the religious life. Although as devout Christians they did not support sexually active same-sex relationships, they believed that religious communities allowed queer people to express their sexuality healthily through close platonic relationships, which gave them a refuge from the strictures of bourgeois convention. Drawing on John Boswell's Same-Sex Unions in Premodern Europe (1994), McGregor forges a link between these modern figures and their devout medieval forebears. Chapter 2 discusses the Anglo-Catholicism of T. S. Eliot and W. H. Auden. It challenges the widespread belief that Eliot and Auden became stodgy conservatives in later life. McGregor acknowledges that Eliot identified as a conservative, but he also states that Eliot was profoundly concerned about economic inequalities and bourgeois shallowness, opining in The Waste Land the need for a massive suburban church-building project to help the unemployed and revive the flagging spirituality of modern people. According to McGregor, this radical streak identifies Eliot as an "inheritor" of the Anglo-Catholic socialist tradition of Cram and Scudder (46). Regarding Auden, McGregor argues that he did not become a supporter of the status quo after his conversion to Anglo-Catholicism. Like Cram and Scudder, he advocated monasticism as a vehicle of social justice, and his queerness helped him avoid a normative bourgeois lifestyle. Chapter 3 discusses the Catholic Worker Movement. McGregor highlights that the inspiration for the movement stemmed not only from recently formulated papal social encyclicals; as with Anglo-Catholic socialism, the movement also took inspiration from medieval traditions. McGregor focuses on the literary contributions of Peter Maurin, the movement's French-born co-founder, which have been neglected until now. title: Isolation of AM Fungi from Rhizospheric Soil and Assessing Their Potential in Revegetating the Mining Wasteland of Gujarat using Inoculated Trees Saplings
venue: International Journal of Plant and Environment
abstract: Fluorspar (CaF2), is a common mineral, occurring in green, purple, yellow, or colorless crystals, which is used in metallurgy and makinga variety of chemicals used in refrigeration. Kadipani in Gujarat has large deposits of this ore. Open cast mining by GMDC has resultedin disturbed ecology. Earlier the efforts have been made by the forest department to grow tree species, in order to restore the forestecosystem, but the plants grew slowly and with stunted morphology and scanty survival. The obligate fungal symbionts known asarbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) present in plants play a key factor supporting plant growth in stressed conditions. Therefore, AMFstrains were first isolated from mining area and were used to raise the saplings first in polybags. Then after 75 days these were used forrevegetating the mine burdens or nearby waste land. The paper presents a pioneering efforts made to isolate and identify, the AMFfrom Fluorspar mines in Gujarat and then Glomus fasciculatum was incorporated in polybags filled with normal garden soil. Plants werealso raised by single spore inoculation method. Preliminary experiments revealed that the inoculated AMF strains promoted seedlinggrowth of Leuceana leucocephala and Millettia pinnata. The inoculation of AMF spores enhanced the growth of both the plants, and suchapplication can be used in sustainable restoration of the mining areas. Review discusses the structure of AM spores and mechanismsinvolved to equip them to survive in stressed situations and as symbionts help the plants to perform better.

title: The Island That Eats People
abstract: The Island That Eats People Joseph Pearson (bio) A current under seaPicked his bones in whispers. As he rose and fellHe passed the stages of his age and youth … —T. S. Eliot, The Waste Land (1922) you will see Click for larger view View full resolution From far away, Samothraki doesn't look like a people-eater island. It is a mound, furry, the shape of the snake in The Little Prince after it has consumed the elephant. And now, it is sleeping. I draw a plastic deck chair close to the railing and open my Mythos beer, staring out at the Thracian coast and the skeletal shape of Alexandroupolis crumpling behind me. Far out there, the waters are said to change nationality, but I cannot make sense of it. The patrol boat speeds past our ferry, its blue and white cross fluttering towards Turkey. I have been warned that each year there are unexplained deaths on Samothraki. The hotel owner in Thessaloniki flinched at my destination: "I wouldn't go there. Bad things happen to people on Samothraki." In Donousa, the brothers [End Page 11] running the beach taverna said, "The island is very strange. You will see." But the café owner in Athens had visited with his wife. When they arrived in Samothraki with the ferry, she stepped to shore, walked only ten meters onto the island, before turning right around to reboard the boat. When asked why, the man replied with a frown, "It's a feeling. You will see." I was told I should be careful on the island of accidents: of sinkholes, waterfalls, whirlpools, cliffs, and snakes. There are trails where you can climb up but not down. The peak, Fenghari, might as well be translated as "certain death without a guide." The earth could open in the night, leaving no one wiser to your fate. And then there is the river, Fonias, whose name literally does mean "killer." Listening to the brothers, I made a mental note of this toponym, Fonias, especially when told that its highest reaches offer the most beautiful pools and views in the Aegean. Mount Fenghari now looms higher above our little boat. Poseidon watched the Trojan War from it, "high on the topmost peak of wooded Samothrace," or so says The Iliad. The summit this late afternoon is not visible, but I have seen pictures of the 1,500-meter volcanic cone, of the kind you'd expect in the Pacific, not in the northern Aegean. Clouds now seep down the obscured slopes, leaving shadows, warped dark shapes cast on other vapors, slipping into the sea. The island is armed against visitors as there is no natural harbor. Samothrace's isolation means historically it has depended on its own cereals and oils and developed an unusual form of Greek. I imagine it is also spoken by the inbred animals and unique plants. As I take the stairs deep into the ferry, the island disappears until the vessel lowers its rusty gangway, so I can disembark with six Bulgarian tourists and four scrawny hippies on motorbikes. I wonder whether I will also walk only ten meters onto the island before turning around. But I am distracted as we disembark because we are forced to pass to one side. There are twenty people waiting to travel to the mainland under armed guard. They are lined up quietly, with uniformed officers at the head and tail of the queue. I notice that most are young men with darker complexions than the Greeks. A woman is unveiled, with two small children at her feet, one of whom runs out from the group, and she calls after him, her hesitant move halted by the guards' watch. But by now, I have passed the refugees and do not see what happens next. I continue another ten meters. Is that uneasy feeling—of something hollowed, from underground—suggested by the stories I have heard, or is it the sound of the island waking? title: What We Remember, What We Forget
abstract: I’m a failure. I have a long history of letting people down. Since I can remember, failure and its synonyms have been used to identify me. A broken ornament, and I was worthless. A lost thing, and I was pathetic. An item misplaced or hidden by another, and I was to blame.Even now, I continue to disappoint myself and others. For I can't recollect the only childhood memory Mrs. Y gifted me.It's the one about an overdose; the one about a baby.All I do know is, thanks to Mrs. Y, it was my fault.It was your fault, as usual. You were eighteen months old. I carried you to my bedroom. There was a small bottle on my bedside table. It was full of pills. I placed you on the bed and left the room.While I was away, you opened the bottle and swallowed the pills.Ten minutes later, I found you unconscious, the empty bottle in your hand.I took you to a neighbor who had a car. He drove us to the hospital, where you had your stomach pumped.A decade after it happened, Mrs. Y sat at an open fire, knitting. It was cold outside, deep snow veiled everything. As if to admonish me for something unseen, Mrs. Y suddenly said, “It was all your fault, as usual . . . . ”There close to the blaze where, four years later, I sat reading Eliot's The Waste Land and Shakespeare's Measure for Measure for Bursary, while Mrs. Y found fault, “You think you're better than us, don't you?”There also the following year when Linda Walker received Dux just ahead of me, Mrs. Y burned with rage at my deficiency, while I—a deformity from a horror story—was shut away at the top of the house, listening to the screams. “She thinks she's going to university! Over my dead body! I'm not fucking paying a cent towards her upkeep. She's staying here; that's an end to it. She can get a job like everyone else. Repay me for everything I've done for her!”There too a few months later, the hearth roaring the night, with a silence heavy as a suitcase, I walked away from all that into a darkness made colder by deep snow. The last bus to the last train awaited me as Mrs. Y closed the door.Such are my memories of the fire.Of “It was all your fault, as usual,” once given oxygen, it was never spoken about again.My memory of that overdose lurks inside me. But it's so deeply buried—in my mind, in my heart—it refuses to resurface.But it is there; isn't it?Why, in defiance of its absence, do I intuitively contend it exists?Firstly, casting on, casting off, Mrs. Y's memory of, “It was all your fault, as usual . . . ” unfurled not just for me, but also for Mr. Y. Secreted behind the sports pages and their oracle of punters’ predictions, he may have been, but he wasn't agitated by Mrs. Y's remembrance. Had it been a fabrication, he would have pointed it out; and didn't.Secondly, I may have been just eighteen months old at the time of the overdose, but I wasn't too young to compose memories. Back then, for instance, I ran along the dirt lane which looped behind that dark and narrow terraced house of my infancy. It was ill-paved and uneven. A protruding cobble snagged the welt of my shoe, upending my small body. As I sought to right myself, blood appeared at my knee and tears spilled from my eyes. I made for home and Mrs. Y's querulous response, “What have you done to yourself?!”When we go into Lockdown, I begin to have dreams in which the lost memory of my overdose resurfaces.Well, almost.In the stupor of sleep, the memory reappears as something kaleidoscopic, entangled and chimerical. For instance, a high moon, pale as a pill, casts weak light over a wilderness. The animal I am is exposed: black-pelted suckling sprouting my first sharp teeth. Eyes barely open, I find the world to be a place of skeletal outlines and disembodied howls.Mrs. Y is a stronger, fiercer beast. Her dark presence rises out of the hollow where we hide. She holds me in her bloodthirsty mouth. I dangle, her fangs clasped to my scruff as she skulks through tall grass towards deep water.There, body possessing a lunar reflection, the inlet is a marble monument, serene and enveloping.The savage jaw releases the scruff, then abandons its offspring.A pool of incandescence draws the suckling toward it.A sudden slip into the shimmery white of it, the high and the low of it, the savage undertow.Looking back at the memory of my drug-induced slumber stitched together for me by Mrs. Y that raw afternoon of needling, I remain troubled by many things.Firstly, its illusiveness. This memory is mine; and yet, it isn't. I was there when it happened; and yet, comatose, I was not. What unfolded, did so to me; and yet, as I was infantile and stupefied, it did not. Is this why the frail memory of this incident fails me; or why I fail it?Secondly, its concision and contradiction. Authored by Mrs. Y, my infant overdose is scant and inconsistent. It lacks details and nuance. It seems to me that to offer a memory is to impart a story, and to impart a story is to maintain its consistency or avoid (perhaps occasionally justify) any inconsistencies. But rather than mitigating the discrepancies, the timeframe of the overdose reconstructed by Mrs. Y amplifies them. Why, for instance, did she leave a baby alone in a room beside a bottle of pills? Why did she walk away? Did she need a moment of privacy? If so, why not place me in my cot? It had railings. There, I would have been restrained and safe once Mrs. Y exited the scene.Of additional incongruity is the length of time I was in the company of the medication. In Mrs. Y's brief recount, ten minutes elapsed before she checked on me. It's so precise. No “almost” or “nearly.” In a memory which lacks specificity, it's odd to find exactness there. It's almost as if this detail illustrates a fault line in the narrative: something observed at the time with such accuracy it belies the apparent nonchalance of the memory.Thirdly, I'm unsettled by its slant. For the absence of this recollection from my memory bank is matched by Mrs. Y's absence from most of her narration. The author of the drama, she portrays herself as its irreproachable adjunct, its fateful wraith and, come the “hastily arrived at, nail-biting” conclusion, its heroine: rescuer of the babe; doom-slayer; redeemer of the lost cause. As a mother, I reflect upon the trauma retold and know that, irrespective of the circumstances, had I almost lost my child, I would have been so guilt-ridden, the devastation would have endured. It would have saturated my recollection of the event, tainting all.You weren't to blame, my son. This I know, because I remember it. You were sitting safely in your buggy, when I turned my back. I was too focused upon a rack of dresses to notice you abandon your buggy, the straps holding you in unbuckled with a dexterity and stealth far beyond your two years of age.When I realized your absence, the department store stretched out wildly before me. Close by, a regiment of shelves displayed knives of every kind, graters and scissors for cutting bones. Behind them, a battalion of stands flaunted glassware a fingertip's touch away from shattering. In the distance, a horde of electrical appliances paraded beguiling traps for tiny hands, inquisitive minds and headstrong personalities. Somewhere among this terrifying muster, your voice rose up, “Come find me, Mummy.”When I called back, there was silence; and in it, the haunting evocation of my neglect.Past inattentive shop assistants, lines of sharp utensils, easily broken things and a rabble of televisions simultaneously screening Jeopardy!, I ran, calling out your name. My mind was ripe with implausible imaginings: your infant body already escaped the store; your infant body already snatched by some unattainable miscreant.Close to collapse, I returned to your empty buggy. Only then did you materialize. A blind spot in an enclave of clothes on a rack surrendered you.“I won! I won!” you shouted, joyous at a game I didn't know I was playing.Another dream, another Lockdown refraction.Mrs. Y is revivified, not as a wraith-like presence in my overdose, but as a hubris-laded savior whose supernatural abilities thwart a poisoned arrow aimed with Artemis-like accuracy at me.Because of Mrs. Y's resilience, I survive, not in doubt or inherited memory, not even in myth, but as a muse resurrected by the arts, bloodied by ink, colored by oils and voiced by those putting on a show.We are our memories. They are a repository of our lives. They remind us our existences encompass the everyday and the dramatic, the successful and the flawed, the loved and the estranged. They also remind us of our origins and maturations. Orbuculums, they even offer us lessons we can use to chart our futures.Our memories hold metaphysical meaning too. In everything we recollect, the small stuff and the life-changing, we find solace and certainty that we exist. Where Descartes instructs us, Cogito, ergo sum, our memories remind us that because we remember, we are. Seven billion creatures confined to a speck of stardust rotating around a balled inferno in a dark pocket of perhaps infinite space, we might be, but our recollections support the otherwise deeply contestable philosophical argument that we—and all that we encounter on our journeys through life—are real.Simultaneously, though, we know that at best our memories are reconstructions of the truth, and at worst, forgeries. We accept, for instance, that two people experiencing the same event can retain opposing recollections of what transpired. Are both valid? Are both false? Or do authenticity and fallacy lie elsewhere, a place peripheral to experience and memory?All answers to such questions instruct us that, like festering wounds we endure, our memories expose our vulnerabilities. Their subjectivity and incompletion, their unreliability and age- or infirmity-impacted deterioration make them defective. And yet, we depend on them to compose fundamental certainties about ourselves.So what does this say about who we really are?In Searching for Memory: The Brain, The Mind and The Past, author and Harvard University professor of psychology Daniel L. Schacter contends that there are three stages to making and retaining a memory: encoding, storage, retrieval. As our brain processes a recollection through these stages, he argues, what we recall and our connection to it alters.As a memory happens, we are its witness. At this moment of absolute accuracy, we have what psychologists call “field” perspective: the unfolding situation observed from our first-person outlook. But thereafter, our viewpoint changes. By the time of retrieval, our perspective is that of the “observer.” This offers us a vision of the experience from the angle of an outsider. Now the accuracy of the event is blurred, we its third-person voyeur observing an incident that features a replication of ourselves. Here we are split by memory: author and protagonist; self and other; original and copy.The process of encoding, storage, and retrieval also transforms the memory. At the time of encoding, it is raw, unedited material filmed on the movie camera of our mind. But during storage, then retrieval, it succumbs to the brain's edit suite. Anything that seems unnecessary is diminished or removed. Anything that appears significant is magnified. The end result replaces truth with a censored, redacted, and rewritten version of the original recollection. The more we replay it, the more we censor, redact, and rewrite.Alien, Mrs. Y plagues my sleep once more. She burns through outer space at light speed. She arrives at an apparent wasteland to discover something awry: a secret facility, guarded and weaponized. She uses her extraterrestrial powers to dissolve barbed wire fences and slay sentinels. Coded security doors are reduced to cinders. Feverish, she roams empty corridors, hunts down the room where, her strange offspring, I am caged.When she finds me, subject to some vile experiment, she tears my chains, rips out my catheters, and stems the potions and sedatives that are being used to deaden me.Amitriptyline; Desipromine; Doxipin: These were drugs prescribed in the 1970s to numb the symptoms of those experiencing extreme postnatal depression (PPD). Experienced by 10 to 20 percent of new mothers, PPD can arise up to year after birth. Its effects include sleep disturbance, feelings of worthlessness and sorrow, and thoughts of self-harm and hurting the newborn.The pills I ingested that unremembered afternoon when I was eighteen months old were antidepressants. Like much else, Mrs. Y never mentioned this to me. Nor did she tell me of the side effects: dramatic mood swings; insomnia; drug dependency; feelings of futility.Instead, she confessed this to a stranger.Of that unsettled evening in 1985, this is what I recall.The air was starved of moisture. The heavens offered the wail of thunder, a storm about to break. Knock, knock, knock . . . The door opened, Mrs. Y invited the visitor in.She shone in the dim light of our house, this neighbor who emanated the faint aroma of Panache. She was young and small, barely a mother herself. She sold the women in her community promises of rejuvenation and eternal youth in a pot, a way to earn—in the colloquial, sexist language of the day—pocket money, and to allow her a respite from nurturing new life.Anti-aging cream and “Cool Peach” lipstick: this was Mrs. Y's order. Paid for, the deluge began. It trapped our pale pilgrim against a windowpane clouted by torrential rain. There, simultaneously sheltered and exposed, she stood silently as Mrs. Y barraged her with a recount of postnatal depression and drugs.At this juncture I should point out that this memory is, like Mrs. Y's recollection of my overdose, an abridgement of what occurred. Also, that my memory is, like my kaleidoscopic Lockdown resurrections, a reimagining of experience.But it offers an answer to the question, what does this say about who we really are?For it's a reminder that memory is a creative endeavor: memory, the director's cut; memory, a book of collected poems; memory, an exhibition of curated portraits; memory, a surrealist retrospective.When I consider Mrs. Y as a woman who has just given birth, I can see she's high-risk. Under 25 years of age; living in poverty; a history of melancholia; a pregnancy unplanned: These are the main factors that increase a woman's exposure to PPD. At the time of my overdose, Mrs. Y fulfilled all criteria. She was the eldest of eleven children, raised in a state house by a problem gambler and his hollowed-out wife. Mrs. Y suffered severe mood swings long before, at 22 years old, she fell pregnant with me.Whether it was these determinants or Mrs. Y's consequent recourse to mind-altering drugs, I'm not sure, but something unspoken led her to silence much of my infancy. Of the months spent carrying me; the length of the labor; the time of my arrival; my first days outside the womb, not to mention my first months, my first year . . . ; the holidays Mr. and Mrs. Y took me on; who in the cast of uncles and aunts cared for me: These remain as much unknown to me as the memory of my overdose, Mrs. Y so drug-addled and traumatized by her depression, her poverty, and my unwanted arrival that she sealed in silence both my treasured early years and her recollection of them.“Stress and trauma,” Schacter outlines, “are sometimes associated with loss of memory for single events or a small number of experiences—a condition I call limited amnesia.”1Considering the amnesia of violent episodes by those who experienced childhood abuse or war trauma, Schacter argues that limited amnesia is more prevalent when the victim is incapacitated.“Most cases that involve amnesia for a single traumatic event can be attributed to such factors as intoxication, head injury or loss of consciousness during the trauma.”2For Schacter, it's the intersection of these extremes—a deeply traumatic experience plus a brain-altering influence of drugs or alcohol—that disrupts the natural memory process of encoding and retrieval, and so causes amnesia.Schacter offers a way to break limited amnesia, outlining how the memory of a traumatic experience can be retrieved when the conditions that framed its encoding are replicated.“Our own states of mind can also serve as valuable cues for remembering. When people drink alcohol or smoke marijuana during the encoding phase of a memory experiment, they later have difficulty remembering what they encoded—but they recall more when they are later given similar doses of alcohol or marijuana. This is known as state-dependent retrieval.”3Sadly, state-dependent retrieval is unfeasible for me. For I would have to take another overdose, risking death a second time, to reconnect to and resurrect the memory I've misplaced or repressed.Mrs. Y suppressed memories, while in my Lockdown refractions, I confabulate them.Schacter makes sense of my subconscious impulse to confabulate. title: International Entrepreneurship and the Impacts of Catastrophes on the Tourism Sector
authors: Adriana Mirelly Silva Spindola Correia; Yákara Vasconcelos Pereira
venue: Revista Rosa dos Ventos - Turismo e Hospitalidade
abstract: Humanity experiences the catastrophic effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. In view of this scenario, studies are needed to understand the impacts of catastrophes in the most varied dimensions. The tourism sector emerges as one of the most affected economic segments when disasters occur. For companies in the sector that operate globally, the consequences influence the actions of international entrepreneurs. This study aims to conduct a theoretical discussion of the relationship between catastrophe impacts in the tourism sector and international entrepreneurship. From this purpose, impacts of catastrophes on the tourism sector are identified, as well as the reactions of international entrepreneurship in this context. Therefore, from the literature, impacts of catastrophes on the tourism sector are observed, as in the case of the crisis in the hotel sector. In addition, it results in the main reactions of entrepreneurs in the face of catastrophes. KEYWORDS Tourism; International Entrepreneurship; Catastrophe; Disaster; Covid-19. RESUMO A humanidade vivencia os efeitos catastróficos da pandemia Covid-19. Diante desse cenário, tornam-se prementes estudos para compreender os impactos de catástrofes nas mais variadas dimensões. O setor do turismo desponta como um dos segmentos econômicos mais afetados quando ocorrem desastres. Para as empresas do setor que atuam globalmente, as consequências influenciam as ações dos empreendedores internacionais. Este estudo possui o objetivo de realizar uma discussão teórica da relação entre impactos de catástrofes no setor de turismo e empreendedorismo internacional. A partir desse propósito, foram identificados impactos de catástrofes no setor de turismo, bem como as reações do empreendedorismo internacional frente a esse contexto. Assim sendo, a partir da literatura observou-se impactos de catástrofes no setor de turismo, a exemplo da crise no setor hoteleiro. Ademais, tem-se como resultado as principais reações dos empreendedores frente às catástrofes. PALAVRAS-CHAVE Turismo; Empreendedorismo internacional; Catástrofe; Desastre; Covid-19. title: The Great Gatsby: A Graphic Novel AdaptationNick: A NovelEl gran GatsbyStepping Out with Scott and Zelda: Touring the Fitzgeralds’ Montgomery
abstract: As the clock approached midnight on 31 December 2020, commentators fretted endlessly over whether the entry of The Great Gatsby into the public domain would diminish its cultural standing. Already a slew of fresh adaptations—not to be confused with the new editions that James L. W. West III discusses in the preceding review-essay—were competing for media attention. Ready for purchase on New Year’s Day would be illustrated versions, modernized versions, even “mash-up” versions in which the familiar storyline was transposed into another genre, such as Kristen Briggs’s The Great Gatsby Undead, a self-published vampire take on the classic (or “revamped” as the back cover declares). As Annabel Gutterman wrote in Time that Christmas Eve, “When the copyright for Fitzgerald’s classic novel of greed, desire and betrayal expires, anyone will be able to publish the book and adapt it without permission from his literary estate, which has controlled the text for the 80 years since his death. That freedom could yield works that add to Gatsby’s legacy . . . or it could open the door to editions that change the text for the worse.”A year later, it now seems that latter worry was unfounded. Although new retellings are still routinely announced, most of the press surrounding this initial wave of adaptations fizzled out within weeks as literary attention turned elsewhere. In the end, only two twists on the almost ninety-six-year-old tale seem to have had any staying power, perhaps because they dramatize two extremes of adaptation. K. Woodman-Maynard’s The Great Gatsby: A Graphic Novel Adaptation (the K. stands for Katharine) reveals both the challenges and triumphs of translating a verbal text into images. Meanwhile, Michael Farris Smith’s more controversial Nick illustrates the limits of mining the cultural capital of a famous work by inventing an origin story for a main character. The attention accorded these two works has overshadowed a third type of adaptation, translation, which in 2021 did a steady business, including a new Spanish version of Gatsby in the respected Letras Universales series from the Madrid-based publisher Ediciones Cátedra.Woodman-Maynard’s graphic novel could have come and gone without a ripple considering that a mere six months before its publication the Fitzgerald Estate commissioned its own official adaptation featuring art work by Aya Morton and text adapted by Fred Fordham. As Kirk Curnutt wrote in last year’s Review, “Morton brings more than enough invention to the job to make the adaptation enjoyable,” particularly in her creative visualization of key moments. Her most striking image remains “George Wilson’s stalking of Gatsby,” which “is powerfully dramatic: a wordless frame in which Wilson . . . pulls his pistol while an oblivious Gatsby floats in his pool [that] better represents both men’s pain than any extant film version” (Curnutt 262; see also Fitzgerald, Gatsby Graphic Novel 185). Woodman-Maynard accomplishes the near impossible by first and foremost revealing how differently one can picture both the characters’ physical features and the color scheme and texture of her images. She also captures the Romantic dreaminess of Fitzgerald’s language, with the dramatis personae appearing to float through scenes rather than be tied down by the realism of the rendered settings. (This is especially evocative when Nick first visits his cousin’s house and discovers Daisy Buchanan and Jordan Baker literally floating above a couch [10–11; GGVar 10]). Her Gatsby is a wholly unique contribution to illustrated versions of the novel, every bit as successful as Morton’s.The most obvious difference between the two is the medium. Morton rendered her images in acrylic, while Woodman-Maynard’s are in watercolor. Her lines are also looser, done more in sketch style than her predecessor’s, which are finer and more exact. Perhaps her most striking innovation is to saturate distinct scenes with different tints to color the mood. Thus, Nick Carraway’s chapter 2 trip with Tom Buchanan into New York City to attend a tacky party with his mistress Myrtle Wilson is dominated by pinks (36–37; GGVar 27–46), while Gatsby’s reunion with Daisy Buchanan in his ornate mansion in chapter 5 is drenched in purples (93–107; GGVar 98–116). The aftermath of Myrtle’s death at the hands of Gatsby’s car (driven by Daisy, of course) in chapter 7 is cast into a light gray shade that conveys the sudden loss of frivolity and gaiety while intensifying the suspense that will culminate in Gatsby’s own murder (172–80; GGVar 163–75), while Nick’s final visit to Gatsby’s abandoned house and his rhapsodic rumination on the naïveté of his friend’s belief in “the green light, the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us” (GGVar 218), is steeped in a somber slate blue.Although there is no shortage in Gatsby criticism analyzing color symbolism, these are not necessarily the hues one expects to be emphasized in an adaptation. As A. E. Elmore wrote more than a half-century ago, Fitzgerald’s Romantic instinct is to emphasize gold, yellow, and other glittering, iridescent shades: “White, even after one excludes near-synonyms such as silver, makes more appearances in the novel than any other single color, and something like three of every four are applied to East Egg or characters from East Egg, especially to Daisy” (428). Several “drab” and “pale” pigments do appear in the prose, usually characterizing the no-man’s-land between East and West Egg and Manhattan. As Elmore writes, “An overwhelming number of the references in the novel to gray, to other dark colors, and to darkness and dimness themselves are applied to the valley of ashes and its inhabitants” (433). While Woodman-Maynard remains true to certain details—one cannot exactly garb Gatsby in anything other than his trademark “pink suit” (GGVar 146), nor picture him driving a car that is black or brown instead of yellow—her emphasis on lavenders, powder blues, and occasional tangerines adds a unique glow to a familiar palette. As one final sign of her inventiveness, we should note that for a novel that asks whether we should believe in the “green light” (GGVar 218), her Gatsby is almost entirely bereft of viridescent tinctures.Woodman-Maynard also manages to establish her own take on the physiognomy of the characters. Her Jay Gatsby sports a cleft chin that amplifies his charisma, while Nick is thin-lipped in a way that whenever he smiles or frowns seems to make half his mouth disappear. As Curnutt wrote of Morton’s depiction of Daisy, “despite the celluloid examples of Lois Wilson and Betty Field, illustrators for the past several decades have been thoroughly baptized in Mia Farrow’s peroxide” (260), so it is no surprise that the Louisville belle is blonde here as well, albeit more flaxen than aureate.1 Woodman-Maynard envisions Daisy’s nose as much sharper than Morton does, almost like a backwards checkmark, a subtle detail that nicely encapsulates her “cheerful snobbery” without sacrificing the sympathy she deserves as a young woman who, raised without agency, wants “her life shaped now, immediately” by “some force” of “love, of money, of unquestionable practicality” (GGVar 181).If one character seems doomed to typecasting, it is Tom Buchanan. Not that he deserves much pity, but Fitzgerald’s reference to the villain as a “hulking physical specimen” with a “body capable of enormous leverage—a cruel body” (GGVar 15, 8)—almost obliges illustrators to picture him with Brobdingnagian heft. Accordingly, Woodman-Maynard’s philandering husband towers over other characters, his brows often furrowed in vexed confusion and his mouth wrenched open with ire. Each time his presence in these types of adaptations is rendered as domineering, his posture veers toward lumbering, almost as if he were the gorilla-like Moose Malloy in Raymond Chandler’s Farewell, My Lovely (1940). One gains more respect for Bruce Dern’s weaselly performance in Clayton’s 1974 film version of the novel. Dern managed to tap into Tom’s underlying insecurities instead of his entitlement, highlighting less his bullying physique than the “hot whips of panic” that flare up when a simple mind like his is confused (GGVar 149).As Curnutt also noted in his review of Morton’s graphic novel, the greatest challenge any Gatsby illustrator faces is addressing what might politely be called the “Wolfshiem Conundrum.” How, in other words, can a contemporary artist sensitive to the accusations of anti-Semitism surrounding the novel’s shadowy gangster figure depict him without perpetuating bigoted stereotypes, especially those surrounding his “flat-nose” and the “two growths of hair” curling from “either nostril,” as well as Yiddish dialect such as “gonnection”? (GGVar 83, 85). Curnutt suggested Morton may have erred too far from the source material by depicting the coconspirator of the assassinated Rosy Rosenthal and the fixer of the 1918 World Series with an “ash-blond complexion” (Curnutt 261; GGVar 84, 88). This surprising revisualization makes the mobster resemble her depictions of both Gatsby and Tom: “Morton’s strategy of rendering Wolfshiem Anglo is subtler if less globally intriguing” than Baz Luhrmann’s approach to the problem in his 2013 film, which was to cast Indian actor Amitabh Bachchan in the role, “but it also adds its own confusion to the text. If Tom looks like Gatsby’s big brother, then Wolfshiem looks like Tom and Gatsby’s suave-but-shady uncle. The only trait we have to triangulate him between the West Egg/East Egg opposites are the wide splashes of gray at his temples” (Curnutt 261). Woodman-Maynard’s approach to the issue is not to change Wolfshiem’s ethnicity but to allow the broader, looser lines of her sketch style to soften Fitzgerald’s racial tropes into shady indeterminacy. Her gangster is bald and bearded and looks vaguely Eastern European rather than overtly Jewish (74–77). He is also cloaked in shades of heavy blue that keep his features as murky as his criminal enterprises. The approach is effective and successful; it reminds us that organized crime in 1920s New York was run by different ethnic factions, whether Jews, Sicilians, or Irish, and that, even as we recognize the need to be sensitive to treatments of racial difference, not every criminal need comes straight from central casting.Woodman-Maynard also finds her own eye-catching ways of integrating text into her image panels, perhaps one of the biggest issues surrounding the design of graphic novels. We refer here not to characters’ speech bubbles, which convey their dialogue, but to exposition and descriptive passages, two forms of narration that are essential to Fitzgerald’s prose. Although recognizable lines from the novel often appear imposed on scenes, usually tucked in corners or unfurling along panel borders, Woodman-Maynard fits others into objects within her tableaux. When Nick first visits the Buchanans’ impeccable estate, Tom’s imposing stance seems to drip with braggadocious condescension: “‘Now, don’t think my opinion on these matters is final,’ he seemed to say, ‘just because I’m stronger and more of a man than you are’” (GGVar 9). Woodman-Maynard places these words in the thick shadow Tom’s legs cast on his veranda as he and Nick survey the property’s lush lawn (2).In one of the graphic novel’s most remarkable moments, she places the revelation of Gatsby’s origins at the beginning of chapter 6 (“His parents were shiftless and unsuccessful farm people” [GGVar 118]) into the rippling rain puddles that Nick must sidestep as he quietly leaves Gatsby and Daisy to consummate their reunion at the end of chapter 5 (109; GGVar 116). And in another example, at the end of chapter 7, Nick spies Tom and Daisy talking over chicken and ale in their kitchen after Myrtle’s death. Into the fabric of the couple’s flapping curtains (a motif in the novel, of course [GGVar 9–10]), Woodman-Maynard stitches Nick’s famous assessment of their marriage (181), which will now be bound more firmly by secrets than it ever was by love: “They weren’t happy, and neither of them had touched the chicken or the ale—and yet they weren’t unhappy either. There was an unmistakable air of natural intimacy about the picture and anybody would have said that they were conspiring together” (GGVar 175). title: Launching the new Reviews section of Journal of Refugee Studies
abstract: From 2021, Journal of Refugee Studies has replaced the Book Reviews section of the journal with a more inclusive Reviews section. We encourage submissions of materials and sources including written texts and academic manuscripts, but wish to expand significantly beyond these formats, and intend to be less prescriptive in terms of how authors wish to review these. Here, the section takes inspiration from a number of other journals, not least the American Historical Review (American Historical Review 2021: emphasis added) which is clear that ‘reviewing books and other historical material of professional interest… is a primary responsibility’ of the journal. The AHR has long welcomed reviews of ‘films, public history sites and museums, collections of documents, websites, podcasts, and many genres of popular culture relevant to historians’, such as video games, graphic histories, television programmes, and textbooks (American Historical Review 2021). Expanding the reviews section of the Journal of Refugee Studies is therefore intended to give due recognition to oral, visual, and landscape-based records of forced migration, all of which can provide insights into experiences of displacement—and resources for teaching and learning—that complement the written word. As academic research outputs also diversify, such as through the ‘Refugees: Forced to Flee’ exhibition of Research Council funded projects at London’s Imperial War Museum in 2020/1, pioneering scholarship and research must also be sought outside of books, particularly recently published, English-language scholarly texts. Scholars studying the history and role of book reviewing have indeed cautioned that in response to a ‘tiredness of the customary forms and formulas of book reviews’, we must ‘approach reviews more creatively and in keeping with our discipline’s approaches to research’ (Sturm 2020: 3). As work on refugee and forced migration studies rightfully integrates more varied approaches to theorizing and producing knowledge, it has raised important questions about how representative or ethical it is to focus so singularly on academics’ outputs and particularly those that are primarily, if not exclusively, textual. Alongside reviewing a wider selection of contemporary records, exhibitions, and materials, we also encourage submissions on pieces that reviewers consider to have been historically overlooked within refugee and forced migration studies, particularly due to the overwhelming dominance of English-language texts and the entrenchment of Euro-American hierarchies of knowledge production, intellectual value and what comprises ‘forced migration’. David Ngendo Tshimba’s review of Samwiri Lwanga-Lunyiigo’s work on Uganda’s history of refugee hosting during and since the country’s colonization shows the importance of doing so, as he uses this rich historical work to reflect on both the dynamics of refuge before the 1951 Convention and more contemporary debates on self-reliance (forthcoming). Widening the scope of this section to include these historically undervalued manuscripts is thus a way to better examine their contributions and impact to our field of study, including through engaging with, and often celebrating, what they offer to teaching, learning, and research on displacement issues. As exemplified in Mezna Qato’s forthcoming review of Samira Azzam’s short stories on life in Palestinian refugee camps, many of which were written in Arabic, the journal also welcomes reviews of books and records that are published in any language. After briefly explaining the critical role that reviews can and should play in defining a field of research and practice that is inclusive, diverse, and decolonized, this brief editorial will return to further explaining the format and aims of the new Reviews section. In the context of a perceived decline in their significance and value, it seems important to briefly touch on what role book reviews play in any intellectual project and field. Leo (2009: 168) does not pull his punches when he states that ‘scholarly reviewing has become a genre marked by increasing degrees of politeness and summation—that is to say, its critical edge has dulled.’ Trends like homophily reinforce this. In the social sciences and humanities, for example, Larrègue et al (2019) note the increasing tendency of the reviewers and authors of reviewed books to originate from the same country, thus reifying existing geographical silos within academia and contributing to an overwhelming focus on books by European and North American academics. Too often, this also contributes to ‘The Matthew Effect’ in book reviewing, whereby the books that benefit from the exposure of being reviewed are by those authors who are already well-established voices in the field (Sturm 2020). If the situation is not addressed, Leo (2009: 167) goes on to argue that ‘we will continue to see a downfall in the quality and quantity of a kind of writing that can, at its best, support the vitality of our intellectual exchanges’. Robust justifications nonetheless exist for strengthening and invigorating reviews sections of journals. From a practical perspective, though some national research councils do not count book reviews as research publications (Obeng-Odoom, 2014), thus limiting the contribution that writing them can make to the reviewer’s career advancement, reviews remain a critical source of professional validation for the book’s author. Books that are reviewed tend to get higher citation counts than books that are not, driving a positive feedback loop of more readers, more recommendations, and more coveted spots on reading lists (Gorraiz et al, 2014). A positive book review can also constitute a key resource in evidencing an academic’s impact in promotion and review boards. In the context then of there being a clear correlation between the exposure a book gains from being reviewed and its uptake as a key resource in teaching and research, there is a clear need to redress the historical omission of many manuscripts and forms of text from the reviews section of journals. In terms of their intellectual importance, Baker (1991; cited in Power 2018) may have overstated the point that it is book reviews and not books that constitute ‘the principal engines of change in the history of thought’, but they certainly have the potential to play a (more) significant role in academia. As Orteza y Miranda, (1996: 191) stated, they should never be merely ‘parasitic on the work being reviewed’. Instead, they should function as ‘a change agent, creating a critical climate of opinion…that encourage possibilities for a renewal of thought and a renewed sense of commitment to our tasks.’ Taking it further, she states that in the book review section of a journal: ‘one reads of old, though still dominant and dominating, views and presuppositions being shown to be inadequate to the intellectual and social demands of the times. In their places, one reads of emerging issues, of new and exciting paradigms being created to solve seemingly enduring problems, and of change, or even, perhaps, of transformation, in the direction of thinking about some intractable problems, raising new kinds of questions. It is, in other words, the knowledge creating/knowledge examining domain of the journal.’ (Orteza y Miranda, 1996: 197) Given their ability to draw attention to these new ‘directions of thinking’ and ‘kinds of questions’, book reviews are thus inextricably wound up with the political economy of knowledge production within academia. Decisions on what to include in book review sections are indeed also implicitly decisions about ‘what belongs (and, conversely, what does not belong) to the “geography” of their domain of research, on the metaphorical, disciplinary, and geographic levels’ (Larrègue et al. 2019: 98). They ‘serve to map what is of value in a scholarly field, namely, what work is valuable and what values are at work in it’ (Obeng-Odoom 2014 referenced in Sturm 2020: 2; Larrègue et al. 2019), which enables them to both reflect and advance a necessary shift in academia towards embracing marginalized forms and fora of knowledge. Here, we see the importance of contributions such as Anne Irfan’s review of Zora Neale Hurston’s Barracoon: The Story of the Last Slave which both contributes towards, and exemplifies, ongoing efforts to historicize and decolonize knowledge production on forced migration. The new reviews section of this journal thus aims to do both: to mirror the work being produced in refugee and forced migration studies while challenging academics to reflect back on new disciplinary priorities and perspectives. Only then may the reviews section ‘realize [its] potential as an interpretive and critical genre capable of participating more consciously in the interpretive practices that are at the heart of the discipline’ (Wiley 1993: 481). In this sense, a question posed by Toor (2012) in her piece ‘Why Bother Writing Book Reviews?’ seems to miss the point of this intellectual exercise. She asks ‘is the time spent reviewing other people’s books more important than writing your own stuff, making your own contributions?’ If we approach the reviews section as providing an opportunity for critical and creative interventions within academia, which push academic debates forward while promoting engagement with diverse sources and forms of knowledge production, then the answer to her question is not simply ‘yes’. Writing a review should in itself be valued as an important, original, and potentially transformative contribution to our field. As mentioned above, however, it is critical that what counts as ‘worthy’ of being reviewed is no longer so narrowly conceived. While this section will thus remain open to reviews of more traditional research outputs, in recognition of their ongoing and important contributions to this field of study, we also hope to encourage reviews of a range of other sources. Amongst these are of course works of fiction. Some of the most powerful stories of displacement, and most trenchant critiques of development and humanitarianism, lie precisely there: in stories. Academia has long struggled to adequately and accurately engage with the lived experiences of a diverse range of individuals, which has raised the need to access and promote different narratives (Doharty et al. 2020). Some of these can be found in work that captures experiential forms of knowledge, including accounts that are fully or semi-autobiographical, such as Dina Nayeri’s The Ungrateful Refugee (Lindley 2021), and in more creative mediums such as collections of poetry, novels, films, plays, art, etc. Literature, performance, and other forms of artistic expression are often lauded as mediums that enable the expression of ‘decolonial thinking rooted in alternative epistemologies besides western paradigms’ (Spiegel et al. 2017: 271), and thus form critical resources for informing and enriching our research and teaching on experiences of displacement and their afterlives. As also discussed above, we welcome reviews of books published at any point in history that reviewers consider to be critical and yet overlooked sources of knowledge, or that would yield fresh insights through being revisited. This has the advantage of supporting what Obeng-Odoom (2014) describes as the ‘deferred review’, whereby reviewing a seminal text decades after its initial publication enables an author to evaluate what impact it had on scholarship, policies, and societal practices both at the point of its release and over the ensuing decades. Offering this approach to reviewing is also intended at least in part to answer Stein’s (2016: 13) question as to ‘What precautions are necessary so that the incorporation of more non-Western knowledges into Western universities does not result in their tokenism, decontextualization, or exploitation?’ While adequate contextualization is of course central to this, as Mezna Qato does so expertly in her review of Samira Azzam’s short stories (forthcoming), so too is revisiting historical texts and applying to them the same standards and processes of review that have historically been reserved for only more ‘traditional’ texts. With reviewing comes recognition and respect for the contributions that these sources have made to our thinking, teaching, and advocacy. Reviewing them alongside contemporary manuscripts is then a further way to flatten out any implicit hierarchies about the relative importance or value of these different but at least equal contributions (Doharty et al. 2020). Part of expanding the types of materials that can be reviewed in JRS is thus about recognizing non-Western and non-academic sources of knowledge and styles of presentation as authoritative texts for the study of forced migration and as critical tools for teaching on it, as Lewis Turner does so instructively in his review of The Clothesline Swing by Danny Ramadan (2021). As Halpenny (1993: 223) states, ‘reviews secure entry for a book’s contribution into an academic teacher’s resource base; they bear information to help research in the present and future’. When done well, they can indeed form a critical part of the robust discussions that underpin academia, forming that ‘interconnected network of ideas yoking the concrete pedagogies we enact in our individual classrooms with the theoretical concerns that are the subjects of research and scholarship’ (Wiley 1993: 480). We therefore encourage contributors to this section to not only target researchers, as is standard convention for book reviews (Hartley 2006), but to reflect on how, when, and why their chosen texts might prove particularly useful resources for teaching too, as Beatrix Eugenia Sánchez’s does in her joint review of Exit West by Mohsin Hamid and World War Z by Max Brooks (forthcoming). Another area of slight departure is around the style and tone of writing, as we wish to support contributions that include more personal reflections on how reviewers’ own positionalities shape their relationships to the materials under review. Our subjectivities, intellectual histories, and own research undoubtedly shape how we approach any process of reviewing and thus this section is intended to provide opportunities, but not pressure, for people to draw that out more explicitly. Central to this is that we will work to solicit more autobiographical book reviews, whereby individuals with experiences of displacement review texts that intersect with their own histories and embodied knowledges (for an example of this in the medical field, see Rankin 2010). In general though, we welcome greater reflexivity on these points of intersection, as is exemplified in Katy Long’s thought-provoking and personal review of Valeria Luiselli’s Lost Children Archive and Tell Me How It Ends: An Essay in Forty Questions (2021). Through this piece, we also see the value of moving away from formats that contextualize books only relative to other literature in the field while remaining largely autonomous from the social and societal context in which they were first written and are now being reviewed. While for some reviews the literature-oriented approach may continue to make the most sense, for others—including the array of new sources we will now be reviewing in JRS—it may prove more appropriate and revealing to foreground this societal and political context. This shift in focus of the Reviews section is also intended to complement broader efforts to ensure that displaced people have greater representation, recognition, and voice within journals and academia more generally, particularly through acknowledging and celebrating their diverse and longstanding contributions to theorizing, researching, and teaching. It is nonetheless clear from the first few submissions in this new format—which are referenced throughout this piece—that the majority of reviews have been written by scholars based in institutions in the wealthy states to which refugees are resettled. While a central aspiration of this section is certainly to facilitate contributions from refugees in order to redress the historical under-representation of their expertise and knowledge, this is not the only answer to the question of who should do the sort of reparative work that we are hoping to promote here. It indeed seems critically important that established academics play a significant role. In an academic world in which there is currently no remuneration for publishing book reviews, and only limited prestige attached to the work of reviewing, the responsibility cannot—and perhaps should not—be placed on displaced populations to do this kind of labour for free or at the expense of working on projects or outputs that carry greater weight for their personal and professional development. Finally then, as Sturm states with reference to Chinnery’s (2010) reflections on the act of book reviewing, book reviews are ‘a critical gift, an act of scholarly generosity not only to readers but also to reviewers’ that ‘serve not the market economy of the neoliberal economy (or, at least, not well), but the still vital gift ecology of the scholarly community’ (2010: 1). To all those who have submitted and will submit to the Reviews section of JRS, thank you for contributing to the huge amount of work that is needed to decolonize and diversify reading lists, theories, and research. In this particular forum, this will continue through documenting the rich variety of sources of knowledge on forced migration that require greater scholarly engagement, recognition, and often respect.

title: Are UN Innovation Labs effective innovation models to meet the needs of communities in the humanitarian sector - Case Study Kosovo
abstract: Humanitarian action involves the provision of goods and services such as food, water, sanitation, disasters medical care, shelter and protection, during and soon after natural and human-made disasters (Sphere, 2004, p. 6). Diverse and often complex causes create situations that make the inhabiting of affected locations challenging. In a 2019 UNHCR report, global forced displacement increased again in 2018 to ca. 70.8 million individuals forcibly displaced worldwide, as a result of persecution, conflict, generalized violence, or human rights violations. In addition to providing humanitarian assistance to such populations in crisis, humanitarianism also deals with partnering with other stakeholders, interconnected entities - a "humanitarian system". Whilst lead responsibility in humanitarian responses lie with the affected State, international UN aid agencies assist by rallying the collective support of States to address the needs of affected communities. However, researchers have found that responses can be inefficient, can sometimes lead to dependency and are often unsustainable. With increasing numbers of displaced persons and related challenges facing aid organisations, researchers have argued that Innovation is now imperative in the humanitarian space. Humanitarian innovation is a means of invention, adaptation and improvement through finding and scaling solutions to problems, in the form of products, processes or service models, facing effective humanitarian assistance. Consequently, UN agencies are introducing mechanisms that seek to address needs through new practices. A preferred mechanism is a Lab model (Bloom and Faulkner, 2015). They have however queried the general understanding of innovation and what Lab mechanisms are truly achieving. Obrecht and Wagner (2016) also suggest that progress of measuring impact, as well as factors that contribute to successful innovations are unclear. Ramalingam, Rush et al. (2015) also note problems associated with fragmentation, coordination of innovation, actor and roles and the need to strengthen skills capacities and enablers of innovation etc. Thus, this research sought to establish whether UN Innovation Labs are effective innovation models to meet the needs of communities in the humanitarian sector? Following on from a preliminary key informant phase, the main data collection comprised 65 semi-structured interviews, 50 surveys and 2 focus group discussions. This study investigated Kosovo's UNICEF Innovations Lab, through a case study methodology, underpinned by constructivist principles, to elucidate what innovation outcomes are achieved through Lab mechanisms. It sought to identify how innovation is achieved by outlining project level features of Lab processes. It interrogated the model employed in light of the Living Lab model of open innovation and innovation ecosystems, identifying thereby key actors and their roles. To answer the main research question, it relied on contingency theory to identify dimensions of effectiveness. It then transposed its findings into contingency factors for effective Lab mechanisms within the context. The study revealed that an inclusive Living Lab model operating a multi - method approach, in a real life environment, with multi stakeholder participation, openness and active user involvement, a congruence of structure and context variables, leadership with distinctive attributes, made the examined open innovation model effective in achieving its goals and objective in the form of programme, product, service and process innovations within the context. The results of this study may be applied as guidelines for similar initiatives in humanitarian settings. However, there is need for further study to be conducted and recommends a multi case study approach to determine whether the model is the effective UN Innovations model to allow innovation to occur and to meet the needs of demographics in entirely humanitarian settings.

title: John O’Brien (1945–2020): A Most Subversive Man
venue: American book review/The American book review
abstract: John O’Brien (1945–2020): A Most Subversive Man Warren Motte (bio) Yesterday evening, I attended a memorial service for my friend John O’Brien. It was both moving and bracing to hear so many people speak about him with such deep affection. Like every other event that we “attend” these days, in this crushingly lousy, godforsaken year of 2020, it was held on Zoom. That medium, as useful as it may have proved in last few months, is not one where I feel immediately comfortable, and yet last night I felt even more dislocated than usual. I finally realized that this time it was not Zoom’s fault; instead, it was occasioned by the fact that I am still shocked by John’s death. For in some sense I had never considered him as a mere mortal, had never consciously imagined the prospect of his death. Click for larger view View full resolution John was a man of many parts. First and foremost, he was a committed, intrepid reader. Though by his own account, he came to reading fairly late, as a freshman in high school. There, a teacher introduced him to William Faulkner, Ernest Hemingway, James Joyce, and T. S. Eliot. At the end of the school year, he gave John a reading list of a hundred titles, and John spent the next few years working through it (beginning with Fyodor Dostoevsky’s The Idiot), with such singlemindedness that he largely neglected his social life. “I was searching for something, and I thought that literature was where I was going to find it,” he remarked recently. He would go on to teach literature at Illinois Benedictine College and Illinois State University. John was an early champion of African-American writers. His book Interviews with Black Writers, published in 1973 and still in print, includes conversations with seventeen authors, from Richard Wright and Ralph Ellison to John Wideman and Alice Walker. And he was also a novelist, though his manuscript, entitled The Man Who Arrived Home after a Trip to London and Was Greeted by His Wife (or Lover) at O’Hare, remains unpublished. I knew John as a smart, curious, warm, engaging man. His kindness toward me was exceptional and unflagging. I was first in contact with him in the early 1980s, when we spoke about projects for The Review of Contemporary Fiction involving Italo Calvino, and then, a bit later, about Harry Mathews. He would subsequently invite me to contribute to the RCF, and to Context, and to play a role in the Dalkey Archive Press, advising him on French literature. He published many of my articles and book reviews, and several of my books. Equally important to me, he persuaded me that I had a home at Dalkey, and a significant role to play there, a precious thought for any academic. And I was not the only one in my family to feel that way: for several years my son Nicholas, a graphic designer, contributed cover art for Dalkey volumes, at John’s kind invitation. John’s sense of hospitality was boundless. And it was a joy to be around him, to chat with him, to argue with him. I remember our cheerful, running disputes about who was (at the time, of course) the most distinguished living writer of English, me arguing sometimes for William Burroughs, sometimes for John Barth, John, always and steadfastly, for Gilbert Sorrentino. John founded The Review of Contemporary Fiction in 1980, “out of a sense of isolation, as well as a kind of outrage at the fact that books and authors were reduced only to marketplace value.” He would later launch another publication, Context, a review intended for free distribution at bookstores and on college campuses. His intent in doing so was “to reach as many people as possible, especially college-age students and younger staff at bookstores, in other words people who are more or less just beginning their serious reading.” It was in 1984 that he founded the Dalkey Archive Press, with the idea of bringing important books back into print, and keeping them there.
